title: Jensen’s Judgment: Broncos Have a Bo Nix Problem They Must Fix Fast
full_text:
I hate to say it, but the Denver Broncos have a quarterback problem.
Before anyone knee-jerk reacts and loses their teeth, understand that I'm actually a firm believer in Bo Nix. I see him as the very franchise quarterback the Broncos desperately searched for for nearly a decade after Peyton Manning retired. The Broncos finally found their guy in Nix, but a few games into his third year, there's no denying that he's in a slump.
In the Broncos' 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers , Nix went 25-of-42 for 214 yards and a touchdown. In a vacuum, those aren't terrible numbers — but digging a little deeper, 14 of those completions were to running backs, and only two of his passes traveled farther than 10 yards.
It's hard to win in the NFL that way, and against the best of the best? Forget it.
The Broncos have managed to start the season 2-2, despite facing arguably the four best teams in the league, but if the coaches can't snap Nix out of his funk, things could quickly spin out of control.
One of the hallmarks of Nix's first two NFL seasons was his poise. Not just pocket poise, but his overall confidence and cool, calm demeanor. No situation or opponent was too big for him, and the Broncos won a lot of games because of him.
That poise allowed Nix to pass for north of 7,500 yards and 50 touchdowns, and helped lead the Broncos to 24 regular-season wins. Now, that's not to say that Nix never showed the foibles of a young quarterback, because of course he did, but his poise in the pocket and under pressure helped lead this team out of the AFC West doldrums.
We're not seeing that poise of late, though. Nix looks spooked out there; he bails clean pockets, looks to escape way too early, and seems just on the edge of panic for 85% of his snaps. A panicked person isn't a poised person or a good decision-maker, and it takes a poised player to lead a team as its quarterback.
So, why does Nix suddenly look so uncomfortable out there? I can't say for sure, but it's likely a combination of his return from two ankle surgeries this past offseason, the vagaries of playing for a new play-caller, and the tier-one level of competition the Broncos have faced thus far.
We could break it down further and point to the Broncos' lack of a run game and the fact that this offensive line is allowing more pressure on Nix than at any point in his young career. We could even throw in the moving pieces of working in a new wideout — Jaylen Waddle — as another potential factor affecting Nix's presence of mind.
The bottom line, though, is that Nix seems reluctant to push the ball down the field. After all, he leads the NFL in passes behind the line of scrimmage, per Next Gen Stats .
Bo Nix attempts through 4 weeks, per @SumerSports : 37 — Behind line of scrimmage 46 — 0-5 yards 23 — 6-10 yards 29 — 11+ yards Leads league in passes behind line of scrimmage so far this season. pic.twitter.com/YaqqjhSsVd
On top of that, Nix is obviously hesitant to use his legs beyond the scope of buying time, too, which is understandable, given how he injured his ankle last January, but eminently unhelpful in digging out of this slump.
The kid is juggling a lot, and I don't know if Nix's season-opening performance against the Kansas City Chiefs — in which he threw an interception on his first pass of the season and fumbled three times (losing one) — has something to do with it, but he seems far more focused on not turning the ball over than he is on trying to make a play.
That might sound too reductive, but we already know that ball security and avoiding the negative play are two of Nix's superpowers. They were a big part of what attracted Sean Payton and the Broncos to Nix as a draft prospect in 2024.
Any coach can appreciate the care and concern with which Nix protects the football and generally avoids negative plays, like sacks. But any coach should also be able to see that, like all good things, it can be taken too far and become a bad thing. It genuinely seems to be inhibiting his ability to push the ball downfield and put up points.
Again, I'll point to the insane level of competition the Broncos have faced so far as an explanation, in part, but this offense ranks 27th in yards per game, 24th in yards per play, and 27th in points per game — all bottom-10 stats — for a reason. It doesn't help that Denver is also fielding the 29th-ranked rushing attack, but as Payton himself said at the podium following Sunday's loss to the 49ers, things " aren't clicking " offensively.
Payton, offensive coordinator Davis Webb, and quarterbacks coach Logan Kilgore need to figure out what Nix is seeing out there and get to the bottom of why he's been so conservative with the ball, outside of a handful of plays here and there, mostly against Jacksonville in Week 2.
The film from Week 4 illustrates in living color how hesitant Nix was to throw the ball beyond five yards. It was one checkdown to a running back after another, and it's not just because the 49ers ran a two-high shell so much, as Payton would have you believe.
Nix left a lot of money on the table, so to speak. Our Lance Sanderson broke it down in this week's Film Room article : Nix passed up some big plays to take the safe checkdown. That's like stepping over a dollar to pick up a dime.
Coaches and quarterbacks often say, "You can't go broke taking a profit." And there's truth to it when it comes to the craft of quarterbacking, but horizontal checkdowns do not an offense make.
56% of Nix's completions last week were of the horizontal variety, and that's not counting screens to wideouts. Meanwhile, the talent of a Pro Bowl receiver coming off back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons — Courtland Sutton — is being squandered, as is Waddle's explosive downfield ability, which the Broncos paid dearly to acquire. Not to mention tight end Evan Engram, whose snap share has increased dramatically while his touches have declined in equal measure.
I get it; quarterbacks have to walk the razor's edge of protecting the ball while also capitalizing on opportunities to push it downfield, even if it puts it in harm's way. It's a pickle, but that's what Nix signed up for as an NFL quarterback. The best passers are able to walk that narrow line and thrive, and we've seen him do it countless times.
We know Nix can do it, but it's not happening consistently in Year 3, and that's alarming. Nobody wants to see him regress, but the red flags are there.
Again, though, with the strength of this early-season schedule, it's hard to know exactly how much to attribute to the level of competition the Broncos have faced, how much falls on Nix's shoulders, and how much blame falls on Payton and Webb.
That's why Payton and his coaches make the big bucks; it's their job to figure out what's holding Nix back and get him on track. We can continue to lament the Broncos' slow offensive starts each game, but until the coaches get to the bottom of why Nix seems so flustered and hesitant, they'll keep sputtering out of the gate.
If the Broncos' coaching brain trust can understand what Nix is seeing and help him snap out of it, everything else will fall into place offensively. The Broncos will only go as far as their quarterback can take them, and if Payton and company don't help conjure a Nix epiphany soon, this team might not survive long enough to weather the first eight-week storm and benefit from the significantly easier schedule it has from Week 9 on.
It hasn't been all bad from Bo. His second-half performances against the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams were special, and the one touchdown drive he put together in each game against the Chiefs and 49ers hints that the quarterback we all know still lurks inside him.
It's on Payton and the coaches to draw out the quarterback we know Nix can be and translate it to the field for 60 minutes each game. Whether it's points of coaching emphasis or Xs and Os, Payton and Webb are running out of time to fix this before half the season is suddenly in the…

title: Broncos Bring Back WR After Injury to Pat Bryant
full_text:
With Pat Bryant expected to miss time , the Denver Broncos on Tuesday bought themselves some insurance at wide receiver, bringing back Cameron Ross to its practice squad.
The signing was confirmed by The Denver Gazette's Chris Tomasson, who spoke with Ross' agent.
“He’s incredibly excited for the opportunity to be part of the Denver Broncos organization and excited that they’re bringing him back," rep Seth Katz told Tomasson.
An undrafted rookie out of Virginia, Ross signed with Denver following the 2026 NFL Draft and appeared in all three preseason games , logging five receptions for 29 yards. He also technically led the club in rushing during its victory over Atlanta, while contributing seven returns for 64 yards across exhibition play.
The 5-foot-10, 186-pound wideout was among several pass-catchers who competed for — but were ultimately waived from — the Broncos' roster at final cuts, along with WRs Kolbe Katsis, Dane Key, and Joseph Manjack. Katsis and Key were re-signed to the practice squad.
Prior to reuniting with Ross, the Broncos worked out free-agent WR Jamari Thrash, who evidently lost the audition.
The Broncos are reeling a bit from the anticipated absence of borderline WR2 Pat Bryant, who was carted off the field amid Sunday's loss to the 49ers with an ankle injury. It's not a season-ending issue, but Bryant is a candidate for short-term injured reserve, which would cost him at least four games.
Barring a surprise, Ross probably won't get promoted to the active roster for Denver's Week 5 road contest against the Los Angeles Chargers, as they may simply lean more heavily on Courtland Sutton, Marvin Mims, and Troy Franklin behind WR Jaylen Waddle and leading receiver, RB RJ Harvey.
"We have to look at, if he's not playing outside and [WR Jaylen] Waddle is, then how do we get him away from the rotation? We've had some opportunities, but there are a handful of things that aren't clicking," head coach Sean Payton said Sunday of Sutton's involvement. "We've got to figure it out fast because we're going into week five. I think you guys have all made some good observations. I thought [RB] RJ [Harvey] did really well. The thing I felt coming away from the game was that our guys left it out there in the heat and everything, and yet, we have to look closely at the things that we can do as teachers to help them.”

title: Broncos Work Out Multiple Wide Receivers and Cornerbacks
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are dealing with a new problem at wide receiver.
Pat Bryant suffered an ankle sprain in the Broncos' 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, and while the second-year wideout avoided major injury, he's expected to miss a few weeks .
The Broncos just got Marvin Mims Jr. back from injury , which is helpful in this situation, but the team is also keeping an eye on outside options.
Enter Jamari Thrash, whom the Broncos worked out on Tuesday, first reported by Mike Garafolo .
Thrash is in his third NFL season. A 2024 fifth-round pick of the Cleveland Browns, he has appeared in  18 games with one career start, totaling 13 receptions for 129 yards.
At the 2024 NFL Combine, the just shy of 6-foot, 188-pound Thrash ran a 4.46-second 40-yard dash. At Louisville, he could take the top off a defense, but there's a reason he slipped to the fifth round.
Among other things, scouts believed Thrash didn't handle physicality well, whether that was getting off the line of scrimmage in press or at the top of the route with the ball in the air. If he could get by a guy, though, his footwork and speed could help him separate.
Time will tell whether the Broncos ultimately choose to sign Thrash.
The Broncos also worked out cornerbacks Paul Manning and Ayo Oyelola, and three other receivers: Cameron Ross, Brenden Rice, and Nick Nash. Manning had a cup of coffee in Denver in the offseason, while Ross was signed by the Broncos as a college free agent.
The #Broncos worked out six players today, four of whom are wideouts, including Brenden Rice, son of Hall-of-Famer Jerry Rice. Cameron Ross was signed the practice squad, though. pic.twitter.com/7kYEEnffk2
All cornerbacks and wideouts. That, unfortunately, lines up with the injuries to Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss, and the aforementioned Bryant.
Rice is the son of Hall-of-Famer Jerry Rice. True Broncos fans will remember that Rice actually spent a summer in Denver training camp in 2005 before officially hanging up his cleats.
The Broncos signed a receiver they worked out on Tuesday, but it wasn't Rice or Thrash. The Broncos reunited with Ross — an undrafted rookie who spent the offseason, camp, and the preseason in Denver.
Ross looked good this past summer and came very close to making the roster. It'll be interesting to see what Denver has in mind for him.
While Bryant is on the mend, the Broncos' receiver depth chart has been reshaped slightly. Keep in mind that Lil'Jordan Humphrey was just placed back on the practice squad , but if the Broncos believe Bryant will need at least four games to get healthy, he could end up on short-term injured reserve, which would open up his roster spot.
Meanwhile, here's a look at the new depth chart:
As you can see, the Broncos are still in good shape at wide receiver, despite the injury. Franklin was the team's No. 2 receiver last year, and he's been playing as the No. 4 this year. He's now vaulted to No. 3.
Once Mims gets his playing legs back under him, he could leapfrog Franklin, but that's not what happened in Week 4. Franklin outearned Mims with a 32-to-18 snap-count difference .
Sutton and Waddle remain at the top of the depth chart, obviously, while Humphrey headlines a four-receiver group on the practice squad.
The Broncos have utilized Bandy before and he's made a modest impact when called upon. Katsis and Key are both rookies, so don't expect to see either of them called up, unless it's the former to handle returner duties as he did in Week 3.
The Broncos still have an excellent receiver depth chart that is four-deep on the active roster. Humphrey and Bandy are both trusted veterans that Denver will have no problem turning to if needed.
Working out Thrash is interesting. It makes me wonder whether the Broncos maybe liked him in the 2024 draft, but the Browns took him off the board a bit earlier than Denver had him graded.
We'll see if he ends up getting signed. Right now, though, I'd guess that Tuesday's workout of Thrash was more of a preemptive look-see than a reflection of imminent action.

title: Sean Payton’s Latest Davis Webb Comments Hint at Broncos’ Play-Calling Outlook
full_text:
Given the difficulty of the Denver Broncos' opening schedule, starting 2-2 isn't the end of the world.
On the other hand, brushing the offense's worrisome struggles under the carpet won't fix anything. In the wake of the Broncos' 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers , new offensive coordinator and play-caller Davis Webb continues to be highly scrutinized.
If Webb is to ultimately succeed, head coach Sean Payton will have to hold the line and withstand the calls to take back the Broncos' primary play-calling duties. To that end, Payton had no interest in discussing the play-calling matter following Sunday's loss.
“Yeah, like I said, it’s too early," Payton said. "It's a fair question; I appreciate it. It's tough to discuss any of that right now. But I told those guys, ‘Hey, we’ve played some tough teams, and this is another good football team.’”
Giving Webb more time to work things out is admirable, but the Broncos' inability to run the ball effectively and score points in the first half has alarmed the fan base and media. Payton hasn't fed into the panic, but the sense of urgency to find answers may have increased coming out of Levi's Stadium.
"We've had some opportunities, but there are a handful of things that aren't clicking," Payton said. "And we gotta figure it out fast, because we're going into Week 5."
Relinquishing the play-calling duties to Webb always carried inherent risk, given Payton's long-standing success in that role dating back two-plus decades. One of those risks was the possibility that it could inhibit Bo Nix's development entering Year 3. Alas, the play-calling changes seem to have affected the suddenly far less decisive quarterback .
Teams have played Nix with a two-deep shell, determined to take away the Broncos' deep passing game, which has led to a proliferation of checkdown passes to running backs that opponents see coming from a mile away. Unfortunately, getting the ground game rolling is the best way to force opponents to play their safeties closer to the line of scrimmage.
Until that happens, though, the Broncos are stuck in a catch-22. They're doomed unless they can either get the run game clicking or Nix can start working the middle of the field to draw the opposing safeties down.
“I think, to your first point, and we had seen this on tape, they did a pretty good job of staying on top of some of the deeper throws and [that is] part of what they’re trying to do defensively," Payton said of the 49ers' defensive approach.
After struggling against the 49ers , Nix seems to be suffering through what the Broncos can only hope is a speed bump rather than a regression in his overall development. Like his head coach, Nix continues to back Webb, and he couldn't help but point out that the Broncos' first four opponents this season happen to be the NFL's four best teams.
I'm not just saying that, either. The Broncos' first four opponents, entering Week 5, are the four top-ranked teams in ESPN 's Football Power Index . That's a tough row to hoe for any play-caller, let alone a first-timer, and it also casts Nix's struggles in a more forgiving light.
“Yeah, I'm real confident in him," Nix said of Webb post-game. "I think when you look at the overall landscape, we've played four of the top teams in the league, and [it's] not easy for a first-time OC as young as he is to go against some of the, quite frankly, the best teams in the league."
Changing things up with Webb could open a can of worms. If the Broncos were to reinstall Payton as the primary play-caller, it would be seen as a demotion for Webb — Payton's young coaching protégé.
Payton and the Broncos would have some egg on their face. But much like a head coach must stay the course when going with a young, highly-drafted quarterback, once such a decision is made, the team has to ride it out, come hell or high water.
After all, Payton can't expect Webb to turn the ship around and thrive without his support, nor could he expect Nix to figure things out from the bench. They're all in the same boat, but so long as this offensive triumvirate keeps rowing in the same direction, the Broncos have the chance to work their way out of these choppy waters and into smoother seas.
Winning heals all wounds. With the 0-4 Los Angeles Chargers next up on the schedule, this Week 5 matchup has suddenly become crucial for Denver, especially with the reigning World Champion Seattle Seahawks following shortly afterward on a short week.
The Broncos can't afford to look past the Chargers and focus on the Seahawks on Thursday Night Football . Payton has never won at SoFi Stadium as Denver's head coach, so despite the Chargers' winless start, fans can only assume L.A. will get the Broncos' full attention and their very best shot.
Hopefully, Webb and Nix can take some big steps forward against the reeling but desperate Chargers.

title: What Broncos’ Snap Counts Revealed in Loss to 49ers
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are coming off an ugly loss to the San Francisco 49ers.
The Broncos looked flat offensively for most of the game, a common theme this season, while the defense hung tough until the very end, bending, bending, bending... and then finally breaking late in the fourth quarter. Denver fell 24-14.
This game was heavily influenced by a trio of injuries to key players: cornerbacks Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss, and wide receiver Pat Bryant . Unfortunately, the Broncos were unable to overcome that many crucial losses against one of the NFL's juggernauts.
On offense, Bo Nix and the offensive line played 100% of the snaps, finishing with 65 snaps on the day. Alex Palczewski was in for one snap in a heavy package; otherwise, the entire starting five and the quarterback played the entire game.
Let's examine the Broncos' snap share in Week 4 and what takeaways can be gleaned from how the coaches rolled once the injury bug began to strike.
This was a Harvey day. Dobbins led as a ball carrier, rushing 11 times for 40 yards, but Harvey garnered the most playing tim e and total touches, finishing with 10 catches for 68 yards and seven rushes for 25.
Credit to Badie, who played a bit more in this game than usual. He made a few big plays for the Broncos as a receiver, and picked up a crucial third down and two-point conversion.
The receivers' snap share was going to be impacted by the return of Mims, but losing Bryant in the third quarter saw Franklin's playing time increase. Waddle scored his first touchdown as a Bronco, but he also dropped a gotta-have-it pass, and was otherwise a non-factor.
Speaking of non-factors, you'd be forgiven for thinking that Sutton didn't play in this game, even though he led in snap share. He was targeted six times, but Nix connected with him just once for four yards.
Mims looked rusty as a receiver, while Franklin failed to garner even one target, despite playing 32 snaps. Nix completing only two passes beyond 10 yards and throwing 14 of his 25 completions to running backs had a lot to do with the receivers' overall lack of production at Levi's Stadium.
Once again, Engram led all tight ends in snap share, which illustrates how much more the Broncos are relying on him as a blocker, but it didn't translate to production as a receiver. He was targeted five times with one catch for six yards.
Trautman was used as a blocker mostly, as usual, but he was targeted once. He took a huge hit from Fred Warner and was unable to haul it in. For the first time since Week 1, Adkins was held without a catch or a touchdown.
It's pretty rare when Allen doesn't lead the defensive line in snaps, but he was edged out by not one but two players against the 49ers. I can only wonder why Roach and Uwazurike saw one more snap than the All-Pro, but Allen certainly had a great game, finishing with a team-high four pressures and four QB hits, while also blocking a field goal.
It's interesting to see the Broncos giving Jackson and Jones more playing time, though it's not resulting in much production. It is ostensibly helping to keep Roach and Allen fresher. D.J. Jones and the D-line did a great job of limiting the 49ers' run game in this one.
For the first time ever, Robinson led all of Denver's outside linebackers in snap share. With Dondrea Tillman sidelined with an injury, Robinson was the only backup edge defender, so he played a lot, finishing with just two tackles and one pressure.
Bonitto was neutralized by Trent Williams, limited to just two pressures and two tackles. Elliss had a bad game, with just one tackle and zero impact on the quarterback. Zero pressures.
Singleton played 100% of the defensive snaps, and turned in his best, most consistent game of the season. He was flying to the football, filling the right gaps, and making the tackles, finishing with a team-high 14.
Strnad was also good in this one, giving up just two completions on four targets for 19 yards. Singleton allowed all four of his targets to be caught for 17 yards. They shined as run defenders and while they weren't perfect in coverage, as a duo, Singleton and Strnad showed progress.
Barron was the first man up when Surtain went down, and he played very well. Barron was only targeted twice in coverage, but he allowed one completion for just six yards and broke up the other pass on third down.
Barron's hit on Kyle Juszczyk injured the 49ers' fullback, alas. But it was a great open-field tackle.
I don't want to speak too soon, but Barron looked like a legit starting-caliber corner out there. Here's to hoping he can sustain it.
Things didn't go so well for Abrams-Draine in coverage, as he allowed all three of his targets to be completed for 33 yards, but only one of them was to a receiver. McMillian was targeted five times, allowing four catches for 49 yards, including a couple to Mike Evans in the clutch. That was a bad matchup.
If Surtain and Moss miss extended time, this is your cornerback trio, Broncos Country: Barron, Abrams-Draine, and McMillian. Hold on to your hat.
Jones had a good game in run support, flying all over the field, and finishing with nine tackles. In coverage, though, he wasn't so good. He only gave up one completion on one target, but it was a 56-yard touchdown by George Kittle that iced the game for the 49ers. Ouch.
After a huge Week 3 performance, Hufanga missed four tackles and gave up a big completion to Evans on his only target (18 yards). Hufanga also played 100% of snaps and finished with just four tackles, but if he had made all his tackle attempts, he would have doubled that number.

title: Film Room: How Bo Nix Held Back the Broncos’ Offense vs. 49ers
full_text:
This Denver Broncos offense has problems, and there’s no other way to put it. Through four weeks, the Broncos have only scored a grand total of 13 first-half points.
Even with the Broncos' late-game heroics, that’s not nearly good enough. It’s a conglomeration of suck, and it’s a big reason the Broncos lost 24-14 to the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday.
You can point to play-calling if you want to, as well as execution and miscues from skill players all over the field. There are issues with the offensive line in both run blocking and pass protection.
To be honest, though, one of the biggest reasons for the Broncos' offensive ineptitude is quarterback Bo Nix .
It’s difficult to nail down all the culprits of the notorious slow starts for this offense, but there were several missed opportunities to push the ball downfield, as Nix opted for check-downs, especially in the first half.
Nix struggled against the 49ers , finishing the day 25-of-42 for 214 yards and a touchdown. He only completed two passes beyond 10 yards, and 14 of his completions went to running backs out of the backfield.
Nothing between the numbers besides what appear to be check downs. Fred Warner is there, so need tape for context. Pretty much nothing beyond 10 yards, either. This is not good. https://t.co/TMtG7jrzAk
This isn’t a full indictment of Nix, but it needs to be talked about on a much larger scale. He has to get better at letting plays develop and fully opening the play designs. There was a lot of meat left on the bone this week, particularly in the first half.
I typically don’t like pausing plays because it dilutes the context, but I did so at the top of Nix’s drop to show the pocket, route concept, and the windows where Nix misses some explosive opportunities. The tape doesn’t lie.
Bo Nix cannot eat this football. He has plenty of time to step up and deliver. Engram is as wide open as you can get. pic.twitter.com/21o4CHWH8X
Most of Nix’s issues stem from escaping the pocket too early or coming off his progressions too quickly. Our first play highlights this on what could have been a massive gain to Engram.
Denver comes out in 13 personnel and runs a two-man concept designed to target Engram on a crossing route. I paused this play at the top of Nix’s drop to show the protection and the window that Nix has to throw into. With max protection and a great pocket to step into, Nix has to rip this ball right when he hits his back foot.
San Francisco is in a Cover 3 look here, and safety Ji’Ayir Brown is sitting in his shallow zone with his eyes on Nix. Marvin Mims Jr. runs a vertical route to clear out the cornerback, opening a massive hole for Engram to run into. There’s no way Brown can recover in time to get his hands on this ball, but Nix double-clutches and checks down to Harvey for a minimal gain.
This is a massive miss from Nix, and an inexcusable one considering the amount of time he had to let this develop.
Good job from Bo here to move the linebacker with his eyes. Waddle has to make this catch. pic.twitter.com/d2KUZ8JD36
It’s not all on the quarterback, though. You need your playmakers to make plays.
A few plays later, Nix gets let down by Jaylen Waddle on a crossing route. This is what a third-year quarterback should look like. He hits the top of his drop, moves his eyes to Harvey coming out of the backfield to draw the linebacker, then fires a missile to Waddle over the middle of the field.
Waddle has to make this catch. The ball is a little bit high, but that’s no excuse for a veteran wide receiver.
This is what Sean Payton was talking about when he said Bo comes off of his reads too quick. You have time to rip the Dig here. The checkdown is way too fast. pic.twitter.com/FPkwiWeLns
After a Mike McGlinchey holding penalty set the offense up in a bad situation, Nix comes off his progression too fast, missing a big play over the middle of the field. This is a frustrating play because Nix has all day to throw this football.
Davis Webb calls up a “dagger” concept for Waddle and Pat Bryant, with Waddle taking the top off on the post route and Bryant on the fig. San Francisco only brings four rushers, and Denver’s offensive line blocks it up perfectly.
Rather than allowing Bryant to open up down the field, Nix checks it down to Engram in front of linebacker Fred Warner, who forces the incompletion. There are no defenders within 10 yards of Bryant over the middle of the field, and Nix’s decision to check it down keeps the offense off schedule.
He has to let plays develop when he has time. There’s no reason to check this play down.
We saw this concept a lot from Drew Brees. Swing under the Dagger. Pump to the flat, rip the Dig behind it. Bo got sped up, but you have to stand tall and take a hit sometimes. pic.twitter.com/D4yK3QLCkx
On the next play, Webb calls a Sean Payton staple: a swing route under the dagger concept. This is designed to draw the cornerback up the field and open the window to the dig route behind it.
Nix does right by pump-faking towards Mims on the swing route, but gets flustered in the pocket by pressure from his right side. Instead of stepping up and driving a throw to the dig, he double-clutches and checks down to Harvey in the right flat, right in front of the slot defender playing in an underneath zone.
Sometimes as a quarterback, you have to be willing to take a hit in the pocket. If Nix were to keep his eyes up and stand his ground, he could have hit Bryant for a nice chunk gain to get the offense back on track.
This play is a little bit more difficult because of the pressure from McGlinchey’s side, but not an impossible ask for a third-year quarterback with experience in the system. We saw Drew Brees make this exact same read for years under Payton with the New Orleans Saints.
Back-to-back plays with back-to-back misses on the same concept to the same player. Bad look for Nix here.
This one is tough because Bo gets some pressure up the middle. Gotta play with some anticipation though. Bryant is wide open on the Post if you step up and deliver. pic.twitter.com/SsaIJXRVJO
After a San Francisco field goal to tie the game, the Broncos are set up at the 20-yard line due to a special teams snafu on the kickoff. Webb dials up a “scissors” concept with Troy Franklin and Bryant, and Nix has to check down to Harvey to avoid pressure in the middle of the offensive line.
Bryant is running the post pattern on the concept, and Franklin’s speed pulls the post safety up the field, opening a massive window between the hash marks. This would have been a massive gain, potentially setting up the Broncos' offense deep in field-goal range.
This isn’t entirely on Nix due to the pressure, but again, sometimes it’s necessary to step up and deliver a throw when you get hit in the chops in the pocket. You have to play with some anticipation in the line of fire. That’s big-boy quarterbacking, and an unfortunate necessary evil of the position.
Again, not everything is Nix's fault.
Poor execution from the offensive line, drops from his receivers, and even some sequencing from his play caller have hampered the offense as a whole. But the fact is, Nix touches the football on every play, and the offense can only go as far as he can take it, even when adversity strikes. Take notice that all the plays in this breakdown came from the first half.
Nix made a couple of incredible plays in this game, including a couple of scrambles where he found explosive plays out of nothing. He hit Tyler Badie for a huge gain early in the first quarter while rolling to his left, as well as finding Bryant for an explosive play while escaping pressure as the pocket broke down.
There is some magic in Nix's play, but the frustrating consistency issues continue to be a problem. If he can start hitting on some of the plays I laid out above, this offense can look much more consistent and explosive, while taking pressure off the defense in late-game situations.
Bottom line, Nix has to be better. Plain and…

title: Broncos Fall Flat in 24-14 Loss to 49ers: The Good, Bad, & the Ugly
full_text:
The Denver Broncos emerged from their trip to California with their second loss of the season, falling to the San Francisco 49ers 24-14 .
The heat was intense, both literally and figuratively, and despite a very lackluster showing overall and a turnover, the Broncos were actually in position to win the game if their defense could have gotten one more stop.
Instead, the Broncos allowed two third-down conversions with under five minutes in the game, trialing by three points, the second of which was the dagger: 49ers tight end George Kittle took a short pass 56 yards to the house.
That was all she wrote on the Broncos' comeback efforts. As we continue sifting through the aftermath, let's examine the good, bad, and ugly from Week 4.
Overall, the Broncos' defense hung tough against the 49ers' heretofore high-flying offense. They put the brakes on Brock Purdy and company until late in the game, when all those weary snaps began to add up.
The Broncos bent, but didn't really break until the worst possible moment. Still, they deserve credit for mostly shutting down Christian McCaffrey, who rushed 15 times for just 52 yards and a late touchdown.
If the Broncos had been able to also corral Deebo Samuel as a rusher, they might be singing a different tune this morning, but his three carries for 44 yards were untimely and costly. As a passer, Purdy was held to just 218 yards, but he was able to scramble 10 times, picking up another 29 yards and moving the chains.
It wasn't a dominant defensive showing; far from it. But the Broncos' defense did enough to give the offense a chance to battle back into this game.
I can say that the Broncos' defense decided to break at the worst possible time, but in truth, it was Nix and the offense waiting far too long to finally get into a rhythm that ultimately doomed the outcome of this game.
Nix was the checkdown king in this game, with 14 of his 25 completions going to running backs. RJ Harvey finished with a team-high 10 receptions, as Nix and the Broncos repeatedly checked down instead of pushing the ball downfield.
“We had seen this on tape," head coach Sean Payton said via conference call on Monday, "they did a pretty good job of staying on top of some of the deeper throws and [that is] part of what they’re trying to do defensively. So I think coming away from that game tape, I think the feeling overall was just more yardage underneath in different ways that I think we feel like we could have taken a little bit more advantage of.”
Payton wasn't saying that Denver should have tried harder to push the ball downfield; what he said was that the Broncos could have made more of the underneath targets. I don't know exactly what he meant by that, but the only way the Broncos could have "taken a little bit more advantage of" the underneath throws would have been if the running backs had broken more tackles.
The 49ers were content to let the Broncos complete passes all day to backs underneath, swarm up, and tackle. The 49ers did play a lot of two-high shell, but the Broncos didn't do anything to even try to force those safeties down into the box. San Francisco's cornerbacks and linebackers tackled so well.
Perhaps it was a game-plan thing; I don't know. What I do know is that Nix was mostly ineffectual as a passer, despite finishing with 214 yards. At least he didn't turn the ball over, nor was he sacked.
Other than that, it's difficult to find a silver lining to the Broncos' offensive showing in Santa Clara. I mean, good on Harvey for catching 10 balls and fighting hard to pick up extra yards when he was being gang-tackled by three or four 49ers.
But if that's the best Payton, Nix, and Davis Webb could come up with against San Francisco, with weapons like Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Evan Engram, and Pat Bryant, fans have every reason to be increasingly alarmed by this offense's outlook.
I could point to the Broncos' seven penalties, many of which were untimely drive killers, but the injuries were a much uglier development. It started with cornerback Patrick Surtain II going down with a non-contact injury to his lower right leg.
Then fellow cornerback Riley Moss exited with a rib injury. Neither returned. In the third quarter, during a 30-yard catch-and-run, wide receiver Pat Bryant suffered an ankle injury and was carted off.
We're still awaiting an update on Moss, but the good news is that both Surtain and Bryant seem to have avoided major injury , although both will miss some time.
Jahdae Barron played well in relief of Surtain. Kris Abrams-Draine didn't fare quite as well, but he and Barron will now be teamed up with Ja'Quan McMillian as the Broncos' starting cornerback trio until Surtain and Moss return.
The 49ers' late-game passing production was greatly influenced by the absence of Surtain and Moss. Losing your top-two corners against an opponent like the 49ers... eventually those chickens will come home to roost.
It was ultimately more than the Broncos could handle at Levi's Stadium. Hopefully, the Broncos will fare better against the Los Angeles Chargers next week, as Surtain will be out and Moss's situation doesn't look great for Week 5.

title: Broncos’ Pat Surtain II Injury Update Could Have Been Far Worse
full_text:
The Denver Broncos have dodged not one , but two major bullets following Sunday's costly loss to the San Francisco 49ers.
The Ringer's Tom Pelissero reported Sunday that Broncos cornerback Patrick Surtain II, who left the Week 4 game with an apparent non-contact injury, "avoided any worst-case scenario" and his Achilles' tendon remains "intact."
Further testing revealed an ankle injury for Surtain, who's classified as "week-to-week" and is expected to miss only a short period of time, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Monday .
Surtain was having a solid game prior to being assisted off the field, recording four combined tackles including two solo stops while helping limit San Francisco's passing attack.
The perennial All-Pro defender was among multiple players to suffer injuries amid the 24-14 defeat in the Bay Area; Denver also lost wide receiver Pat Bryant to an ankle injury and fellow starting cornerback Riley Moss to a rib injury.
Predictably, head coach Sean Payton offered little by way of an official update.
"Of course today and throughout the week, really we’ll stay away from any updates," Payton told the media on Monday. "Guys were all in today getting work and rehabbing. We’ll make sure we go through the process well, and then we’ll have a report Wednesday."
The Broncos stay on the road to face the 0-4 Los Angeles Chargers in Week 5.
The Broncos' schedule doesn't get any easier after Week 5, with matchups against the Seattle Seahawks, Arizona Cardinals, Kansas City Chiefs, and Carolina Panthers yet to come over the next month — all teams with viable passing games.
Much will hinge on the status of Moss, who may or may not play through his rib issue. If he does, he'll be locked in as the club's No. 1 corner, with Jahdae Barron or Kris Abrams-Draine starting opposite him and Ja'Quan McMillian holding down his familiar slot role.
If Moss cannot go in Week 5, Barron and Abrams-Draine will be the top two CBs. In that instance, it's likely Denver would comb the market for help at the position, as they have only Brent Austin on the practice squad.
“Relative to their play yesterday, I thought they came in and did a real good job. It was good to see," Payton said of Barron and Abrams-Draine on Monday. "I think it’s a position we have depth at, and those guys both kind of got thrown into the fire and I thought they handled it well.”

title: Insider Provides Key Pat Bryant Injury Update—What It Means
full_text:
Exhale, Denver Broncos fans. Second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant will only miss "a few weeks" with an ankle sprain.
ESPN 's Adam Schefter broke the news Monday morning, reporting that Bryant suffered an ankle sprain in the Broncos' 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers .
Broncos WR Pat Bryant sprained his ankle during Sunday’s loss at San Francisco, and now is expected to miss “a few weeks” per source. pic.twitter.com/uwZA3UYou2
We're still awaiting an update on cornerbacks Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss, who exited Sunday's game at Levi's Stadium with a lower leg and rib injury, respectively.
As for Bryant, "a few weeks" could mean two or three, or it could mean four-plus. If the Broncos expect it to be at least four games, they'll place him on short-term injured reserve.
Hopefully, it doesn't come to that, but even if it does, that would put Bryant back on the field somewhere around Week 9 and beyond. He'd still be back in time to contribute to the Broncos' stretch run, even if it's an IR designation first.
Bryant's injury occured on a 30-yard catch-and-run that helped set up a Wil Lutz field goal. Bryant finished the day with three receptions on three targets for 47 yards.
Beyond the running backs, Bryant and Jaylen Waddle have been the Broncos' passing attack. Courtland Sutton and Evan Engram have been disappearing acts thus far, while RJ Harvey caught as many passes against the 49ers as Bryant, Waddle, Sutton, and Engram combined.
How much of Bo Nix's checkdown obsession was game-plan oriented or quarterback-driven we don't know, but it became so predictable that even fans watching the game knew what was coming on a down-to-down basis.
Outside of Week 2, the Broncos' passing game has been anemic and frustrating to watch. We're mystified by this failure to launch, and it's hard to see it suddenly improving with Bryant being gone for the next few games.
A third-round pick out of Illinois last year, Bryant had an impressive rookie showing. He started off a bit slow, but as the season wore on, he slowly began to eat into Troy Franklin's snaps.
Bryant was on the cusp of doing great things when he suffered a brutal concussion in Week 16 that hospitalized him. He was back in time for the Broncos' playoff run, but another concussion, followed by a hamstring injury in the AFC championship game, sidelined him for most of it.
Entering Year 2, Bryant had one heck of a training camp, easily earned the No. 3 receiver spot behind Sutton and Waddle. Bryant was a big reason for both of Denver's wins this season, so he will be missed.
Fortunately, the Broncos still have Franklin, who's very experienced for a third-year player, and Marvin Mims Jr. is healthy again. That gives the Broncos a four-deep receiver rotation, plus Lil'Jordan Humphrey is on the practice squad.
If Bryant ends up on short-term IR, expect Humphrey to promoted back to the active roster. We'll hopefully learn more about Bryant's outlook soon.

title: Why I Don't Trust Detroit Lions GM Brad Holmes To Sign Good Cornerbacks
full_text:
Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes actually did proclaim once that he loved sitting in the film room to watch defensive backs play.
"I love corner play," Holmes said at the 2024 NFL scouting combine. "I just love it. I could watch DB individuals all day every day. It’s poetry in motion. I love DB play. But yeah, we just want to get the right fit."
Holmes later added, "They’re not growing on trees. Although that’s arguably, them and wide receivers, probably the most volumous group, position group in the draft. But that doesn’t mean that they’re all going to be good, especially as high as you might have to pick them, because of their physical qualities. If you get wooed by the physical qualities too much but they don’t have the intangible qualities you can get yourself in trouble."
Unfortunately, after six years on the job, there is no other conclusion to draw other than he is not aware of what a good cornerback looks like.
Since his arrival, the former Los Angeles Rams Director of College Scouting has an abysmal cornerback track record, both in the draft and in free agency.
In 2024, he targeted Terrion Arnold and Ennis Rakestraw with the Lions first two picks. Unfortunately, the Philadelphia Eagles were able to land two better defensive backs (Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean) with their two early picks in that year.
Ifeatu Melifonwu could not stay healthy, as he was the Lions 2021 third-round draft choice. He is no longer with the team.
Free agency has also been horrid for Holmes.
Cam Sutton was cut after an arrest warrant became public. Holmes invested $33 million in the veteran in March of 2023.
Emmanuel Moseley also did not work out. Injuries derailed his chances to succeed in Motown.
Even when good defensive backs find their way to Detroit, Holmes has been too cheap to keep them around.
Darius Slay expressed the biggest mistake made by the Lions was letting Carlton Davis depart. After making the decision to trade for him, the team allowed him to depart in free agency to the New England Patriots, where he has excelled.
Commanders veteran Amik Roberston is certainly a better nickel cornerback than what the Lions feature presently.
Khalil Dorsey has found his niche on special teams, but he is not a starting caliber cornerback.
Kindle Vildor has bounced around the league, but Lions' fans are only going to remember him for the football bouncing off his head against the 49ers in the 2023 NFC Championship Game.
D.J. Reed has lost a step and is nowhere near worth his $16 million salary. He is having a slow start to the season and is coming off a bad game against the Carolina Panthers.
With how poor the defense is, with the secondary not able to execute in either zone or man-to-man coverage this season, is it not really conceivable that Holmes can fix the problem.
The front office reportedly tried to land Joey Porter Jr., but he is now with the Dallas Cowboys. All other options seem not as appealing at this point.
This writer is at the point that if Holmes targets a defensive back, something is likely wrong with that player, whether it be injury related or a lack of coverage skills needed to play at the NFL level.
Pundits are now floating many names that Holmes should target, but if the defensive coordinator also is in over his head, how can that formula actually be expected to work.
A poor cornerback evaluator with a poor defensive coordinator.
The math ain't mathin to make anyone feel better about improving the secondary that much this season.

title: Cardinals Have Talent, But Lions Can Exploit These Holes
full_text:
On Sunday, the Detroit Lions will battle with an Arizona Cardinals team that certainly has talent but has struggled through the first four weeks of the 2026 campaign.
In fact, since beating Jim Harbaugh and the L.A. Chargers in Week 1, they have lost three straight games. And they have allowed at least 31 points in each of their three losses, including a season-high 36 points in Week 4 against John Harbaugh and the N.Y. Giants.
While the Nick Rallis-coordinated defense has struggled (29.3 points allowed/game), the offense has fared better.
The Cardinals are led under center by Jacoby Brissett, who has completed 67.8 percent of his passes so far this season but has also thrown for just six touchdowns while tossing four interceptions. It's been iffy play from the veteran passer.
However, the Cardinals, which are averaging 21.8 points a game through four weeks, have the potential to be more productive. It's because Mike LaFleur's squad possesses multiple high-end offensive weapons, including rookie running back Jeremiyah Love and tight end Trey McBride.
With time, Love has a chance to be one of the very best at his position, and McBride is already viewed as that among tight ends. Fourth-year wideout Michael Wilson, who amassed 1,000-plus receiving yards a season ago, is also off to a solid start in 2026.
Subsequently, it's fair to say Arizona's offensive attack has room for growth, and could exploit the Lions’ beleaguered defense on Sunday.
With that said, the Cardinals still possess their fair share of weaknesses. Quite notably, they struggle to get after the quarterback. In fact, through three games, they've accumulated just four sacks, and have recorded one of the league's lowest pressure rates. It should bode well for Lions signal-caller Jared Goff, who presently ranks No. 10 in QBR (66.3) among qualified quarterbacks.
Then, there's this: Arizona will enter this Week 5 contest with multiple injuries on the offensive line. Not only is left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. out for the season, but right guard Isaiah Adams was also banged up against the Giants. It's far from an optimal situation for the Cardinals’ pass protection, and Detroit direly needs to take advantage of this Sunday.
And if the Lions can generate enough consistent pressure against Brissett and force him into a turnover or two, it would go a long way toward Dan Campbell's squad securing the Week 5 win.
It will be far from a cakewalk for Goff & Co. in the desert. However, at the same time, there is a clear path to a much-needed victory for Detroit.

title: Darius Slay Analyzes Detroit Lions Biggest Mistake: They Can't Cover
full_text:
Former Detroit Lions cornerback Darius Slay was like many fans of the team during their loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday Night Football.
Slay, who retired this past offseason after 13 NFL seasons, watched as the Lions were picked apart by Bryce Young. The Alabama product tore up Detroit's secondary, adding to what has been a litany of struggles over the first four weeks of the season.
The former Lion noted what he feels is the biggest mistake the front office has made over the past few seasons. Carlton Davis, who the Lions acquired in a trade, departed after just one season in free agency as Detroit elected to not re-sign him.
This move has come back to haunt Detroit in the eyes of Slay, as he believes Davis' style was an ideal fit for Detroit's defensive scheme. On a recent appearance on "Woodward Heavyweights," Slay expressed his opinion on a pivotal choice the Lions made.
“Honestly, the biggest mistake I think that the Lions did to that secondary was letting Carlton Davis go. That’s who I felt like was the most complete corner and could’ve been a stamp there since I left there. I feel like Carlton Davis was a guy that fit that scheme. Them guys want to play a lot of man, a lot of matching, and I think Carlton Davis was a great addition to that.”
Slay began his career in Detroit as a second-round pick in the 2013 NFL draft, and blossomed into a Pro Bowl cornerback throughout his time in Detroit.
He quickly became a well-loved figure in Detroit, as he provided stable cornerback play that the fan base is currently yearning for. However, a rocky relationship with then-head coach Matt Patricia ultimately pushed him out as he was traded to Philadelphia.
With the Eagles, Slay ultimately won a Super Bowl ring and enjoyed plenty of success. Still, he expressed his appreciation for his time in Motown.
“I always wanted to stay in Detroit. But thankfully, I did go to Philadelphia and won a championship," Slay said. "I’m loving it, I loved that part of my life, I am not lying. I always wanted to spend the rest of my career in Detroit, but I’m damn sure thankful that I went to an organization that really appreciated what I brought to the table and it shows. That’s why I’ve got a lot of love in Philly."
Slay admitted he'd consider exiting retirement for the right price, but noted that he feels comfortable with his current situation post-NFL career.
"I still work out. I still do my little dues. I train, I stay in great shape," Slay said. "I've got a couple of DBs that I train, high school mostly. I'm still in a groove, but it'd take a nice, pretty, pretty penny to get me to come out of retirement. I can go for real, I can really go. I just chose not to continue because of the fact that I'm good, man. But I can really still go."
Detroit's defensive struggles have called the job security of coordinator Kelvin Sheppard into question. Schematically, the Lions seem to be struggling and at times appear out of sorts.
Slay noted that Sheppard is well thought of throughout the league, but ultimately hasn't been able to get the most out of the players at his disposal. When asked what is the defenses identity, Slay noted it is clear the secondary cannot cover opposing wideouts effectively.
"Shep’s a good dude. I played with Shep, he’s known well, I’ve got a lot of respect because he coaches hard, he holds players accountable," Slay said. "I just don’t see them playing complete defense. I see the linebacking corps isn’t in sync with the secondary, and then I see the secondary is trying to play a lot of man but you don’t have man corners at this time. I know Shep still wants to be aggressive, but he needs to address with the players."
The Lions have played a plethora of man-to-man coverage since Campbell became the head coach, first with Aaron Glenn as the coordinator and then now with Sheppard. Yet, Slay believes a switch in philosophy could be more beneficial for the personnel Detroit has at its disposal currently.
"It’s more about the coaches adjusting to what they have. D.J. Reed can play ball, but 60 plays of man, you’re gonna lose. You’re gonna lose some reps like that. I was in a Matt Patricia defense, we played man 85 percent of the time. I lost some, but I won way more than I did. But this group, as a group, is just not a winning group in the back end with that coverage scheme.”

title: Lions Are Demanding Even More From Offense: How Greatness Is Determined
full_text:
The Detroit Lions' defense has been under a heavy amount of scrutiny to start the 2026 NFL season.
For head coach Dan Campbell, there is an understanding why supporters are feeling anxious about Kelvin Sheppard's unit.
During his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket this week, Campbell also took the opportunity to demand more from his offense.
"Man, if you want to be great, they should want to score 35 points a game, at a minimum. That's what greatness is. That's what they're charged with. We've got plenty of weapons on offense and if we're gonna accept mediocrity, then yeah, we can make all the excuses in the world," said Campbell. "If we want to spit and sputter and be average, that's one thing. We're not going to be average. We're going to raise the floor on these guys, man. We're going to push 'em.
"We've got too much offensively right now. Our quarterback's too good, our playmakers are too good, and we've got a young, hungry offensive line that's got a ton of room to grow."
The former NFL tight end has received a fair amount of pushback, due to how poor the performance of the defense has been.
Campbell has not shied away from discussing defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard and avenues the defense can improve.
He has indicated since the Panthers loss a few new players could be given opportunities to assist the ailing defense.
Another avenue to improve the play on the field, highlighted by the former NFL tight end, has been the undisciplined penalties. Against Carolina, Detroit incurred a total of nine penalties.
“I think you just go back to what we did when we started. You pull them out and then if it continues to be an issue in the game, you put other guys in. I mean, that's kind of what you have to do. And if you're on the clock, then you keep them in for a play and then you get them out the very next play. So that's really the only way to do it to this point," said Campbell. "I trust that we'll get there and that's on us as coaches.
"Starts with me and we're the ones who have to demand that," Campbell added. "And I thought we did a pretty good job during training camp, but you get on the road, and you don't respond very well to it. It's an issue because that's what this League is.”

title: Good, Bad and Ugly From Lions Loss to Panthers
full_text:
On Sunday Night Football, the Detroit Lions traveled to Carolina to take on their second NFC South opponent of the year. The Lions looked to keep pace with their division after all three NFC North opponents won their matchups this week.
Additionally, the Lions were hoping to snap a losing skid in Charlotte, as they had lost their last six games in Bank of America Stadium.
It is safe to say that did not happen on Sunday night, as the Lions fell 32-26 to Bryce Young, Chuba Hubbard, Tetairoa McMillan, and the Panthers.
There was plenty of bad and ugly in this week’s good, bad, and ugly.
Jared Goff had a very strong game. There were issues with ball placement at points, alongside his receivers having drops, but Goff managed what he could. The quarterback spread the ball well, with four pass catchers over 75 yards.
Goff kept the Lions in the game after Carolina was able to bottle the run, something they previously had not done all season. This came in spite of a defensive interior that was aggressive and able to bat down multiple balls after getting a push against the Lions interior offensive line.
The receiving trio of Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, and Amon-Ra St. Brown had their first ever game where they each went over 75 yards. On top of catching the ball well, there were strong downfield blocks and adjustments that helped keep Detroit in the game.
Williams rallied from an early concentration lapse to grab a ball before half that gave the Lions a game-tying field goal. TeSlaa had a career day , including a career-long 57-yard catch. St. Brown provided multiple clutch first downs as the Lions tried to rally.
In the end, all three receivers had a ‘what if’ day, as they were open a few more times when the football got deflected at the line of scrimmage.
The special teams unit got a lot of time on Sunday, kicking four field goals and being brought out to punt multiple times. Jake Bates was perfect on field goals and extra points, Jack Fox had strong punts, and the Lions shined while the Panthers missed two extra points.
The lone mark against the Lions occurs from a running into the kicker penalty on a late punt, but that was a desperation block attempt.
The Lions struggled on the interior of their offensive line today. The front three could not get a push against Carolina, which held Jahmyr Gibbs in check. The back finished under 50 yards.
The lone Goff sack of the day occurred via a rush up the gut. In addition to the sack, Juice Scruggs was whistled for holding, Tate Ratledge was whistled for a false start, and Christian Mahogany got pushed into Goff multiple times. All three were the primary blocking lineman on plays where their defensive tackle batted the ball down after surrendering ground blocking the pass.
The linebacker play was subpar on Sunday. Jimmy Rolder recording a tackle for loss during some of his first defensive snaps, but was otherwise a nonfactor. Jack Campbell continues to not make much of an impact, also recording two missed tackles during the game that resulted in first downs on scoring drives.
Derrick Barnes and Malcolm Rodriguez lacked any noticeable plays on the game, and the linebacker unit was exposed by the Carolina RPO scheme on multiple occasions. The last linebacker from the group to play, Trevor Nowaske, had his most memorable play occur when he was held on special teams.
The secondary’s tape was unwatchable for the fourth week in a row. Ennis Rakestraw had a solid game last week, but that was not the case on Sunday. Rakestraw, Roger McCreary, DJ Reed, and Jalen Mills all struggled. Christian Izien got burnt a few times.
Reed entered the game allowing over 20 yards per catch, and he was the lone man in coverage on the opening touchdown drive. During the contest, it was noted that the Lions could not play man or zone with their struggles.
After the game, former head coach Mike Tomlin discussed that the Lions had to figure a way to “slow down their dying.” When asked about the comments after, he did not walk them back. The Lions’ secondary is killing any chance of postseason thoughts in Motown.
The disturbing fact for the Lions is that they have only faced one top quarterback in the league. They have looked abysmal against the likes of Geno Smith, Tyler Shough, and Bryce Young.
The line started strong for Detroit, with multiple Alim McNeill run stuffs and a McNeill sack. Aidan Hutchinson was disruptive and forced a few pressures and throwaways. DJ Wonnum finished off a chase down run for no gain. Besides that, the defensive line was tossed around on Sunday.
On most RPOs, there was a positive gain awaiting Carolina no matter what Bryce Young chose. Chuba Hubbard ran for over 120 yards, including multiple runs for over 20 yards when he did not have any in the 2025 season.
Young was not flushed from the pocket much by anyone besides McNeill and Hutchinson . Derrick Moore rarely made an impact as a second-round pick. Skyler Gill-Howard lined up offsides. Tyler Lacy’s lone contribution was a run stuff.
The secondary’s struggle amplified matters, but allowing Hubbard’s massive day on the ground while not recording much pressure in an ugly day.

title: 3 Risers, 4 Fallers After Detroit Lions Loss to Panthers
full_text:
The Detroit Lions are entering a pivotal Week 5 contest against the Arizona Cardinals.
After a disappointing primetime loss in Week 4 to the Carolina Panthers, the Lions are set to take on the Cardinals in their final game before their bye week. As a result, it's an opportunity for them to generate some momentum heading into the week off.
Here are risers and fallers following the Lions' Week 4 loss to the Carolina Panthers.
Goff has had some good performances glossed over by the performance of the defense. He remains turnover-free through four games, and ranked second in the league behind only Bryce Young in passing yards ahead of Monday Night Football with 1,214 yards after a 400-plus yard performance against Carolina.
The veteran passer has some flaws that got exposed by Carolina's pass-rush, but has been very efficient and consistent for a majority of his snaps in Detroit's first four games. He has clear chemistry with Drew Petzing, which has led to a strong start to his 2026 campaign.
After a slow start to the season, TeSlaa has had two big games in a row. He's had back-to-back career-high totals in receiving yards, including Sunday's game in which he set a new personal best with 95 yards on four catches.
There were high expectations facing TeSlaa entering training camp, but his momentum cooled off after an up-and-down performance leading up to the start of the regular season. He seems to be trending up as of late, which has been a big boost to Detroit's offense.
McNeill is up to three sacks in four games after recording another one on Sunday during Carolina's first offensive possession. He seems to have regained his explosiveness that he missed last year post-ACL injury, which has added another element to Detroit's pass-rush.
With so many questions about the state of their defense, the Lions should take some solace in the fact that McNeill has been producing consistently early in the year. His career-high for sacks in a season is five, and he's on pace to double that at this point.
There were some concerns about McNeill given the hefty contract extension he signed in 2024 and his performance last year, but he continues to quiet those with his performance early in the season.
The Lions' secondary has taken its lumps throughout the start of the season, as the defense has been the worst in the league against the pass up to this point. Reed, who was signed last offseason with the expectation that he could be the team's top option, has not lived up to expectations.
Against the Panthers, Reed allowed three completions on five targets for 58 yards and a touchdown. It was emblematic of the team's performance, as wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan gashed them for 192 yards and two scores on 14 catches.
Through four games, Reed has allowed an opposing passer rating of 141.7 and has been called for four penalties. It has been a less than ideal start for the veteran who is being counted on to be a big part of Detroit's defensive attack.
Signed to a four-year extension this offseason, Campbell has struggled out of the gate. In particular, Campbell has been struggling in pass coverage allowing 16 completions on 19 targets according to Pro Football Focus.
Campbell is expected to be a leader of the defense for the foreseeable future, and he still has plenty of time to turn things around. However, given the high expectations he faced the results up to this point have been disappointing.
Through four games, Campbell has a PFF pass coverage grade of 44.5 which is a significant drop off from the 71.7 mark he posted last year in his All-Pro season.
The Lions traded up to land Moore in the second-round of this year's draft, but have yet to see any significant results through his first four games. His snap count has diminished over the last two weeks, as he's totaled 17 snaps in that timeframe after playing 35 total in his first two outings.
Moore has not been impactful in Detroit's pass-rush, as he hasn't recorded a tackle and has just three pressures in four games. He's still a young player, and D.J. Wonnum's emergence has played a part in his smaller role.
However, for a player the Lions traded up to get, the results have not been what the team expected up to this point.
Wright had a pair of penalties in Sunday's game, and while he has some value as a run-blocker he has not been as impactful as years past. He has four catches for 20 yards up to this point, and the team has an intriguing young option in Jackson Meeks waiting in the wings.
Meeks has already supplanted Tyler Conklin to become the third tight end on the depth chart, and if he demonstrates reliability as a run-blocker could continue to get an extended look. This could spell trouble for Wright, who is in the final year of his contract.

title: Detroit Lions Power Rankings: After Bad Loss, Mediocre Defense Exposed
full_text:
Here are the latest Week 5 NFL power rankings and how the Detroit Lions fared, following a 32-26 loss to the Carolina Panthers.
Power ranking: 18th Previous ranking: 14th
"A tip for Amon-Ra St. Brown: if you would like the quarterback of the Detroit Lions to come back on your podcast, you can’t blow him up for being a distant teammate on the first visit!"
Power ranking: 16th Previous ranking: 13th
"Like the famous line from the 2000 film "Gladiator," you're guaranteed some level of entertainment with this 2026 Lions team. Detroit scored at least 31 points in three of four games while also allowing 30 or more points in each. After the Week 3 win over the Jets, even coach Dan Campbell had to jokingly admit the Lions are worth the price of admission. "Tell you what, you're coming to our games? You're loving this now," Campbell said. "I mean, these are exciting games . Nobody's leaving early. And that was the point. We're not going to let anybody leave early this year.""
Power ranking: 12th Previous ranking: 6th
"This season, the Lions were supposed to be good enough to take advantage of an easy schedule. Instead, they’re coming off a loss because they couldn’t slow down Bryce Young, who threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns, and the vaunted(?) Panthers offense. The secondary is going to have nightmares about Tetairoa McMillan (14 receptions, 192 yards and two touchdowns)."
Power ranking: 13th Previous ranking: 14th
"The Lions never had a great defensive outfit in the Dan Campbell era, but they were at least decent for a while. Now? Despite 15 sacks — second in the NFL — they’re giving up an NFL-worst 31.8 points per game. You know who they are? They are the Dallas Cowboys. They play like they have to win games 38-35. Even mediocre defensive play would make this team a Super Bowl contender ."
Power ranking: 15th Previous ranking: 10th
"They're certainly leaning on their stars, RB Jahmyr Gibbs with the most touches (102) in the league and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (46) with the most targets. Gonna be hard to deviate from that formula given how bad the league's most permissive defense has been … a state of affairs that seems unlikely to change any time soon."
Power ranking: 21st Previous ranking: 18th
"I guess their super power is running behind an extra lineman as much as anyone and trying to run the ball down your throat under center as much as possible. I feel like there is limited high upside in that. The defense, even when they get healthy, is probably not going to be nearly as good as they would like. They just give up big plays like crazy."
Power ranking: 18th Previous ranking: 13th
The Detroit Lions' defensive issues go beyond their missing starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. The Lions had no answer for Tetairoa McMillan, who caught 14 passes for 192 yards and two touchdowns, or Chuba Hubbard, who ran for 122 yards and two scores.
Head coach Dan Campbell needs to re-evaluate the team's defensive structure and game plan with coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. At some point, even with professional backups, the unit must adjust when the opposing team's best pass-catcher and lead ball-carrier go up and down the field with little resistance.
The Lions have a top-five offense and arguably the league's worst defense, which is a recipe for mediocrity.
Power ranking: 18th Previous ranking: 11th
The Lions' defense has been terrible for most of the season, save for Aidan Hutchinson. That's putting too much on Jared Goff when Jahmyr Gibbs gets contained, like he was at Carolina.

title: After Six Years, Dan Campbell Has Been "Lionized"
full_text:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell has now reached the inevitable point in his tenure we are all familiar with.
A simple word that encapsulates a worn down coach forced to watch his team play undisciplined football.
A simple word that describes a coach that is far too loyal to subpar coaches leading a unit that is trending towards being not only horrid, but one of the worst NFL defenses ever to take the field.
A simple word that describes a coach who used to boast a big personality now putting everyone to sleep during his media sessions.
A simple word that describes a coach who must deliver rah-rah messages to his team via the teams radio parter. After only four games.
On Monday afternoon, Dan Campbell sounded defeated, resigned to the fact not many more players are going to arrive at Allen Park to save the defense.
On Tuesday morning, the former NFL tight end got fired up during his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket .
"I would like to believe that we would have cleaned some of this stuff up, but I also know it's a work in progress," said Campbell. "You continue to coach it up and we'll make a tweak on some of this personnel a little bit. We're going to give some other guys an opportunity. But, we're not going to accept mediocrity. That's not what we're doing here. So, we got too many guys playing at the high level, and we're going to raise the floor on this team."
Campbell later added, "Our discipline is not good enough across the board, and we're playing very average football right now. And that's everywhere. That's everywhere. That's not just defense. We've going to pick up the slack on offense and special teams right now. That will alleviate a lot of our defensive issues. So, it's certainly going to help. That's what I'm tasked with, man. I'm about solving problems and I'm going after this thing, man. We're not going to be mediocre . I don't accept that."
Prior to the season, the new mantra from the sixth-year head coach was to take a more serious, no-nonsense approach.
A far cry from the knee-cap biting message he shared back in 2021.
It appears the Lions are actually the ones in the deep end, drowing with a group of undersized cornerbacks that cannot cover a wide receiver or a tight end.
In the past, a public challenge to his team could be taken a little more seriously.
Now, you just have to chuckle at the thought of someone from the defense stepping up, actually wanting to guard Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.
Sorry. My money is on McBride.

title: Injured Detroit Lions OL Could Return to Practice This Week
full_text:
The Detroit Lions could now have two key members of the roster return to practice this week.
According to head coach Dan Campbell, who spoke during his weekly radio interview on 97.1, shared an injury update on center Cade Mays.
After suffering a wrist injury, Mays started the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list, meaning he needed to wait until after the team played their first four games to participate in practice, or play in a regular season contest.
"He's doing great," said Campbell. "He and (Brian) Branch are on the same plan right now. So, the plan is to get them worked in the practice. We're waiting on the final call from the doctor on both to say,  Yes, they can practice.' We'd love to get them going this week. Doesn't mean they're going to play ."
Mays, 27, inked a three-year free agent contract extension this offseason, following a stint with the Carolina Panthers. In previous talks with reporters, the former NFL tight end expressed the team was likely targeting a return following the Week 6 bye.
Additional Detroit Lions NFL Insider Analysis: Branch, Williams, Ya-Sin Injury Updates
Juice Scruggs has filled in admirably in Mays' absence. The veteran offensive lineman was included as part of the deal that sent running back David Montgomery to the Houston Texans.
Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing shared last week how the success of the offensive line early in the season positively impacts the entire offense.
“You hit on it. It all starts there. It all starts up front in both phases," said Petzing. "And when you can control the line of scrimmage, it gives you a chance to do anything you want on offense and allows those skill players to do what they do best, starting with the quarterback. And you saw it there on the last big play, being able to step up, slide to the left and hit (Isaac TeSlaa) Tes for the big one . I mean, that was such a big play in the game, and it's all based on pass pro and winning your one-on-ones and the communication upfront. So, it's a big deal.”
