title: 3 NFL Coaches on Hot Seat Who Could Replace Kelvin Sheppard
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have some tough decisions on the horizon if things don't change defensively.
Through four games, the Lions' defense ranks near the bottom of the league in a number of different categories. Coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has struggled to manage the game, and his defense has been caught out of position several times leading to explosive plays.
In particular, the s econdary has really struggled as shown in front of a national audience on Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. This performance sparked a debate on whether the defense's difficult fortunes are the result of coaching or personnel.
Ultimately, Sheppard will enter the team's Week 5 game on the hot seat given the team's start to the season. This naturally leads to speculation about who could be next if the Lions were to part ways with him.
While the most likely path forward would be an in-staff promotion on an interim basis, the impending offseason hiring cycle is beginning to take shape based on the start of the season. In particular, there are several defensive-minded head coaches currently on the hot seat who could be candidates to land coordinator jobs if they aren't able to salvage their respective seasons.
Here are three head coaches who are viewed as being on the hot seat that could be potential candidates to replace Kelvin Sheppard in the event that the Lions elect to move on from him at defensive coordinator.
After a promising start to his tenure in Tampa Bay, things have gone south in a hurry for Bowles. He took over for Bruce Arians in 2022 and inherited a roster that featured Tom Brady, but a rough start to the 2026 campaign has things trending downward.
Bowles has made three playoff appearances as the leader of the Buccaneers, but has won 10 games in just one season since taking over. His team started the 2025 season 6-2, but is 2-11 in the 13 games since then including an 0-4 start to the season this year.
With Baker Mayfield sidelined due to injury, the Buccaneers were unable to salvage a win at home against Green Bay on Sunday. Bowles has had some success as a defensive coordinator, however, most notably winning a Super Bowl with the Buccaneers prior to being promoted.
If the Buccaneers can't get back into what is considered a weak NFC South division race, they may have no choice but to move on from the defensive-minded leader.
If he were to be available, he has some history working with Campbell dating back to their time together with the Miami Dolphins and could be an intriguing veteran option to add to the coaching staff.
Like Bowles, Quinn has seen some of the good will generated early in his tenure erased by a tough start. However, his situation is somewhat different than Bowles as he's just two years removed from an upstart run to the NFC title game in the first year of his partnership with quarterback Jayden Daniels in Washington.
Quinn is in his second stint as a head coach, as he previously reached a Super Bowl during a six-year stint as the leader of the Atlanta Falcons. However, he was fired after an 0-5 start that followed two straight losing seasons after that Super Bowl run.
After leaving Atlanta, Quinn put together three years of top-10 defenses as the coordinator for the Dallas Cowboys, and found his way to Washington for a second chance at being a head coach.
Quinn's success has been somewhat derailed by injuries, which makes it tough to project his future. Daniels has dealt with elbow injuries early this year and most of last, which has left the head coach shorthanded at arguably the most important position.
If Washington continues to struggle and Quinn becomes available, he's a no doubt candidate to help stabilize Detroit's defense .
Glenn may have the hottest seat of any coach in the NFL at this stage, as the Jets have had some struggles in big situations with regards to game management leading to a 1-3 start. This comes after a 3-14 record a season ago, and leaves him facing plenty of criticism.
This begs the question of whether or not Campbell would be open to a reunion with the coordinator he spent the first four seasons of his tenure in Detroit with. There's no doubt that Campbell and Glenn have plenty of camaraderie, based on their interactions ahead of and after the Lions and Jets met in Week 3.
Often times in the NFL, coaches don't return to places they've been in the past to take the same role. However, if Glenn can't cut it in the eyes of the Jets as a head coach, perhaps Campbell would be willing to facilitate a reunion if Sheppard is unable to right the ship.

title: Three Stats That Show Why Packers Could Be In Big Trouble Against Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – For the Green Bay Packers, this will be their big opportunity.
On Sunday, the sputtering Packers will face the rival Chicago Bears. The game will be played at Lambeau Field, where the Packers beat the Bears last season. And the Bears will be playing with backup quarterback Tyson Bagent as Caleb Williams will miss a third consecutive game with a hamstring injury.
A victory could be a season-changing achievement for the Packers. Imagine, after a difficult first quarter of the season , they would be 3-2 and in second place in the NFC North.
It won’t be easy. The Packers will have to overcome these statistical mismatches.
Only one game separates the teams in the NFC North standings, but the tale of the statistical tape shows a different reality.
The Bears have outscored their opponents by 47 points, or 11.8 points per game. That’s the third-biggest point differential in the league. They are plus-six in net touchdowns, trailing only San Francisco in the NFC.
The Packers have been outscored by 32 points, or 8.0 points per game. That’s the fourth-biggest negative point differential in the league. They are minus-five in net touchdowns, better than only Arizona in the NFC.
Both teams beat the Jets. Green Bay scored the final 13 points and won in overtime 20-17 at New York in Week 2. The Bears with Tyson Bagent at quarterback won 23-12 at home last week. The stats from the games show the difference in the teams.
Yards gained on offense: Green Bay, 199; Chicago, 492.
Yards allowed on defense: Green Bay, 285; Chicago, 157.
Net passing yards allowed: Green Bay, 218; Chicago, 98.
Rushing offense: Green Bay, 63; Chicago, 232.
Third-down offense: Green Bay, 1-for-9; Chicago, 7-for-15.
Third-down defense: Green Bay, 8-for-19; Chicago, 0-for-7.
Time of possession: Green Bay, 26:57; Chicago, 42:45.
The numbers show teams that are on a completely different trajectory.
After the game on Sunday, coach Matt LaFleur seemed annoyed even in victory. On Monday, LaFleur said, “What makes you say I was annoyed?”
When told it was his focus on the negative things, LaFleur replied: “I think there was a lot of things to build upon.”
But then, without missing a beat, he went right back to the negative.
“The one thing that I’d tell you is when you have opportunities, you have to capitalize on them, especially in this league. It’s so competitive and, certainly, the penalties are inexcusable. Putting the ball on the ground is inexcusable, especially when you have an opportunity to make a game a two-score game.
“That’s stuff that we have to absolutely clean up. I told the guys that whoever holds that ball, you hold it for everybody in the organization. Every player, their families, we’re all dependent on that. You can drill it, you can do ball-security drills all you want, but you have to have the mindset and you’ve got to have good fundamentals when you do it, as well. But we can’t be doing stuff like that.”
He’s right, obviously. The Packers can’t beat a good team until they stop beating themselves.
The Bears are first in the NFL in rushing with 196.3 yards per game. The Falcons, who routed the Packers at Lambeau a couple weeks ago, are second with 181.0 rushing yards per game. The Bears also are fourth with 4.94 yards per carry.
The Packers are last in the NFL with 58.0 rushing yards per game and 31st with 3.18 yards per carry. That puts them on a 17-game pace of 986 rushing yards. The lowest number since the 1970 merger was the 1970 Boston Patriots, who rushed for 1,040 yards in a 14-game season. The lowest 16-game total was the 2000 Chargers with 1,062 rushing yards.
MarShawn Lloyd leads the Packers with 81 rushing yards, or a season pace of 344 yards. That would be the lowest team-leading total since Michael Haddix’s 311 yards in 1990.
“I think – and he’ll probably tell you that, too – that there’s more out there,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday of Lloyd. “The one run that I saw that got me excited was a third-and-1. We ran an inside zone to the right, he bounced it left, made a guy miss and just had a really nice play. That’s kind of what I’m expecting to see from him, so that was good to see him just create a play like that. It was really good.”
Here's, “The one run that I saw that got me excited,” Packers OC Adam Stenavich said yesterday. It's MarShawn Lloyd on third-and-1 turning a TFL into a first down. pic.twitter.com/PiByEF55MI
An occasional run with vision and acceleration provides some hope but what the Packers need is production. Much better production. Much more consistent production.
The Packers have 232 rushing yards. The Bears have almost 3.5 times that number with 785. Their dynamic duo of Kyle Monangai (324 rushing yards) and D’Andre Swift (311) are two of the 17 individuals with more rushing yards than the Packers have as a team.
NFL rushing leaders pic.twitter.com/WWuESV5ffs
“For most of the day, it felt like we were moving the line of scrimmage,” Bears tight end Cole Kmet said after the Jets game. “When we’re doing that, we’re pretty tough to beat. … I know everyone loves the flashy plays. But, at the end of the day, it’s about how physical you are up front. That’s what we pride ourselves on.”
The rushing numbers play into what’s next.
A picture is worth a thousand words. So is this third-down graphic.
3rd Down Conversion Rates through Week 4 Offense: #1 SF, ..., #32 GB Defense: #1 CHI, ..., #32 DET pic.twitter.com/u6ImD7sAny
The Packers are last in the NFL in third-down offense. By a wide margin. They’ve converted 26.1 percent of their third-down opportunities; Seattle is next at 31.1 percent. Rather incredibly, even with better offensive line play, Green Bay was actually worse last week against Tampa Bay (2-of-10, 20.0 percent) than it had been all season.
The Packers’ conversion rate would be the 12th lowest since the NFL began keeping that data in 1972.
The Bears are second in the league in third-down defense, according to the official league stats. Opponents are converting only 23.7 percent of the time, just behind Minnesota’s 22.6 percent. As noted above, they pitched a third-down shutout against the Jets.
Looking at the defenses, the Packers have allowed 29 third-down conversions while the Bears have allowed only nine, even though opponents are facing similar down-and-distances.
Four games marks the unofficial quarter pole of the NFL season. With the Packers off to a 2-2 start, here are some winners and losers from @JacobWestendorf . ⬇️ https://t.co/uY53cQhVxT

title: Packers Winners and Losers After First Quarter of NFL Season
full_text:
That went fast. The Green Bay Packers are at the quarter pole of the season. They are 2-2 and have not played their best football to this point of the season.
Heading into Sunday’s home game against the Chicago Bears, the early part of the season has seen some young players emerge, while others have been on the wrong end of a few things.
There is still time for those who end up on our list of losers to work their way back to the winner’s circle. The same is true for the winners. They could end up on the other side of things by the end of the season.
Football has a way of seeing the cream rise to the top. Who has done that so far this season? Who has work to do? We have that and more in our list of winners and losers.
Coming into the season, was there a player who had to emerge as a playmaker more than fourth-year edge Lukas Van Ness?
Van Ness was a first-round pick in 2023 who had yet to live up to his billing due to injuries and inconsistent play.
Micah Parsons is not coming back anytime soon. Rashan Gary was shown the door in the offseason. The same was true for Kingsley Enagbare. That meant Van Ness had to start the first game of his career Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings.
He’s certainly taken that leap to start the season. The standard numbers look good. He has 2.5 sacks, which is second on the team. He has 4.5 tackles for losses. He’s looked more disruptive now that he’s fully healthy and appears more comfortable in his role.
He has 13 pressures in 191 snaps, according to Pro Football Focus. For comparison’s sake, Van Ness had 18 pressures in 366 snaps in 2023 and 20 pressures in 427 snaps in 2024. He missed half of last season due to an injured foot but had 23 pressures in 263 snaps.
Van Ness is on pace to blow by those numbers. He ranks among the top 20 in pressures and pass-rush win rate. The Packers’ pass rush has not been great through four games, but Van Ness has kept them afloat. The Packers are hoping to welcome Parsons back to the lineup sometime in the next month, which could lead to a pairing that could help slow down some of these dynamic passers the Packers are set to face as fall turns into the winter.
We’ll have more in a little bit on contract extensions that have turned into lemons for Brian Gutekunst, but Christian Watson certainly has not been one of them.
Watson’s $92 million contract extension raised a few eyebrows around the league. It’s clear that anyone who was asking that question wasn’t aware of how much Watson means to Green Bay’s offense. This year, he has the production in the box score to match some of the gravitational pull his skill-set brings to the offense.
He has a team-leading 331 yards and five touchdowns, including an electric 81-yard score for the first touchdown of the season at Minnesota.
Watson is on pace to break the 1,000-yard mark for the first time in his career. Heck, he’s on pace for 1,400 yards. Gutekunst has had a lot of bad luck with recent contract extensions, but Watson’s is aging well, so far.
The other part of Green Bay’s dynamic duo at receiver is Matthew Golden. Any concern about his lack of production a season ago was a misunderstanding of how the Packers typically handle their rookies.
Golden had some things to learn, and the Packers had four veterans they trusted in front of him.
This year, Golden is starting to break out. He leads the team in targets. He often looks like the guy that Jordan Love is targeting in the biggest moments. His strong hands have been on display at times, though the drop against Tampa Bay was the fourth of the season.
Golden has 274 receiving yards, which don’t include the league-high four pass-interference penalties he's drawn. After having zero touchdowns in the regular season last year, Golden has two on the young season. If he can stay healthy, he should only get better and, like Watson, challenge the 1,000-yard mark.
Edgerrin Cooper could, unfortunately, make both the winners and losers lists because he has been lost for the season with a torn Achilles.
It feels a little bit like last year’s ACL injury with Tucker Kraft. Kraft felt like he was on his way to an All-Pro-caliber season when he went down for the year in the eighth game of the season.
Cooper seemed to be on a similar trajectory. He had three sacks, six tackles for losses and one interception through three games and some of a fourth. He was their most dynamic player with Micah Parsons out of the lineup, and someone new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon could build his defense around.
Now, Cooper is lost for the season, and the hope is that he can be the same player he was when he returns to the lineup.
Would the Packers be 1-3 without Evan Williams in the lineup? It’s certainly possible. Edgerrin Cooper was the guy that the Packers were building their defense around in the absence of Micah Parsons. When Cooper was carted off the field, who did Gannon turn to in order to save the day against Tampa Bay?
Williams had a sack and narrowly missed another on the final possession to clinch the game, and he had an interception that led to Green Bay’s first score. It was just another good day in what has been a string of those in 2026.
Williams leads the team with 32 tackles and four pass breakups, and will likely be asked to do more as Gannon tries to rework his defense with Cooper sidelined and Parsons’ return still on hold.
Should Matt LaFleur have been retained after Green Bay blew a 21-3 lead in a playoff game last year against Chicago?
That was up for debate at the time, but it doesn’t really matter at this point. The Packers did keep him, and gave him a contract extension.
Through four games, LaFleur has done little to justify keeping his job. The Packers are 2-2, and the two teams they’ve beaten have combined for one win. Their two losses have been humiliating, which has become the norm over the last 10 games in LaFleur’s tenure.
They’re undisciplined, with their penalties and penalty yards on pace to set a dubious NFL record . The offense looks like it doesn’t have anything to hang its hat on. Not all of that is LaFleur’s fault; he can only work with what he is given by his general manager.
It’s also true that after two years of going out of their way to not play Jacob Monk in any capacity, the Packers installed him as a starter at right guard early in training camp and never looked back.
Monk was arguably the worst preferred starter that LaFleur and his staff have put on the field during his tenure. Decision-making along the offensive line has been a bugaboo for years for LaFleur, but this one nearly got his quarterback killed.
A lot of the bad traits that have reared their ugly head under LaFleur still exist. The Packers gave up at least 17 unanswered points in each of the first three games. They were able to dig out of that against a bad Jets team, but were blown away by the Vikings and Falcons.
Now, LaFleur is set to face his nemesis on Sunday with Ben Johnson coming to town. Johnson is playing without his starting quarterback, but made it clear to his team what week it was after it knocked off the Jets on Sunday.
LaFleur is not engaging in any back-and-forth banter , but it’s clear his team needs to win. Furthermore, they need to start looking like a functional offense.
For all the talent that is on Green Bay’s offense, they have not scored more than 22 points in a game this season. They are 27th in points, 32nd on third down and 32nd in rushing.
His track record on offense is presumably a big reason why the Packers kept him despite last season’s failure.
It’s early, and LaFleur will be given time to turn the season around. For now, the Packers look a lot like a team who should have moved on from their head coach, but did not.
The worst unit on the team by far to start the season was the offensive line coached by Luke Butkus. Jordan Love took a whopping 31 hits in three games. Everyone was a culprit. It did not matter who the Packers played on the interior, they all…

title: Packers Make Predictable Roster Moves (Along With a Telling One)
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – In the wake of Edgerrin Cooper’s torn Achilles, the Green Bay Packers placed their star linebacker on injured reserve on Tuesday and promoted fellow linebacker Kristian Welch from the practice squad.
Cooper had three sacks, six tackles for losses and 30 tackles in about three-and-a-half games. Of the 20 players with at least three sacks, Cooper was the only player who was not an edge rusher or defensive tackle. He also has more tackles than any player with three-plus sacks; Houston’s Will Anderson (23) is the only other player with 20-plus tackles.
It’s not just the rudimentary stats.
Aaron Schatz has a stat called “defeats” that measures turnovers, tackles for losses and any other play that prevents the opponent from moving the chains on third or fourth down. Cooper has 12 defeats; only Anderson with 13 has more.
2026 leaders in Defeats (TO, TFL, and plays to prevent conversion on 3/4 down) 13: W.Anderson HOU 12: E.Cooper GB 10: Z.Baun PHI, N.Dean LV, D.Lloyd CAR, J.Rodriguez MIA, G.Rousseau BUF, D.Tranquill KC, T.Watt PIT DB leaders 9: K.Hamilton BAL, M.Harris TEN
How will the Packers pivot beyond simply plugging Isaiah McDuffie or Ty’Ron Hopper into the lineup?
“I think in my brain: Who do we have? Who are we playing? How do we deploy them to affect the game in a positive way?” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said on Tuesday. “That’s always my standard-issue answer to those questions, and hopefully you guys see it’s really not lip service.
“We try to do that as much as we can if it can impact the defense, too. I’m all about individuals, but it can’t get other guys stressed out with what you’re asking them to do as well. Football is the greatest game in the world because it’s 11 guys out there, and everyone’s got to do their job at a high level to have success. It’s more about the collective unit doing a good job.”
The promotion of Kristian Welch from the practice squad won’t do anything to replace Cooper. However, it will take the sting out of special teams coordinator Cam Achord probably losing Isaiah McDuffie from his units.
McDuffie, who was voted the team’s captain on special teams, leads the kick-coverage units with four tackles. If he’s going to be an every-down player on defense, then he can’t be a core player on special teams.
“I think we’re still going through all that right now, but I think as is any position, you’ve got to go through the depth, and that’s why we work to get so many guys ready to go,” Achord said. “That’s a credit to other players being ready to go. Other guys had to step up in that game just the other day.
“That’s why we work more guys at positions throughout the week, is if someone goes down, it’s not one guy, it’s multiple units. Is it four phases, five, six, whatever it is depending on the position, so you’ve got to work multiple guys throughout the week.”
Welch is a proven player on special teams. The native of Iola, Wis., is in his seventh NFL season. He’s played 1,498 snaps on special teams and 99 snaps on defense, according to Pro Football Reference.
“Yeah, anytime you’ve got a veteran like that who’s done it at a high level, especially in the kicking game – he’s already played one game for us – so there’s some comfort there,” Achord said. “He does a tremendous job. We challenge those guys every week to be ready to go, because you don’t know when something’s going to happen. Does it happen during the game? Does it happen Wednesday, Thursday or Friday? Somebody gets sick on a Saturday morning.
“So, I think our guys do a really good job – not just the guys who are on the 53, but the practice squad guys. You’ve got to challenge those guys to be ready to go. Because when your number gets called, that’s your opportunity. We try to, as a coaching staff, to get all those practice guys involved, and they know what roles they may have to play if they’re called upon.”
The Packers still have an open spot on their 53-man roster, with Warren Brinson going on injured reserve on Saturday.
The other transaction made by the Packers on Tuesday was bringing back running back Damon Bankston to the practice squad. He signed to the practice squad on Sept. 8 and was released on Sept. 29.
This is a noteworthy move. Running back Chris Brooks started on Sunday at Tampa Bay but dropped out with an ankle injury in the first half. Coach Matt LaFleur on Monday said the team was doing testing to figure out the severity.
If Brooks potentially is going to miss some time – whether it’s one game or one month – the Packers probably will be giving a chance to Pierre Strong, either on the 53-man roster or as a practice-squad elevation. If the Packers are going to be counting on Strong to play in the games, he can’t be taking the scout-team reps at practice.
Hence, the importance of this move.
This is actually Bankston’s third time with the Packers. He had a predraft visit with Green Bay but chose to sign with the Giants after going undrafted.
“I had brought it down to three teams which was the Giants, the Packers and the Raiders,” Bankston told KRQE . “Out of those three, I just thought the Giants were the best fit for me to make an impact right away. This type of opportunity I’ve been waiting for pretty much my whole life and right now I’m just focused on taking advantage of it.”

title: Packers-Bears ‘Is About Players,’ And That’s Where Coaches See Challenges
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – After Ben Johnson’s Chicago Bears shocked the Green Bay Packers in last year’s playoffs, he excitedly told his players in the postgame locker room, “F*** the Packers.”
Packers coach Matt LaFleur wasn’t going to add any gasoline to the fire.
“Because this game is about players, and so we’ll keep it about the players,” he said on Monday. “You know, I’m not the one out there playing, so I think that’s always been my mentality, and we’re going to keep it about those guys.”
The Packers have enough problems with the war between the lines to not have to wrestle with a war of words between the coaches. The Packers are struggling, obviously, with a 2-2 record. Their two wins have come against teams with a combined 1-7 record.
Just as obviously, the Bears are good. Really good. They are 3-1, with their last two wins coming with a backup-to-the-backup quarterback and a backup quarterback.
The coordinators in their weekly conversation with reporters at Lambeau Field on Tuesday outlined the challenge they’ll face on Sunday at Lambeau Field.
The Bears, allegedly, were supposed to have one of the worst defenses in the NFL. They were saved last year only by an abundance of takeaways.
Well, the Bears entered this week ranked fourth in points allowed. They are third in passing yards allowed per game, second in sack percentage, ninth in interception percentage, second on third down and 10th in the red zone.
It’s not the 1985 Bears. It’s also not the 2025 Bears.
“Really good defense,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “They can test you on the edges with their DBs. They’re going to have an extra hat in the box a lot of times in the run game. They’re physical up front. They do a nice job of playing their gaps, being physical.
“They’re a well-coordinated defense. They do a nice job tying their secondary with their linebackers and their front, just making it hard for you to run the ball. In the pass game, again, they’re going to contest you and they have some really good players.”
The Packers were rolling to a wild-card blowout last year with a 21-3 halftime lead. But they punted on each of their first four possessions of the second half with one first down gained and 9 net yards. Jordan Love was under siege throughout the second half, and the Packers couldn’t find answers to stop the avalanche.
Stenavich watched that film “many times.” While there are new players, Dennis Allen is back as defensive coordinator.
“When you get done with it, you watch it a few times just to see what you can do in the future to improve,” Stenavich said. “As the offseason went, once you get into your Bears prep, you come back to it and just see anything that you didn’t catch the first time or first or second. So, yeah, watched it a few times.”
Chicago is coming off a 23-12 win against the Jets. Green Bay’s defense played well in its Week 2 win at New York. Chicago’s defense dominated in its Week 4 win at Soldier Field, limiting the Jets to seven first downs, 0-for-7 on third down and 157 total yards.
Dayo Odeyingbo leads the team with three sacks. Austin Booker and Montez Sweat have two apiece. Rookie first-round safety Dillon Thieneman and rookie fourth-round cornerback Malik Muhammad each have one interception.
Star quarterback Caleb Williams will miss a third game with a hamstring injury. Tyson Bagent will be the quarterback for a second consecutive week.
Bagent has a fleet of quality pass catchers, but it’s the run game that powers the engine.
When the Packers beat the Jets, Kaleb Johnson, MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks combined for 18 rushes for 63 yards (3.5 average). The Bears bludgeoned that same Jets defense for 232 yards on 54 carries, a 4.3-yard average lowered by Bagent kneeling out the clock. Kyle Monangai led the way with 146 yards (4.9 average) and two touchdowns.
“Time of possession was like 42 to 18 or something like that,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said. “It’s a really good offense, man. Ben does an unbelievable job. I think his coaches do an unbelievable job of getting their guys to schematically execute, technically execute plays the right way.
“They block really well, they run really well, they throw and catch really well. And he puts them in positions to put the defense at a disadvantage. That’s why he is who he is. So, we’ve got a big-time challenge. We got to play good, sound football. But I always say, it’s always going to come down to the fundamentals of the game, and we’ve got to do those at a high level.”
It’s also going to come down to replacing star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper. He’s been the team’s most impactful defensive player, especially in key moments.
2026 leaders in Defeats (TO, TFL, and plays to prevent conversion on 3/4 down) 13: W.Anderson HOU 12: E.Cooper GB 10: Z.Baun PHI, N.Dean LV, D.Lloyd CAR, J.Rodriguez MIA, G.Rousseau BUF, D.Tranquill KC, T.Watt PIT DB leaders 9: K.Hamilton BAL, M.Harris TEN
“He’s a really good player, can do a lot of things for us, as you guys have seen through four weeks,” Gannon said. “My heart hurts for him. Nobody wants to be out for the year.
“This might sound cold but, to me, it’s kind of a known-unknown. You know guys are going to get injured. You don’t know who and you don’t know how long it’s going to be. With him, it’s a tough break. Hard to replace a guy like that obviously, but we’ve got to collectively do a good job.”
The Packers signed Skyy Moore in free agency to give the special teams a lift. The Bears did the same thing when they signed Kalif Raymond away from the rival Lions.
Raymond has been a solid addition. In fact, on an offense with Rome Odunze and Luther Burden at receiver and Colston Loveland in the slot, it’s Raymond who leads the team in receptions.
On special teams, Raymond is averaging 10.5 yards per punt return. With the Lions, he had punt-return touchdowns in 2022, 2024 (when he was a second-team All-Pro) and 2025.
“That’s going to be a great challenge for our coverage units,” special teams coordinator Cam Achord said. “Obviously, the punting game, he’s done it in this league at a very high level. Obviously, in this division, particularly, at a very high level. We’ve got to do a great job spreading the field, getting out there covering, and it’s up to everybody. It’s all 11 out there.”
Punter Daniel Whelan is sixth in the NFL with a 44.4-yard net average and first with 12 inside-the-20 punts.
“He’s a tremendous weapon for our team,” Achord said. “When he’s at the top of his game, I don’t know that there’s anyone better.”

title: Packers-Bears Matchups: Does Green Bay Have Any Advantages?
full_text:
Last year, the Green Bay Packers’ season ended at Soldier Field against the Chicago Bears. The Bears overcame a 21-3 halftime deficit to knock the Packers out of the playoffs, then had plenty to say after the fact.
Bears coach Ben Johnson has had a lot to say about the Packers and coach Matt LaFleur, which is something that LaFleur has said he’s not going to engage in this week. Why not?
“Because this game is about players and so we’ll keep it about the players,” LaFleur said on Monday. “I’m not the one out there they’re playing. Don’t get me wrong. I love the rivalry. It’s awesome. It’s great. It’s intense. You can feel it on gameday.
“You can feel it throughout the course of the week and also the significance – I mean, they’re the defending North champions. So what a great opportunity, great challenge for us in our home stadium to play against the defending champs.”
Will LaFleur’s passive approach to that situation work? Who knows. The Packers have lost three of the last four games against Chicago, including the last two. The Bears have not won three games in a row against Green Bay since 2005-06. The Packers went 4-12 in 2005 and were swept by the Bears. They lost the season opener in 2006, 26-0 in Mike McCarthy’s head coaching debut.
It’s been a long time, but the Bears have a chance to get their third in a row this weekend. Can they?
Here is a look at the matchups for Sunday’s showdown.
No Caleb Williams, no problem? That’s an exaggeration, of course. Williams is more talented than Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent, the latter of whom will start this week against Green Bay.
Through two games, however, Chicago’s offense has been just fine without Williams the past two weeks. Keenum played the game of his life against the Eagles in a Week 3 blowout victory. Bagent threw for 268 yards against the Jets on Sunday.
Green Bay’s pass defense is better than the Jets, but how are they going to rebound without Edgerrin Cooper in the lineup? When Cooper left the field during last year’s wild-card loss, that is when Chicago’s comeback attempt started.
Their two big tight ends, Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland, could have some favorable matchups in coverage against Zaire Franklin and Isaiah McDuffie.
Brandon Cisse left the end of the Tampa Bay game with a neck injury. Will he be good to go on Sunday? If not, Johnson found ways to exploit Carrington Valentine and Keisean Nixon last year.
The Bears have quality targets. While Luther Burden (second round, 2025) and Rome Odunze (first round, 2024) are the big-name players, 5-foot-9 Kalif Ramond leads the team with 21 catches, including a 41-yard touchdown. All three have more than 200 receiving yards.
Yes, it’s a backup quarterback, but the Packers are walking wounded into Lambeau. Unless their pass rush, which has run hot and cold, makes Bagent uncomfortable – the Bears have allowed two sacks the last two games – Green Bay’s defense could struggle.
For all the fanfare that Ben Johnson gets about the explosive plays he can create and dial up in the passing game, it’s his work in the run game that has been the most impressive. His run game when he was the offensive coordinator in Detroit was excellent, spearheaded by David Montgomery and Jahmyr Gibbs. He’s brought that over to Chicago with D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai.
Chicago leads the league in rushing at 196.3 yards per game. The next-closest team is Atlanta, which employs Bijan Robinson, who ran for 194 yards against the Packers in Week 3. The Bears ran for 232 yards against the Jets. They have four games of 230-plus rushing yards since the start of last season; no other team has more than two.
Green Bay has been good against the run in three out of its four games. It was not good at all against Atlanta two weeks ago, and Chicago’s rushing attack is better.
Coupled with the loss of Edgerrin Cooper, Green Bay is going to need to find some answers in the spine of their defense or the Bears could run wild at Lambeau Field.
Coming into the season, Chicago’s defense was supposed to be a major question mark. When it gave up a bucket of points to Carolina in the first week of the season, those questions only got louder.
Since then, however, the Bears have responded nicely. That comes with the caveat of facing Geno Smith and Carson Wentz in two of those games. Their other game in that stretch was against an Eagles offense that is a mess at the moment.
Chicago is ranked third in the NFL in passing yards allowed per game. It has 10 sacks in four games. Dennis Allen did a good job last season of confusing Matt LaFleur and Jordan Love, especially in the second half of the playoff game. The Packers have struggled mightily against pressure packages.
If Love has time, and that’s a big if, there are plays to be made against Chicago’s secondary. Christian Watson, in particular, has played well against Chicago, lighting them on fire last year at Lambeau Field for two touchdowns.
Will Love have time? That’s the million-dollar question.
Green Bay’s run game was better last week at Tampa Bay, but it was still bad. Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd put the ball on the ground, which prompted Matt LaFleur to threaten benching them in his postgame press conference.
Chris Brooks, who was their starting lineup against the Buccaneers, might be out this week with an ankle injury. He had a 27-yard run last week and is their trusted pass-protecting back.
Chicago is in the top half of the league in rush yards allowed, giving up 102.5 yards per game, but just 29th with 4.94 yards allowed per carry. The Packers got long runs by Johnson (31 yards) and Brooks (27), but their backs gained 27 yards on 17 carries otherwise.
Until Green Bay shows any sort of life consistently, it’s not going to have an advantage in this phase of the game.
Cairo Santos has been a thorn in Green Bay’s side since making a game-winning field goal to knock them off in the finale of the 2024 season at Lambeau Field. Santos making his kicks versus Brandon McManus missing them was arguably the difference in last year’s wild-card game.
In the return game, Zavion Thomas has been the primary kickoff returner and Kalif Raymond has handled punts. The Bears are last in the league in kickoff-return average but 13th in punt returns Raymond returned punts for touchdowns for the Lions in 2022, 2024 and 2025. Raymond is averaging 10.5 yards per runback this season.
The Packers’ return game has had a spark this year with Skyy Moore, despite him being quiet over the last two weeks.
Trey Smack has proven to be a weapon. For the first time in a long time, the Packers have an advantage over Chicago in the third phase of the game.

title: Did Packers’ Win Provide a Bump in Our Week 5 Consensus NFL Power Rankings?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – What does an ugly win mean in the eyes of the NFL beholders?
The Green Bay Packers rank 24th in the Packers On SI Consensus NFL Power Rankings after Week 4. That’s where they were last week, as well.
What are the Consensus Power Rankings? We take eight sets of national power rankings and turn them into one ultra-powerful power ranking.
The Packers moved up in five rankings, moved down in two and were steady in the other.
There’s a new No. 1 team with the San Francisco 49ers moving into the top spot. They are followed by the Kansas City Chiefs, Seattle Seahawks and Jacksonville Jaguars. Last week’s No. 1 team, the Buffalo Bills, fell to fifth.
The Packers, who have beaten the No. 28 Jets and No. 30 Buccaneers, will host the sixth-ranked Chicago Bears on Sunday.
Here’s where you’ll find the Packers in the national power rankings, with more extensive analysis available by following the links.
Conor Orr kept the Packers at No. 22 in his rankings. He noted the direction of the teams in this week’s matchups.
“Matt LaFleur trying to simply get his house in order while Ben Johnson constructs three-dimensional mindgames through the media is such an incredible subplot to this game on Sunday. I’ve written it before , but this is the kind of antagonist this league desperately needs.”
Mike Florio moved the Packers up two spots in his rankings, even though he wrote, “It never felt like they truly wanted to beat the Buccaneers.”
The Packers are up four spots from No. 27 in the rankings selected by Chad Graff and Josh Kendall.
“The Packers are not feeling good even though they’re coming off a win. They still can’t run the ball, and the whole offense looks disjointed. And what’s looming? A visit from their bitter rivals that could really put a damper on this already frustrating season.”
The Packers slipped three spots from No. 20 in the rankings voted on by ESPN’s team beat writers.
This week’s theme was four words to describe the first four weeks. Rob Demovsky wrote “Help wanted: RBs apply.” He noted the team’s worst-in-the-league running game and fumble problems.
“Without Josh Jacobs and with an offensive line in flux, the Packers haven't been able to run the ball. They're last in the league in rushing yards per game (58), and they haven't scored a rushing touchdown yet. There were some signs of life Sunday, but Chris Brooks left because of an ankle injury and both Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd fumbled.”
Then, Demovsky quoted coach Matt LaFleur on the fumbles: “‘I think a great teacher's the bench.’ … The problem is he doesn't have any other options at this point.”
The Packers moved up one notch in Frank Schwab rankings. “A win is a win,” he noted, while pointing out the Packers had to hold off a rookie quarterback in the waning moments.
“Green Bay comes home and plays the Bears in Week 5, a game that was flexed out of the late-afternoon time slot in part because of Caleb Williams' injury but also because the Packers aren't that interesting. A third straight loss to the Bears, including last season's horrid collapse in the wild-card round, will have Green Bay fans again calling for LaFleur's job.”
The Packers won but fell two spots in Pete Prisco’s rankings.
“It wasn't pretty against the Bucs, especially with two bad turnovers, but they found a way. The heat is off Matt LaFleur for now but here come the dreaded Bears.”
The Packers inched up one spot in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings, who noted the team’s two wins have come against bottom-feeder teams.
“Is it time to start talking about head coach Matt LaFleur’s job security yet? The Packers barely hung on to beat a decimated Bucs team that is playing worse football than almost any team in the league, and that came two weeks after they needed overtime and an Aaron Glenn brain freeze to squeak by the Jets.”
The Packers moved up one spot in Nick Shook’s rankings. He noted the Packers won the game but lost star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper to a torn Achilles.
“The Packers won on Sunday, which is nice. It was an ugly one and included the loss of linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (for the season), but at least Green Bay held off the angry mob for a week. The rushing attack was a little bit better (finally), taking some pressure off Jordan Love, but this is still far from the product we expected from the Packers.”
The Bears are fourth in Fox’s rankings. They won their last two games without injured quarterback Caleb Williams, though he’s the player who brings the “extra dimension” to make them a Super Bowl contender.
“They outgained the Jets 492 yards to 157 (232-59 on the ground), but replacement QB Tyson Bagent had trouble getting the Bears in the end zone,” wrote Ralph Vacchiano. “Clearly, they’re not the same team without QB Caleb Williams, so this lofty place in the rankings presumes he’ll be back relatively soon.”

title: Packers’ Options to Replace Edgerrin Cooper Range from Backups to Legend
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers suffered a devastating blow on Sunday when linebacker Edgerrin Cooper sustained a torn Achilles during the victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
“He’s a tough one to lose,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “We all saw what he was able to do in basically a half of football and the player that he is. My heart hurts for him and his recovery and what he’s going through, but it’s an opportunity for those other guys.”
Those “other guys” are headlined by the backup linebackers, Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper. Linebacker was arguably the deepest position on the roster. That depth will be tested for the rest of the season.
“McDuffie’s played a lot of great football for us,” LaFleur said. “I think Hopper’s shown really well. Those guys will get an opp.”
Here’s a closer look at the backup plans.
Knowing they couldn’t re-sign Quay Walker, the Packers pivoted by trading for Zaire Franklin. Franklin made an immediate impact on the field and in the locker room, so was appointed a team captain by his teammates.
He hasn’t done much in the games, though. Playing every defensive snap, he’s produced 29 tackles, including one tackle for loss. After playing second fiddle to Cooper for the first quarter of the season, he must step up his level of play considerably.
“We put a lot on his plate,” LaFleur said. “He directs traffic down there. I think he’s done an outstanding job, and I just love the guy, how engaged he is in the game, bringing everybody up, supporting his teammates. When the offense is out there, you see him standing up after they make the corrections, he’s supporting the offense … He’s been a great leader for us and he does a great job of getting all 11 on the same page.”
That’s noteworthy praise, to be sure. But there wasn’t a word about his performance.
Franklin is one of 60 linebackers to have played at least 150 defensive snaps. For what it’s worth, Franklin is 58th in PFF’s grades. Cooper, who had three sacks and six tackles for losses, made his average tackle 1.3 yards downfield and allowed 5.3 yards per target, according to Sports Info Solutions. Franklin’s average tackle has come 3.7 yards downfield and he’s allowing 9.5 yards per target.
When Cooper was injured, the next man up was Isaiah McDuffie.
McDuffie is as solid as they come as far as backup linebackers go. In the old 4-3 scheme, he typically was the third linebacker. A sixth-round pick in 2021, he started one game his first two seasons but eight in 2023, all 17 in 2024 and 12 last season.
“It’s just having that next-man-up mentality,” he told reporters after the game. “At the end of the day, I got to have his back. That’s what he would want. He would want us to go out there and get the dub for him so, at the end of the day, we’re a unit, we’re a room, and we rely on each other, and it’s always that next-man-up mentality.”
McDuffie is a productive tackler with 86 tackles in 2023, 97 in 2024 and 92 in 2026, but he’s not a big-play performer with career totals off two sacks, 12 tackles for losses, one forced fumble, zero interceptions and five passes defensed.
The Packers drafted Cooper in the second round in 2024. In the third round, they drafted Ty’Ron Hopper.
He’s missed one game in his career – this year’s opener – but hasn’t had many opportunities on defense with 156 career snaps.
“Everything,” LaFleur said of where he’s improved. “From technique, his footwork, his ability to diagnose plays, and go out there and play winning football. So, I think he’s done a great job. I think Sam (Siefkes) does a great job with the linebackers and every year we’ve seen Hop get better and better and better.”
While McDuffie is a steady, sturdy commodity, is there more big-play upside with Hopper?
Obviously, Kristian Welch isn’t going to be a factor on defense but he almost certainly will be added to the 53-man roster from the practice squad.
The native of Iola, Wis., entered the NFL in 2020, He’s played 1,498 snaps on special teams and 99 on defense. In 23 career games with the Packers, he’s played two snaps on defense.
The Packers, at their core, are a draft-and-develop franchise. They drafted McDuffie and Hopper and developed them into the players they are today. Presumably, the Packers will go forward with that duo.
However, general manager Brian Gutekunst went out and signed two veteran guards last week, 36-year-old Kevin Zeitler and 34-year-old Laken Tomlinson. Those were out-of-character transactions by Gutekunst but also a sign that desperate times require desperate measures.
Are these desperate times? That’s what the Packers will have to contemplate.
Bobby Wagner is 36 and – by far – the best free agent. From 2014 through 2024, he was a first- or second-team All-Pro for 11 consecutive seasons. He spent the last two years with the Commanders. In 2024, he started all 17 games and had 132 tackles, two sacks, 10 tackles for losses and four passes defensed. In 2025, he started all 17 games and had 162 tackles, 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for losses and four passes defensed.
In a sensational 14-year career, he had missed nine games before watching the start to this season from his house.
Whether he wants to play at all is unknown – former teammate Von Miller didn’t think so.
“If he wanted to play football, he'd be on the team,” Miller told The Dallas Sports Journal . “He's a man of many talents. He went and got his master's degree during the season last year. If he wanted to be on the team, he would. I think it's probably something else that he's doing right now.”
It might be worth an exploratory call to the future Hall of Famer to gauge his interest in eventually pairing with Micah Parsons to make a run at the playoffs – and beyond.

title: Victory Monday Fact or Fiction: Packers’ Season Is Lost Despite Beating Bucs
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The old ABC Wide World of Sports slogan was, “The thrill of victory and the agony of defeat.”
There was no thrill of victory for the Green Bay Packers after edging the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Only the muted feeling of another lackluster performance, the agony felt by linebacker Edgerrin Cooper following his torn Achilles and the anguish felt by teammates knowing what that injury meant to the rest of the team.
How will the Packers pick up the pieces without their star linebacker?
“Yeah, I don’t know, Pete,” coach Matt LaFleur said to Pete Dougherty of The Green Bay Press-Gazette after the game. It was an atypically short answer, a combination of equal parts frustration over the way his team played and honesty in knowing there’s no way to replace Cooper.
At least he didn’t utter the next-man-up nonsense. No offense to Isaiah McDuffie, who probably is one of the better backup linebackers in the NFL. There’s just no way any player can replace Cooper, a chess-piece defender for coordinator Jonathan Gannon.
The reality, of course, is there’s no next man up for Cooper. It’s going to take the other 52 players on the roster, all playing harder and better, to pick up the slack.
Let's take a closer look at the Packers' predicament in this week's Fact or Fiction.
Cooper was Gannon’s best option in replacing Micah Parsons to start the season. He leads the team with three sacks and six tackles for losses. He’s second with 30 tackles. In just more than one half of work against the Buccaneers, he had one sack on the opening possession and an interception to end the half. He had a team-high nine tackles while playing barely more than 50 percent of the snaps.
That dynamic skill-set was a reason why the defense was able to adapt as well as it did without Parsons.
On Saturday, NFL insider Tom Pelissero reported that Parsons probably won’t play in a game until November . A peek at the schedule shows there are four games between now and November. Those games are against:
The Chicago Bears, who have won back-to-back games with backup quarterbacks. They are first in the NFL in total offense and ninth in scoring.
The Dallas Cowboys, who are tied for second in the NFL in scoring and are fifth on third down behind the high-flying combination of Dak Prescott throwing to George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb.
The Detroit Lions, who are fifth in the NFL in scoring and sixth in total offense behind the elite combination of quarterback Jared Goff, running back Jahmyr Gibbs and receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams.
The Carolina Panthers, who are fourth in the NFL in scoring and total offense with rising quarterback Bryce Young and big-time receiver Tetairoa McMillan.
Can Green Bay’s defense, which has played well enough for the team to be 3-1, somehow stop those offenses without one of the best pass rushers in football and one of the game’s top linebackers?
That seems like almost an impossible mission. Cooper is ninth in the NFL in sacks. Of the eight players ahead of him, he’s No. 1 with 30 tackles and one of only two players with an interception. He is a field-tilting player, whether it’s stopping the run, dropping into coverage or rushing off the edge.
If the defense is going to suffer without Cooper, which would be the predictable result, then it will be up to the offense to pick up the slack.
Matt LaFleur is the offensive mastermind given a new contract. Jordan Love is one of the highest-paid quarterbacks in the NFL.
And yet, the offense, in a word, stinks.
The Packers are 27th with 18.3 points per game. They entered the week ranked last in the NFL in third-down conversions at about 27 percent. They actually performed worse on Sunday at 20.0 percent.
After their best day of the season, the Packers are still last in the NFL with 58.0 rushing yards per game and 31st with 3.2 rushing yards per attempt.
The Packers are last in the NFL with 2.5 fumbles per game. Jordan Love has been victimized by the most drops and the highest drop percentage. They have been guilty of the second-most holding penalties and the fifth-most pre-snap penalties on offense.
“There was some positive things, but we’re never going to be satisfied with scoring 17 points in the game,” LaFleur said. “That’s just not to our standard and we’ve got to find ways when we have opportunities in the red area to convert. We can’t be turning the ball over, can’t have penalties.
“That is a stingy defense … but I also think that we also have to clean up a lot of stuff. Like, too many penalties (and) turnovers. Ball-carriers have got to hold onto the ball. We put the ball on the ground way too much. And this stuff’s got to get fixed, and it’s got to get fixed now.
Now, with the rival Bears next on the schedule, would be good timing.
If the blockers learn how to block without holding, if the linemen can learn the snap count, if the backs can hold onto the ball, if the receivers can catch the ball then, yes, the Packers have a chance. A real chance.
The addition of Laken Tomlinson at left guard paid dividends against the Bucs, and the addition of Kevin Zeitler at right guard should do the same. This could quickly become a decent offensive line, which might not sound like a tremendous compliment until you remember Love getting knocked into the middle of next week by unblocked defenders the first few games.
Love has shown he can be a high-level quarterback. Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft are legit weapons. Maybe the line will rescue the running game.
There’s just too many “maybes” and “ifs” to believe the Packers can save their season. Sure, they could wind up being playoff contenders heading into January, but nobody should be satisfied with another nine-win season and one-and-done playoffs.
This is Titletown, after all. It’s not Seventh Seed City or Playoff Bubble Boulevard.
“We won, but it’s the same thing I said after the Jets game,” said tight end Tucker Kraft, who dropped what should have been an easy touchdown catch. “We’re still out there making [mistakes]. We’re excited, we’re happy, winning on the road is hard. But we’re still beating ourselves up.”
Between Cooper’s torn Achilles and the self-inflicted black eyes, the Packers look like a team that’s on the ropes.
For the coaches and high-priced players who remain healthy, it’s time to put up or shut up. Learn the snap count. Hang onto the ball. If they can’t do the simple things, how on earth are they going to do the hard things necessary to beat the really good teams coming up on the schedule?
Verdict: Fact, unless the Packers really can get things “fixed now.”

title: Three Overreactions From Packers’ Win Over Buccaneers Include Pain, Slop
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – A win is a win. The Green Bay Packers took care of business, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 17-14 on Sunday.
It was a huge win, let’s make that clear. The distance between 2-2 and 1-3 is one game in the standings but miles apart in reality. However, speaking of reality, a reality check is coming.
The Packers’ two wins have come against teams with one win. Their four games have come against teams with six wins. The FCS portion of the schedule is over. The big boys are coming.
Let’s dive in with this week’s Overreactions.
Leave it to center Sean Rhyan to provide the real talk.
Asked about Edgerrin Cooper’s Achilles injury, Rhyan said: “We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse, it seems like.”
There’s no such thing as curses. Right? Well, here’s the season-ending carnage from the last 11 months.
From 2025: Tight end Tucker Kraft’s torn ACL, center Elgton Jenkins’ broken leg with ligament damage, defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt’s broken leg with ligament damage, right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele’s partially torn patellar tendon, edge rusher Micah Parsons’ torn ACL.
From 2026: Receiver Jayden Reed’s neck injury, Bako-Bewele’s complete tear of the same patellar tendon and, now linebacker Edgerrin Cooper’s torn Achilles.
Those are just the big-name players. It seems like every injury is a major injury, whether it’s Warren Brinson slipping on the practice field or Cooper looking to see who tripped him following a noncontact injury on Sunday.
Statistically, the Packers weren’t especially injured last season. It’s just that they suffered some season-ending injuries to big-time players at about the worst possible time. This year, according to Rotowire’s weighted severity score , the Packers entered Week 4 ranked 10th in injuries.
Some injuries are easy to explain. Last year, Rhyan’s foot hit Kraft’s knee against Carolina. Brinson fell on Wyatt at Detroit. Other injuries are harder to explain because of their noncontact nature. Why did Parsons’ knee give out on him at Denver? Why did Cooper’s Achilles tear at Tampa Bay? Should Bako-Bewele have had a more extensive surgery last season in hopes of preventing this year’s injury? Who knows – that decision was made by the team and Bako-Bewele’s team using the best information available.
Everyone wants to know who to blame, and the answer is I don’t know. It would be impossible to figure out how much the Packers spend on their strength and conditioning program, let alone get those numbers from the other 31 teams to add some context. Money wouldn’t be the only measuring stick, anyway.
The Packers hired a new strength and conditioning staff in 2024, led by Aaron Hill, and he implemented some obvious changes in creating a more extensive and dynamic warm-up routine. The reality, though, is if there was one tried-and-true way for players to stay healthy, every team would be doing it. In last year’s NFLPA report card, the training room and staff got a C (the training room has since been updated, to Parsons’ approval ) and the strength coaches got a B.
Coach Matt LaFleur played his starters in the preseason based on a study that found that players who play in the preseason tend to be healthier in the regular season. Well, so much for that.
It would be easy to chalk it up to bad luck. Or a curse. Maybe the Packers really have just been unlucky and the Injury Gods will grace them for the rest of the decade.
What’s undeniable is injuries ruined last season – they were 9-3-1 entering the Denver game in which Parsons and Bako-Bewele went down – and probably have ruined this season, too. In our preseason roster rankings, which are based on skill and salary (rather than just skill), Parsons was second, Bako-Bewele was eighth, Cooper was 11th and Reed was 16th. They are critical players, and they’re all out of the lineup with major injuries.
How does a team that had a limited margin for error, anyway, overcome the losses of some of their best players? That seems impossible, especially with how the healthy players have performed.
The Packers really should have blown out the Buccaneers. Jordan Love vs. an undrafted rookie at quarterback? Especially Love with time in the pocket against a rookie quarterback? That’s an all-time mismatch.
Instead, the Packers held on for dear life because of their own inability to do elementary-level things.
The Packers were guilty of 10 penalties for 66 yards. The Buccaneers were guilty of only four penalties for 17 yards. This wasn’t one-sided refereeing, as you might argue was the case at Minnesota in Week 1. This was a one-sided lack of discipline.
“We’ve got to clean up the penalties,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “We’re stagnant right now, we’re moving backwards a lot of the time and not having positive plays and it’s putting us in some tough third-down situations.”
If you think that was a postgame comment, no, it wasn’t. That’s what Love said on Wednesday.
Good thing everyone was listening to the captain’s message.
The Packers have been guilty of 48 total penalties and 42 accepted penalties. Only the Browns with 51 and 43, respectively, have been guilty of more. By penalty yards, the Packers are first (or worst) with 344. There have been 17 pre-snap penalties and 10 holding penalties.
The NFL records for most penalties and yards in a season belong to the 2011 Raiders, who were guilty of 163 accepted infractions for 1,358 yards. This year’s Packers are on pace for 179 penalties for 1,462 yards. The franchise records are 135 penalties for 1,103 yards.
Plus, there were two red-zone fumbles – MarShawn Lloyd foolishly trying to run over Antoine Winfield and Kaleb Johnson at the goal line.
On offense, the Packers lead the NFL in fumbles and drops. On defense, they are second in first downs allowed by penalties.
“We also have to clean up a lot of stuff,” LaFleur said, rightly agitated after the game. “Like, too many penalties, turnovers. Ball-carriers have got to hold onto the ball. We put the ball on the ground way too much. And this stuff’s got to get fixed and it’s got to get fixed now.”
That sounds good, but will it actually happen? The reality is the Packers are an undisciplined team with no signs of progress. Penalties and fumbles are part of the game, but LaFleur’s team has an ongoing problem. At this point, the only Super Bowl that the Packers will be competing for is the Super Bowl of Slop.
The Packers are 2-2, which is probably what most of us were thinking at the start of the season by projecting a loss to the Vikings, a win at the Jets, a win over the Falcons and a loss to the Buccaneers. The path to 2-2 veered a bit, but they are .500.
But now what? The Bears are coming to town on Sunday; they are 3-1 and just won back-to-back games with backup quarterbacks. After that, they will host the Cowboys, who are 2-2 with a walk-off loss to the powerhouse Ravens. Then, it’s off to Detroit, which is 2-2 with a superb top of the roster. Then, it’s a short-week home game against the Panthers, who looked phenomenal on offense in beating the Lions to improve to 2-2.
It doesn’t get easier after that with a game at the Patriots (2-2 but reigning AFC champs), a home game against the undefeated Vikings (4-0), road games at the Rams (2-2 and Super Bowl favorites ) and Saints (1-2; host Atlanta on Monday), and home against Buffalo (3-1).
The Packers went 2-1 against the Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers, who have a combined record of 2-9. Those eight teams coming up have a combined record of 21-14.
The Packers had to hang on for dear life against the winless Bucs. An offense led by Jordan Love and Matt LaFleur ranks 27th with 18.3 points per game.
On the bright side, the offensive line was solid against the Bucs and should get better once Kevin Zeitler enters at right guard and the new front builds chemistry week after week. With time, Love can carve up defenses. If Love has time, Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft can make things happen.
Losing Edgerrin Cooper was a…

title: Snaps, Studs and Dud From Packers’ Win Over Buccaneers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wasn’t artistic but it was important. Over the last 10 years, teams that start 2-2 have a 41.0 percent chance of reaching the playoffs while teams that open 1-3 tumble to 14.5 percent.
So, it wasn’t pretty, but the 17-14 victory, which was powered in part by a new offensive line, was pretty important.
Here’s a look at the snaps along with a couple studs and one dud following a 17-14 victory.
The Packers played 60 snaps on offense against the Buccaneers.
Quarterback: Jordan Love played every snap. After taking a beating in the first three games – he had been on the receiving end of more quarterback hits than any player in the league – he was not sacked and hit only twice, according to the official stats.
Running backs: Last week against Atlanta, Kaleb Johnson outsnapped MarShawn Lloyd. Against Tampa Bay, Lloyd played 33 snaps, Johnson played 17 and Chris Brooks played 10. Brooks started and had an explosive run but missed most of the game with an injured ankle.
Johnson broke two tackles on his 31-yard run but fumbled for the second time in his three games. Lloyd caught a career-high five passes, including a 16-yarder that he punctuated with a hurdle, but also fumbled.
“I think a great teacher’s the bench,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “If guys don’t start holding onto the ball, they’re going to be sitting on the bench.”
That’s a great statement and we all know his point. But, from a practical perspective, it would have left the Packers with you or me playing running back.
Receivers: On a sweltering day, Matthew Golden played 53 snaps – by far the most of the group. Christian Watson played 41, followed by 23 for Skyy Moore, 11 for Bo Melton and two for J. Michael Sturdivant. Including the Jets game in which Jayden Reed was injured, it’s clear the Packers are opting for more of a player-for-player replacement in the slot with Moore than a committee approach.
Watson and Golden through three games were on a pace to blow by 3,000 combined receiving yards. The Bucs limited Watson to three catches for 47 yards and Golden to three catches for 21 yards. Golden caught a touchdown pass but had a drop that was oh-so-close to being a fumble. He has a drop in every game, which is stunning considering how well he caught the ball in camp.
Tight ends: All is normal at tight end with Tucker Kraft playing all but five snaps. It was a typical workload from before last year’s ACL tear. Mark Redman’s value as a blocker is evident. That’s why he played a season-high 28 snaps. Josh Whyle, who was banished to special-teams work the past couple games, played 14 snaps, one more than Jonnu Smith.
Kraft had one touchdown catch but should have had two. His first two receptions were vintage run-after-catch plays. He finished with six catches for 42 yards; by our count, 41 yards came after the catch.
“My drop rate right now is terrible,” he said. “I’m on the JUGS. I’m trying to fix it. But I got to continue to press on my ball-catching ability because I can’t do anything with the rock if I don’t get it.”
Redman had a 25-yard catch and Smith had a 19-yard catch. Getting two explosive gains from the backups would be huge going forward.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line for this week went the distance. Travis Glover, who hadn’t played in a game since the 2024 playoffs, was the surprise starter at right guard and rewarded the team for its decision. Glover was never in the mix to be the starting right guard – the coaches went from Anthony Belton to Jacob Monk early in training camp and never changed direction – but clearly should have been.
Laken Tomlinson, who was signed last Saturday, deserves credit for being able to play every snap after not being in a training camp.
The line was guilty of four penalties (two by Tomlinson) and five pressures (three by Morgan). The run blocking was hit or miss. Take away the big runs by Johnson and Brooks, the other 17 carries by the backs gained 27 yards.
The Packers played 63 snaps on defense against the Buccaneers.
Defensive tackles: The Packers were shorthanded with Warren Brinson placed on injured reserve and Anthony Campbell out again with an ankle injury. Things only got worse after Devonte Wyatt left the game with an ankle injury.
Fortunately for the Packers, Wyatt returned, so the rest of the unit didn’t melt into a puddle at crunch time. As usual, Karl Brooks led the way with 35 snaps. Javon Hargrave was next with 29, followed by Wyatt with 25, Chris McClellan with 24 and Jonathan Ford with a season-low 13 as the Packers spent most of the game in nickel.
They combined for two solo tackles (one each by Wyatt and McClellan) and seven assisted tackles. Hargrave had the only quarterback hit in by far his best game of the season.
Edges: Lukas Van Ness, as usual, led from a snaps perspective with 46. A week after playing less than backup Dani Dennis-Sutton, Barryn Sorrell was second with 33 snaps. Dennis-Sutton and Brenton Cox played 24 apiece.
Van Ness had three pressures but couldn’t make the play on two potential sacks. Cox went from 0 to 100 in 0.5 seconds when he saw a bad shotgun snap and almost took down Jalon Daniels for a safety.
Linebackers: Zaire Franklin played every snap. He’s going to have to step up big time following Edgerrin Cooper’s Achilles injury. Is he capable? The eight tackles were solid from a box-score perspective.
Cooper dominated in what probably were the final 34 snaps of his season. He led the team with nine tackles and added one sack and one interception. Isaiah McDuffie played 25 snaps and Ty’Ron Hopper played five snaps when McDuffie was being checked with an injury.
Cooper’s injury doesn’t only impact the defense. McDuffie is a core player on special teams, where he is the unit captain. How much can he play on special teams if he’s an every-down player on defense?
Hopper and Nick Niemann played a team-high 16 snaps on special teams apiece, followed by McDuffie with 14.
Cornerbacks: Keisean Nixon played all 63 snaps and Brandon Cisse played 54 before dropping out late to be evaluated for a concussion. Carrington Valentine, not Benjamin St-Juste, was the next man up.
Nixon made one of the big plays of the game when he blew up a receiver screen for a loss of 3 on Tampa Bay’s second-to-last series. It was a relatively easy day, given the quarterback, but Nixon was excellent.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams went the distance – they’ve played every snap this season – and Javon Bullard played a season-high 60. Including special teams, Williams has played a team-high 305 snaps this season.
There’s no getting around the enormity of Cooper’s injury. He’s been arguably the team’s best player this season and was on his way to establishing himself as one of the best linebackers in the NFL. In three-and-a-half games, he had three sacks and six tackles for losses – more than he had all of last season.
Cooper had a third-down sack on the first possession and an interception just before halftime. The Packers wouldn’t have beaten the lowly Buccaneers without him; now they’ll have to somehow win the rest of the season without him.
“ We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse , it seems like,” center Sean Rhyan said.
Williams had a huge day, too. Tampa Bay’s second possession of the game crossed midfield when Williams made a spectacular interception on a pass intended for top receiver Emeka Egbuka. And then he played the role of closer with a second-down sack and fourth-down pressure.
“Hell of a game,” fellow safety Xavier McKinney said. “He can be really f***king good.”
A player who’s not “f***king good” is MarShawn Lloyd. There are glimmers. On Green Bay’s opening possession of the second half, which resulted in a touchdown, he turned a tackle for loss into a 5-yard gain on third-and-1. It was a low-key huge play. The hurdle on the 16-yard catch was impressive, as well.
However, he fumbled at the end of the play when he foolishly tried to run…

title: Texans Sign Undrafted QB to 53-Man Roster Heading Into Week 5
full_text:
The Houston Texans are making an addition to their quarterback room heading into their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans.
And it's actually a signal-caller they had in the building this season already, considering he was on the practice squad for two weeks.
According to the Texans' transaction log, the team is signing quarterback Mark Gronowski to the 53-man roster.
Gronowski was signed to the Texans' practice squad right before Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills last month, which came right after he was waived from the Miami Dolphins' roster, where he initially signed as a UDFA out of Iowa.
He'd spend two weeks with the Texans on the practice squad, was released after the events of Week 2, but in a short amount of time, now finds his way back to Houston in an even bigger capacity from where he left off last month.
Ironically, Gronowski’s college career before hitting the NFL as a UDFA rookie this season is a lot of what the Texans could benefit from this year: winning.
Gronowski is the all-time NCAA leader across all levels for total quarterback wins in a career. He won a 58 games between his time at both South Dakota State and Iowa, and has some pretty solid numbers in the process.
Gronowski had a college career completion percentage of 63.7% with over 12,000 total yards, 103 touchdowns, and 27 interceptions. He's also gained some noteworthy numbers on the ground, as he has over 500 carries for 2,312 yards and 53 rushing touchdowns.
That dual-threat ability is really what makes Gronowski shine. It was enough for the Texans to give him a spot on the practice squad to start the season, and now just about a month later, he now becomes QB3 on the 53-man roster behind C.J. Stroud and Davis Mills .
The Texans walked into this season with the expectation of having a select three quarterbacks on their roster: that was C.J. Stroud, Davis Mills, and Graham Mertz.
However, it wouldn't take long into the new year for those plans to change within the quarterback room. Graham Mertz suffered a torn ACL in the Texans' first preseason game vs. the LA Chargers, was ruled out for the season, and thus slimmed this quarterback room to two names heading into Week 1.
That two-man setup within a quarterback room that the Texans had for the first four weeks of the season isn't exactly uncommon in the NFL. But having that emergency third quarterback on the roster who can be called up in case of injury is always a nice layer of security to have.
So that's what the Texans are getting here: a third quarterback in Gronowski who will likely be inactive on most gamedays, work behind Stroud and Mills in practice as he had been in Weeks 1 and 2, and likely only get a chance to get on the field if an injury arises to either of the pair ahead of him on the depth chart.
Nonetheless, any player getting the call-up to a 53-man NFL roster is certainly a step in the right direction for their stock moving forward. So Gronowski undoubtedly walks into Week 5 as the biggest winner of anyone in this move.

title: Texans' Defense Could Solve Its Problems With This One Change
full_text:
The Houston Texans' defense––through the first four games of the 2026 season––has been a massive step below where they stood when wrapping up their previous campaign; a year in which many considered this group as the best defense in the NFL next to the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.
And now in part because of those defensive woes, which were most recently displayed in Week 4 against the Dallas Cowboys , the Texans now sit at a brutal 0-4 record.
So moving forward, seeing some type of change for this side of the ball could be recommended. Not a massive panic move, but something to flip the script defensively from what this team has seen through the last four weeks.
The easiest way for the Texans to try and flip the switch in a short amount of time? That might just be by giving head coach DeMeco Ryans primary defensive play-calling duties; a role he hasn't had since the start of the 2025 season when he handed that spot to defensive coordinator Matt Burke.
This isn't a spot that Ryans hasn't been in before. The Texans' fourth-year head coach, with a defensive-minded background, started his tenure in Houston controlling the defensive operations, while handing the offensive duties to then-Bobby Slowik, and now, Nick Caley .
But the Texans' coaching setup changed last year after Houston sunk to 0-3. Ryans handed over his defensive role to Burke, who would instead take more of a CEO role, and that led to the team finishing with a 12-5 record.
Naturally, the Texans entered this season with the same plan. Burke runs the defense, while Ryans oversees the whole project. But that's only led to Houston falling to an even deeper hole than they were in this time last year.
So at this point, why not make a similar change this time around, only to put Ryans in charge of the defense?
There is some good reason for the Texans to consider this, rather than simply making changes for the sake of doing so, because Ryans knows how to coach a defense.
Ryans led the Texans to a pair of top-half finishes through both 2023 and 2024 and a couple of playoff appearances when he was running the ship defensively.
He's also unlocked some of Houston's top talents on that side of the ball into what we know them as today, whether that be Kamari Lassiter and Jalen Pitre in their rookie seasons , coaching up Azeez Al-Shaair in his first season with the Texans, or helping Will Anderson Jr. en route to a Defensive Rookie of the Year award in 2023.
The numbers will tell you that Burke's defense from last season certainly produced better than Ryans' over his first two years in Houston. But over that stretch, this defensive unit has gotten better individually, built more chemistry collectively, and might set up for an easier task for Ryans to take on.
When Ryans was asked about the possibility of taking those duties after the Texans' Week 4 loss, he didn't exactly shoot the idea down. So perhaps it's something that's already being considered behind closed doors heading into this weekend against the Tennessee Titans.
Texans HC DeMeco Ryans was asked about the possibility of taking over defensive play calling duties from Matt Burke. #Texans #Sarge pic.twitter.com/LyJL5Ee4rP
The two key aspects that Ryans needs to get right? Limiting explosives and tuning up Houston's pass coverage. Houston's run defense has remained stout, pressure on opposing quarterbacks has remained mostly consistent, yet it's those two glaring holes in defending the pass that have left Houston's defense back at the drawing board like they are now.
This team certainly has the talent on that side of the ball to get it right, but might need a new mind leading the way for this group to really key in on their same successes seen from 2025. Maybe Ryans can be just that.
