title: 4 Texans Players Who Need a Big Week 5 vs. Titans Amid 0-4 Start
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into Week 5 desperate to cling onto their first win of the 2026 season––having lost their initial four games of the year as a few players on both sides of the ball have been a bit underwhelming for one way or another.
Which means, as Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans arrives for the Texans, those struggling players will have to pick up their slack to help change the narrative and get a win on their record books.
Let's take a look at four players in the Texans' lineup who need a big Week 5 against the Titans this weekend, and might just help Houston get over the hump for their first win:
The Texans' run game really just hasn't found any sense of life since their first outing against the Buffalo Bills, where David Montgomery hauled in three touchdowns with nearly 80 all-purpose yards throughout the day.
In the games that Montgomery has played since that three-touchdown debut, he's logged a total of 27 carries for 67 yards, coming out to less than 2.5 yards per carry throughout. That lack of efficiency and explosiveness has really put a damper on the ceiling of this ground game, and has even led to Woody Marks claiming close to 50% of the snaps in the backfield.
The Texans need a big game from Montgomery against a lackluster Titans team to back up their investment of a fourth-round pick and Juice Scruggs given up for him earlier this offseason. Because right now, it feels as if Houston would like to have that one back .
Another name on the Texans' offense who had a strong start to the year, yet has been a bit disappointing in recent weeks is tight end Dalton Schultz. In Week 2 against the Cincinnati Bengals, Schultz put together an impressive 12 catches for 140 yards without Nico Collins that inspired confidence in what the rest of his season could look like .
But the Texans haven't exactly involved Schultz, or any of their other tight ends on the roster, much at all through the past two games––really in a bit of a head-scratching decision from Houston's coaching staff.
From a broader perspective, the Texans could certainly benefit from giving more opportunities to more than just one of their tight ends. Yet, seeing a pass-catching threat like Schultz start clicking again would be a positive step forward for this offense.
We now have had two of the Texans' first four games on the calendar where cornerback Kamari Lassiter has had some of his most overwhelming games as an NFL pro.
In his first game against Buffalo, Lassiter allowed Josh Allen to have a perfect passer rating when he was targeted. Last week against the Dallas Cowboys, he allowed 136 yards and eight receptions on the 11 plays he was targeted on––a lot of which allowed for star wideout CeeDee Lamb to have a career day.
For this Texans secondary to be at its best, Lassiter has to hold his own as the high-end complement to Derek Stingley on a way more consistent basis. Whether it be an individual fix or for the coaching staff to address, Houston's defense has to find better success in the passing game if they want any hopes of climbing back to .500.
The addition of Reed Blankenship into the Texans' secondary this offseason was done with the intent of getting a bit more consistency, talent, and another leader within their safety unit after the position had suffered from a ton of turnover throughout the course of 2025.
However, Blankenship's placement in this Texans defense seems as if it's led to more problems created than problems solved.
He did secure Houston's first interception of the year in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts, yet has allowed at least a 109.0 passer rating when targeting, and hasn't seen his zone-heavy fit mesh with the rest of this secondary that excels in man-to-man.
Blankenship showing that his presence really can be valued in this lineup will be big for his stock moving forward. Because if there are any similar secondary struggles from what's been seen over the past few weeks, the coaching staff might just make a change to plug newly-healthy veteran M.J. Stewart into that strong safety spot instead.

title: Texans Add New Trio to Practice Squad, Lose Noteworthy DB to Rival
full_text:
The Houston Texans have made a several roster changes following the events of their Week 4 loss to the Dallas Cowboys — all of which came from their practice squad.
Per KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson, the Texans hosted visits for cornerback Jaden Davis and running back Deuce Vaughn on Tuesday, and will be signing both to their practice squad.
Wilson notes that Houston hosted a visit with free agent linebacker Chad Muma, who CBS Sports ' Matt Zenitz also signed to the practice squad.
The #Texans are signing linebacker Chad Muma to their practice squad, sources tell @CBSSports . Former 2022 third-round draft pick with 103 career tackles. pic.twitter.com/xTPVH0uThn
In the process of the Texans' three signings, though, they also wound up losing out on one of their practice squad defensive backs, Alijah Huzzie, who has been signed to the Jacksonville Jaguars' roster.
It's a lot to take in as it relates to the Texans' practice squad movement. So to break things down a little easier, let's sort through each of Houston's new additions (and their single departure) one by one, and sort through why each move might matter heading into Week 5:
Vaughn, a 5-foot-6, 176-pound running back out of Kansas State, was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NFL Draft by the Dallas Cowboys
Vaughn has played 16 career games throughout his two years in the league––both of which being with the Cowboys––where he recorded 40 rushing attempts for 110 yards, along with 10 catches for 58 yards.
Why the Texans Signed Him: The Texans' running back depth is pretty shallow right now. Outside of their regular contributors on offense, David Montgomery and Woody Marks, Houston has three backs between their roster and practice squad: Dare Ogunbowale, British Brooks (injured reserve) , and Jawhar Jordan. Adding Vaughn gives Houston another layer of security at the position with someone who hasn't played in an NFL game since 2024, yet has some appealing quickness and ability to work as a runner and pass-catcher that helps his stock.
Davis, a 5-foot-10, 182-pound defensive back out of Miami, was selected in the seventh round of the 2024 NFL Draft by the Arizona Cardinals.
He's played in three career games with the Cardinals, all of which came in 2025, where he recorded three tackles with a little over 60 total snaps played.
Why the Texans Signed Him: The Texans' cornerback depth saw a couple of changes on Tuesday. For one, they saw Jaylin Smith hit injured reserve with a hamstring injury. But Houston also lost Alijah Huzzie to the Jaguars in a move will discuss a bit more later. But with that in mind, it felt obvious the Texans were going to add some form of depth within their secondary, and Davis winds up being just that.
Muma, a 6-foot-3, 239-pound linebacker out of Wyoming, was selected in the third round by the Jaguars in the 2022 NFL Draft, and has gone on to turn into a five-year NFL veteran playing for Jacksonville, the Indianapolis Colts, and the Jacksonville Jaguars.
He's played in 58 career games, recording 103 tackles, three TFLs, 1.5 sacks, and three passes defended. He's also been listed as a starter for seven games.
Why the Texans Signed Him: The Texans have had to shuffle around their linebacker room in recent days because of the groin injury to sideline Azeez Al-Shaair for Week 4 against Dallas . That led to Kenneth Murray being elevated to the 53-man roster as the green-dot signal caller and starting linebacker on the defense, yet he would go down with a concussion at the end of the game.
So Murray might be sidelined for at least one game, and we don't know much about Al-Shaair's availability for Week 5 just yet. Adding a linebacker felt due, and it winds up being Muma.
Alijah Huzzie, a 5-foot-10, 195-pound defensive back who's been with Houston dating back to the 2025 season, has been a bit of a fixture on their practice squad as someone who could even be worthy of a 53-man roster spot.
Many projected Huzzie to make the 53-man roster before the start of the season as a depth corner and backup nickel to Jalen Pitre, yet he would wind up falling short of that nod. He wound up on the practice squad, and in short time, he's now on another AFC South team in Jacksonville less than five weeks into the new year.
It matters for the Texans in two ways: one, Houston loses a talented defender in Huzzie; someone who's been in the system for close to a year, and might've been worthy of a 53-man roster spot over one of the five tight ends or six linebackers the team decided to bring onto the roster, yet now heads elsewhere for nothing.
Two, Huzzie's departure comes at a time in which his services could be utilized by the Texans now that Jaylin Smith is going to miss some time. Whether it be as a backup nickel or a contributor on special teams, a role could've easily been there for Huzzie to make his mark on Houston’s roster for Week 5.
That fit for Huzzie, though, now resides in Jacksonville––a team that the Texans will coincidentally be facing up against as soon as Week 6 in London, so expect a bit of a reunion to take place for both sides.

title: Texans Should Be Concerned About Latest Injury to CB Jaylin Smith
full_text:
It looks like the Houston Texans will be without some depth in their secondary for at least the next four weeks.
That's because second-year cornerback Jaylin Smith has been placed on injured reserve.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson, Smith is reportedly dealing with a Grade 2 hamstring injury that'll effectively sideline him for multiple weeks, thus leading to the Texans placing him on injured reserve.
Smith had been receiving secondary opinions on the hamstring injury he had suffered this past week against the Dallas Cowboys. However, it won't prevent him from missing a bit of time in the Texans' lineup, which is seemingly becoming a bit of a trend for the young second-year corner.
With the newest absence now forcing Smith out of the mix for the next few weeks, this now marks the third time that the Texans have been forced to place him on injured reserve throughout his young career.
Smith has played in eight of his 23 available games between the regular season and playoffs with the Texans thus far, and will be slated to miss the next four, at the very least.
Smith was sidelined for four games just two weeks into the 2025 season with a similar hamstring injury before returning in Week 8 against the San Francisco 49ers . Just one game later, though, Smith would suffer a torn meniscus against the Denver Broncos to sit him out for the remainder of the year.
Wilson reporting that there is optimism for Smith's eventual return to the lineup is certainly encouraging that he won't be missing the entire season. Once those four weeks on injured reserve are up after Week 9 against the LA Chargers, then perhaps the team can re-evaluate.te.
However, seeing that this is now the third instance of Smith missing extended time, you can't help but be a little bit concerned about what his future looks like as a valuable piece in Houston.
Smith was brought in just a little over a year ago with a day two pick in the 2025 NFL Draft with hopes of being a valuable future asset in the secondary, largely because of his versatility and prowess in man-coverage.
Yet, nearly a season and a half into his career, Smith hasn't really had a chance to show off the appealing skills Houston initially brought him in for.
And for the next few weeks, it'll be the same case.
Smith has only recorded 38 defensive snaps through the eight games he's been active in thus far, with only seven of those coming this season. Instead, he's been a primary part of Houston's special teams game, as he's been on the field for 65% of their special teams snaps this season.
Since he arrived last spring, the Texans have liked what Smith brought to the table as a future CB3 behind Derek Stingley and Kamari Lassiter . However, without being able to stay consistently healthy, now approaching his third IR designation in a little over 20 games, it hurts his chances of being able to cling onto a bigger role in the secondary––both in the short and long term.
For the stretch that Smith is forced out of the mix, however long that may be, we can expect for Tremon Smith to claim those CB3 duties, and the primary backup to fill in on the boundary behind Stingley and Lassiter.
For the stretch that Jaylin Smith was out over the course of his rookie season, it was now-nine-year veteran Tremon Smith who stepped up to the occasion for his role and played relatively well throughout the season too.
Over the course of his 2025 campaign, Smith recorded 23 total tackles, two passes defended, and a forced fumble while also being available in all 17 games.
So considering the team was in this same spot last year, expect the Texans to lean on Tremon Smith a bit more while shorthanded in their cornerback room, both as a depth piece in their secondary and a contributor on special teams.

title: Texans Week 5 Consensus Power Rankings: Houston Hits New Lows at 0-4
full_text:
The Houston Texans have fallen into the treacherous territory of being one of five teams in the NFL to have an 0-4 record now four weeks deep into the 2026 season–– which comes after their latest 30-34 loss to the Dallas Cowboys suffered in Week 4 .
It's a steep 0-4 hole entering the season that the Texans haven't seen since 2020. Even in DeMeco Ryans' notoriously slow starts since becoming head coach in Houston, who started 0-2 in 2023 and 0-3 in 2024 , he hasn't seen a four-week stretch as brutal as this one.
And as a result of that slow start for the Texans, several power rankings around the league have gone on to drop Houston pretty far down their list compared to the title contenders they were seen as before Week 1 .
Let's sort through a new batch of consensus power rankings to see just where the Texans stack up as they roll into Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans.
Conor Orr was pretty high on the Texans entering the season, putting them as far as third before Week 1 arrived. Now though, his expectations for this team have come crashing back down to Earth as they just barely sneak into the top 20.
"Of the teams whose seasons are theoretically dead in the water, Houston provides the faintest glimmer of hope. Braden Smith, Tank Dell and Kayden McDonald are on the way, the Titans are up next on the schedule and 1–4 looks far better (with three examples of playoff teams in the last 25 years, by the way)."
Nick Shook actually wound up placing the Texans one spot higher from where they ended up last week. Yet, even as Houston's stock technically rose, he certainly has some concerns about how this defense has performed as of late.
"I think it’s safe to remove the “elite” tag from the Texans’ defense. For a second straight week,C.J. Stroud gave Houston a late lead, and the defense failed to protect it. Kamari Lassiter had an especially terrible day, giving up eight receptions for 136 yards on 11 targets as the closest defender, per Next Gen Stats. Houston’s defense didn’t generate organic pressure, resorting to blitzes against a quarterback (Dak Prescott) you certainly shouldnotblitz often. The Texans paid the price and have wasted a rather strong stretch from Stroud, who is no longer the problem in Houston."
ESPN 's writers have pulled the Texans down three spots from last week's ranking. DJ Bien-Aime also was tasked with highlighting Houston's start to the season in just four words: "pass defense is struggling."
"The Texans' pass defense has fallen off a cliff in 2026. Last season, Houston was fifth in passing yards allowed (179 per game). So far in 2026, it's 28th (260). For a team with three Pro Bowlers in the secondary, that's inexcusable. There are a bunch of reasons, but a noteworthy one is that Houston hasn't pressed as much as last season. The Texans have the second-lowest press rate (25%), per ESPN Research, compared to the 12th highest in 2025 (56%). That has been a little confusing, as All-Pro cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. and Pro Bowl corner Kamari Lassiter are best when pressing."
Josh Kendall and Chad Graff’s concerns on the Texans are "sky-high" right now. That centers around this defense being far from the Super Bowl level they were expected to be at entering the season.
"This was supposed to be a team that could compete for the Super Bowl in a wide-open AFC. Instead, a defense that we thought had a chance to be an all-time great has looked awfully mediocre through the first four weeks. It’s the main reason for the Texans’ winless start."
Pete Prisco is someone who has also pushed the Texans up one spot from last week's ranking, as they now sit right outside of the top 25 at 26th. As for the optimism surrounding what's next in Houston, though, things might not be as strong.
"They've made the playoffs after opening 0-3. But this year it's 0-4. Can they climb out from that hole to make the playoffs? Good luck."
Ralph Vacchiano points to one aspect of the Texans' defense that has caused them trouble throughout the past four games: turnovers. Houston has just three takeaways over their four games played thus far, and all of those came back in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts.
"The DeMeco Ryans-C.J. Stroud era in Houston has been wildly successful. So what’s gone wrong in 2026? The defense, mostly. It has just three takeaways this season — a stark drop from when the Texans had 29 last year (third in the NFL).  Considering they get good pressure (14 sacks, including 4.5 from DE Will Anderson), that’s a ridiculously low number."

title: 10 Texans Tidbits: What Led to Houston's Week 4 Collapse vs. Cowboys
full_text:
The Houston Texans are now one of five teams in the NFL sitting with a brutal 0-4 record after the events of their Week 4 loss to the Dallas Cowboys , 30-34.
While the Texans' offense was able to show some much-needed signs of life, it was a combination of a rockstar performance from the Cowboys, and a lackluster job by Houston's defense and their coaching staff that now forces them into an even steeper back to .500 over the coming weeks.
Let's break down the Texans' Week 4 disappointment vs. the Cowboys in full with our weekly edition of 10 Texans Tidbits ; sorting out a handful of stats and results that led to this weekend ending up as it did.
The biggest story of the day in Houston this weekend was just how dominant Cowboys wideout CeeDee Lamb ended up being , who had a whopping 17 receptions for 189 yards and a game-winning touchdown in the fourth quarter.
The Texans' defensive game plan was a bit of a mess. Even with the talent they have in their secondary with corners like Derek Stingley and Kamari Lassiter, and even in their back-end at safety, this was the last team you'd expect to allow a career day for Lamb. Yet, Houston's defense fell victim to much of the same explosive chunk plays that they saw in Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills.
According to NFL Pro, Lamb was targeted on 21 of 45 routes in Week 4, the most targets by any receiver to have run 45 or fewer routes in a game since 2016.
It was yet another week of the Texans hoping that their struggling run game could find some traction in terms of potency and efficiency, yet ultimately fell short in what was an uninspiring performance on the ground.
David Montgomery had 10 carries for 24 yards , while Woody Marks complemented him with a little less than 50% of the offensive snaps, recording six carries for 22 yards.
So the Texans' running backs combined for less than three yards per carry again, run blocking was still subpar, and Houston's play design in the run hasn't been the most stellar as well; multiple jumbo packages, more futile runs up the middle, etc. Really, it looks like it hasn't taken any steps forward from how their results looked in 2025.
The Texans aren't known to be the most blitz-heavy defense in the NFL by any means. Through their first four games of the season, Houston ranks among the bottom-five in the league for blitz rate (20.8%).
However, in the snaps where the Texans did want to blitz this Cowboys offense, it was Dallas and Dak Prescott who wound up dissecting that coverage extremely well. Prescott completed five of seven passes for 116 yards against the blitz, averaged 16.6 yards per attempt––his most in a game since Week 4 of 2024 against the Giants.
So if the Texans' pressure and success in the blitz were underwhelming, and their secondary had even more flaws on their end due to CeeDee Lamb's day, putting two and two together will tell you this one can be chalked up as a defensive calamity for Houston.
This weekend marked the third game of the season for the Texans, where their defense failed to come away with a single turnover across the day. No interceptions. No fumble recoveries. Zero turnovers, which happened on just two occasions for Houston last season.
Sure, the Texans' defense doesn't have to generate a whole bunch of takeaways to win games. Yet, not only with the talent Houston's defense has, but also when factoring in just how well C.J. Stroud has controlled the football on the other side of the ball (zero turnovers in three straight games), getting an edge in the turnover battle could be a huge help for their aspired success.
After the Texans entered this season with five tight ends as a part of their 53-man roster, many expected offensive coordinator Nick Caley and this scoring attack to lean on those 12, 13 personnel packages more, and get their tight ends more looks compared to their limitations at the position in 2025.
However, now approaching a quarter of the way through the new season, it seems as if the Texans are doing their best to increasingly take their tight ends out of the game plan.
Dalton Schultz was a non-factor yet again after his 140-yard day from Week 2. No other tight end landed over 40% of the offensive snaps, and perhaps most surprisingly, second-round rookie Marlin Klein was a healthy scratch . What is going on here?
On a more positive note, the Texans' passing game–– particularly the connection between Stroud and Nico Collins–– really shined in this one more than we've seen throughout an otherwise gloomy season thus far.
Collins––in his first game returning from a two-game hamstring injury absence––led Texans receivers in targets (8), receptions (7), receiving yards (118), and receiving touchdowns (2) against the Cowboys. If Collins were to keep up his current pace of production for the rest of the season, he'd finish the year with a career-high in both receptions and yards by far.
We can expect the Texans' star wideout to come back down to earth after a double-touchdown performance over Dallas, yet having him back in the fold clearly gave a much-needed lift for an offense severely struggling in Weeks 2 and 3.
The Texans got to see newest Cowboys cornerback Joey Porter Jr. on the field for his official debut with the team. And even while he was limited in terms of his snaps for most of the day, he performed pretty well in the reps he got.
Porter Jr. played 24 of 52 defensive snaps against the Texans (46.2% of the snaps), including 19 snaps in coverage without allowing a single reception on just one target faced. He matched up with Nico Collins five times and was not targeted once.
This is now the second week of the Texans' season where Pro Bowl cornerback Kamari Lassiter has looked to be the weak link in a disappointing secondary performance.
Against the Cowboys, Lassiter allowed eight receptions for 136 yards on 11 targets; all marking the highest numbers he's seen for each since kicking off his third year pro.
Perhaps it's an individual concern for Lassiter. Maybe it's a message that the Texans' secondary needs to play to their star corners' strengths a bit more by playing more press coverage. Regardless, something's got to give for Lassiter to return to the high-end level he was in 2025, and for Houston's pass defense to turn around as a whole.
After many were eager for 2025 third-round wideout Jaylin Noel to get on the field more after a limited first three games of the season, Noel had the second-highest snap count among Texans receivers this weekend, where he was able to turn in an eye-catching stat line.
Noel turned in his three targets for three receptions and a career-high 85 yards, which largely came off of the Texans' biggest offensive play of the day, a 52-yard catch-and-run for a 24-year-old.
With the quickness and explosiveness that Noel can clearly inject into this offense, the Texans would be foolish not to give their second-year wideout a few more looks moving forward in hopes he can be a consistent complement to Collins.
The Texans now find themselves at a gloomy 0-4, a spot that only one team has made the playoffs in NFL history after an 0-4 start: the 1992 San Diego Chargers.
And the Texans do have a bit of reason to believe they can make some history. It was just last season when Houston became the first team in the 2020s to come back from an 0-3 start to make the postseason, and now they find themselves in a similar situation.
For Houston to make that surge up the standings again, though, it'll rely upon them taking advantage of their next slate of games before the bye. The Texans have three meetings to go until that Week 8 bye, coming against the Tennessee Titans, Jacksonville Jaguars, and New York Giants.
The hope would be for a 3-0 run here, but that's clearly much easier said than done.

title: Why a Texans-Tyreek Hill Signing Makes Sense — and Why It Doesn't
full_text:
The Houston Texans could be among the teams paying attention to the latest Tyreek Hill news surfacing after the events of Week 4.
According to ESPN 's Adam Schefter, the agent of free agent Tyreek Hill, Drew Rosenhaus, is setting up visits for the veteran wide receiver this week to begin negotiating a deal. Among those visits is his former team, the Kansas City Chiefs, where he spent the first six years of his NFL career.
Developing: Tyreek Hill’s agent Drew Rosenhaus said he plans to begin negotiating a deal for his veteran wide receiver with multiple teams today. One of those teams is the Chiefs, who have maintained contact with Hill. “I would anticipate Tyreek  potentially signing with a team… pic.twitter.com/RBn7ju28Ku
It's a big development as it relates to what's next for Hill, who's been stuck rehabbing from a torn ACL suffered around this time last NFL season, and has been a free agent since his release from the Dolphins earlier this year .
So now that Hill's recovery has seemingly taken another step forward and ready to start talking to teams about a contract, it begs the question of where his next destination could be.
And in the mix of teams who could be in the race to sign Hill, the Texans stick out as a team who might have some interest in a deal. They're 0-4 on the year, have seen a few offensive ups and downs through the first four weeks, and maybe a signing of a five-time All-Pro could help alleviate those woes.
With that in mind, let's break down as to why a Texans signing for Hill might makes sense, and also sort through why a signing isn't quite as seamless as it may appear:
While the Texans did see their offensive production take a big boost this weekend with Nico Collins healthy and in the fold , this group could still use an extra, experienced set of hands next to their No. 1 in order to truly round out C.J. Stroud's arsenal better than they ever have.
And the Texans––if interested in signing someone like Hill––could see a much-different skillset within Hill compared to Collins that makes the signing add up even further. Collins is the more physically imposing jump-ball receiver, while Hill can utilize his speed and quickness to truly take this passing offense to the next level.
The last time Hill played a full 17-game season, it came in 2024 with the Dolphins when he recorded 81 receptions for 959 yards and six touchdowns. The year after, he played only four games before a torn ACL derailed his entire season.
So he might not be the annual 1,000-yard receiver he was in both Miami and with the Kansas City Chiefs–– especially post-injury–– he offers a layer of experience and proven production at the wide receiver position that Houston just doesn't have right now.
And for a team that sits 0-4, every avenue that can upgrade this offense should at least be explored. If the interest is there from both sides, the situation in Houston feels like a much better fit than many others in the league could provide for Hill.
When it comes to a potential Hill signing for Houston, there are a few concerns that might arise within the Texans' front office, which ultimately might prevent them from seriously pursuing a signing.
Let's sort through them one-by-one:
1. The Texans could have some underlying concern about Hill's status and potential production post-injury. It was only a few weeks ago that Hill himself said that he had no power in his injured leg, and there's a chance his explosive quickness and speed aren’t near what they were in either Kansas City or Miami. If that's the case, then maybe signing him for the season isn't worth the trouble.
2. Houston has two noteworthy investments at the position outside of Nico Collins in second-year wideout Jaylin Noel and recent trade acquisition Kayshon Boutte . So if Houston feels as if they already have enough talent at the position, maybe they just need to scheme around them better instead of adding further pieces.
3. Tank Dell is set to see his practice window opened from injured reserve heading into Week 5, which tends to hint towards a return to the field being imminent. As Dell is just now starting to work his way into the Texans' offense, then maybe adding another pass-catcher like Hill into the equation isn't the most ideal setup for his return.
So the idea of adding Hill into the mix of this Texans offense is fun, sure. On paper, he’s an easy weapon who can add a dose of speed and explosiveness into a passing game that hasn't been the most inspiring through four weeks.
However, there are certainly a few more hurdles to his fit in Houston from what meets the eye. Knowing that, there might be better options that Hill turns to on the market instead––like the Chiefs––where he can have a bit more certainty and familiarity for how his role could look.

title: Texans Open WR Tank Dell's Practice Window: What It Means & What's Next
full_text:
After stretching four weeks into the 2026 NFL season, we've finally got an update from the Houston Texans on what's next for wide receiver Tank Dell as he looks to make his return to the field for the first time in over 20 months.
And based on the newest intel heading into Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans, things seem to be trending in a really positive direction for Dell's pending recovery, despite what some previous buzz around the league may have hinted at .
According to Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans, the team will be activating Dell's 21-day practice window from injured reserve, along with offensive tackle Braden Smith and defensive tackle Kayden McDonald.
"This week, we expect to open the window for Tank Dell, Braden Smith, and for Kayden McDonald," Ryans said on Monday.
Knowing that Dell is going to be off the injured reserve list and on the practice field this week, it's the most noteworthy development that the Texans wideout has faced in his lengthy recovery process thus far.
Dell has been sidelined since December 2024 with a devastating knee injury he suffered against the Kansas City Chiefs, effectively damaging his ACL, MCL, LCL, meniscus, and kneecap, and has kept him out of the action for Houston's offense since.
However, knowing that Dell is going to be practicing this week, it means we're one step closer to seeing the Texans' pass-catcher and one of C.J. Stroud's favorite targets back on the field for a regular-season game.
As Dell's 21-day practice window is now opened, the Texans have three weeks from when their practice starts to make a decision on their wide receiver's roster status.
By the end of those three weeks, the team will have to elevate that player to the 53-man roster, trade or release that player to another team, or place them back on season-ending injured reserve.
For Dell, it's eye-catching for two reasons: he's finally able to get back on the field for an organized practice for the first time since training camp, but it also marks the next step in his long-awaited return to the field.
The Texans opening his window is a hint from the team that they know Dell is close to returning. The coaching staff will certainly want to get a look at their returning pass-catcher in multiple practices before they set him loose as a part of the 53-man roster, though this is a huge step towards getting to that point.
While the Texans are now on the clock with Dell's 21-day recovery, they have a bit of time on their hands before they're forced to make a decision on his roster status.
If the Texans open Dell's practice window this week, it gives them three full games before that 21-day stretch expires, which connects perfectly to Houston's Week 8 bye that begins at the end of October: they'll face the Titans in Week 5, the Jacksonville Jaguars in London for Week 6, and the New York Giants at home in Week 7.
After that Week 7 game finishes up–– and if all goes well in practice through the next three weeks–– the Texans will then likely be due to officially activate Dell to the 53-man roster, and give him another full week on their bye before he'd have a chance to make his season debut against the LA Chargers in Week 9.
So there's still patience to be had before we get to see Dell catching passes in-game from Stroud once again. Yet, knowing that his practice window is live certainly gives some extra optimism that his return will be coming sooner rather than later.

title: Texans' Snap Counts vs. Cowboys: What Stood Out in Week 4 Loss
full_text:
The Houston Texans have now lost the first four games on their 2026 schedule after the events of Week 4's loss to the Dallas Cowboys, 30-34 .
And in the fallout of the Texans' Week 4 loss, we've now gotten our hands on the snap count totals from both Houston and Dallas in this weekend's game, giving us a glimpse at who on the roster played a good chunk of the day, and who might've seen a bit more of the opposite:
And by looking at the Texans' side of things when it comes to their snap totals seen this weekend, there are a few noteworthy outcomes that deserve a bit of attention more than the rest for one reason or another.
Let's sort through four interesting aspects of the Texans' snap totals that stood out from their Week 4 loss to their in-state rivals :
After weeks of much clamor for Noel to get more snaps and targets his way compared to the first three games of the year, this game against Dallas really felt like the Texans were eager to involve Noel a bit more than they had before. And in the reps he got, he took advantage of them in a big way. Noel had the second most yards (85) and snaps (34/62% of the offense) within the receiver room behind only Nico Collins. And with the multiple explosives he generated, it gives the Texans more reason to get him involved moving forward.
After the Texans had known Azeez Al-Shaair was going to miss this week with a groin injury, the expectation remained that fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz would be the second starting linebacker to fill in next to Jake Hansen within Houston's front seven. But it wasn't Woodaz to get the call up. Practice squad elevation Kenneth Murray was the one claiming a lion's share of those linebacker snaps, outside of the eight that he was out of the mix due to injury. Only then was Woodaz thrown on the defensive side of the ball, which might be a sign of just how polished the Texans view their day three rookie at this point in his career .
This was the first weekend the Texans' defensive line has had to do without Mario Edwards Jr., who tore his ACL in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts to sideline him for the rest of the season. As to how the Texans pushed forward without Edwards, Jaden Crumedy took the snaps as Houston DT3 behind Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai. He was mostly a non-factor, but the good news is that second-round rookie Kayden McDonald is gearing up to be elevated from injured reserve heading into Week 5.
This piece doesn't show up within the Texans' snap totals, which is because the player in reference didn't see a single look in any capacity in Week 4––that being second-round rookie tight end Marlin Klein . If anything, the Texans' first three weeks of offense seemed to hint that Klein was due for more snaps moving forward, not less. Instead, Houston sat their day two rookie out entirely, were limited in their tight end usage as a whole, and leaves you wondering as to what the front office's plan was when bringing the Michigan tight end into the building in the first place.

title: Colts' Wide Receiver Room Is Becoming a Problem
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back to .500 after winning two straight, but there is still something missing from this offense.
Indianapolis simply does not have enough explosiveness at wide receiver right now.
Daniel Jones averaged a career-best 8.1 yards per attempt last season, helping create one of the most dangerous offenses in football before his Achilles injury. That number has dropped considerably through the first month of the season, and the absence of Alec Pierce has been impossible to ignore.
Pierce isn't just another receiver in this offense. He led the NFL in yards per catch in back-to-back seasons, averaging 22.3 in 2024 and 21.3 in 2025 before signing a four-year, $114 million extension this offseason.
He opened this season with four catches for 61 yards against Baltimore, but aggravated his surgically repaired left heel against Kansas City after just one catch for 11 yards.
Now he is on injured reserve and is not eligible to return until the Colts' October 25 matchup against Minnesota.
That has left Indianapolis searching for somebody to replace the vertical threat he brings.
The Colts signed Darius Slayton shortly after Pierce went down, and the move made perfect sense. Slayton has averaged 15.0 yards per catch throughout his career and spent six seasons playing alongside Jones in New York.
Slayton even said that he and Jones "see the field pretty similarly," which made him seem like about as close to a plug-and-play option as Indianapolis could find.
Yet he has been inactive in back-to-back games.
The first one was understandable. Slayton had just arrived and was still learning the offense.
But being a coach's-decision inactive again in London, especially with Pierce on injured reserve and Keenan Allen out with a groin injury, is much more concerning.
Ashton Dulin finally returned against Washington and caught three passes for 29 yards, including a 23-yard reception, but even he is now dealing with a hamstring injury.
The Colts did sign veteran wideout Quez Watkins to their practice squad on Tuesday, reuniting him with head coach Shane Steichen from their days together in Philadelphia, though he hasn't played in the NFL since 2023, so it's hard to imagine he'll surpass Slayton on the depth chart anytime soon.
Josh Downs remains the reliable volume option underneath, and guys like Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell certainly have their roles.
But none of them replace what Pierce does.
Indianapolis does not need another possession receiver. This offense needs somebody who can consistently threaten a defense vertically and create explosive plays.
Whether that means exploring free agency or attacking the trade market, the Colts at least need to be looking.
I understand the complicated part. Indianapolis just committed $114 million to Pierce, and once he returns, a room featuring Pierce, Downs, Allen, Slayton, Dulin, Treadwell and Burks suddenly looks crowded.
But crowded on paper doesn't mean much when the players expected to provide your explosiveness are either injured or not playing.
The Colts are 2-2 and still right in the middle of the AFC South race heading into Pittsburgh.
There is too much talent on this offense to allow one missing element to hold it back, and right now, the lack of a legitimate downfield threat is doing exactly that.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Week 5 Power Rankings: Jury Still Out on Indianapolis Colts
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are starting to turn things around, but are doing so very quietly.
After opening the season 0-2, Indianapolis has won back-to-back games and enters Week 5 at .500. Despite the improved record, there still isn't much consensus on what to make of this team.
Some see a team that could make a run at the playoffs. Others aren't convinced the Colts have done enough to prove they're ready to compete.
Here's where some of the biggest names in NFL media have the Colts ranked heading into Week 5.
The Colts dropped two spots in Connor Orr’s rankings, despite Indianapolis getting a win in Week 4, noting the team needs to continue improving its roster as the season progresses.
“I don’t really care what happens to this iteration of the Colts, but following the Sauce Gardner trade last year, literally the only sensible follow-up is to continue pouring resources into this team and trading for Colts legacy son Marvin Harrison Jr.,” he wrote.
Indianapolis jumped up just one spot to No. 22 in the power rankings voted on by ESPN’s team of beat reporters.
Stephen Holder is unconvinced that the first four weeks have given any answers as to who the Colts are. His four words to describe the start: Who are these guys?
The Colts have managed to get to .500 with consecutive wins, but there are so many questions about their viability as playoff contenders,” he wrote. “The defense has played better but hasn't faced a major test in the past two weeks…Sunday's win somehow produced 30 points despite QB Daniel Jones posting his lowest passing total in a full game since joining the Colts last season (143).
The Colts came in at No. 22 in Mike Florio’s power rankings , two spots better than last week.
Florio kept his analysis brief. He’s not sure Indianapolis is capable of winning the division, and questions its ability to win enough games to “steal a wildcard berth.”
No change from last week in Chad Graff and Josh Kendall’s updated rankings, but concern is growing, particularly over the quarterback play.
The Colts went to London and didn’t have to do much to beat up on the undermanned Washington Commanders,” they wrote. “But there’s rising concern about (Daniel) Jones, who completed 19 of 34 passes for just 143 yards with no touchdowns and an interception.”
Clearly, the duo is not moved.
Another one-place jump for the Colts . Ralph Vacchiano believes the team is a playoff contender, and are better than it gets credit for. At the same time, the quarterback remains a wildcard.
“They are an overtime FG away from being 3-1 this season. So they’re a playoff contender, but how much longer can they thrive if (Daniel) Jones keeps making big mistakes?”
Vacchiano also cites concerns over the pass defense, which has allowed the third-most yards so far this season (1,105).
Nick Shook dropped the Colts two places in his new rankings, arguing that Commanders’ quarterback Marcus Mariota’s injury gave Indianapolis a “favorable outcome.”
“You’ll take any and every win in this league, although this one doesn’t inspire a ton of confidence,” he wrote. Shook shares the same worry over Jones’ turnover problems that several have already pointed out.
Bleacher Report’s analysts collectively ranked Indianapolis at No. 23 , no change from the week prior.
Brent Sobleski writes that the Colts are a shell of the team they were a year ago, and a big reason why is the drop off from Daniel Jones.
“He's been part of the problem to start this season despite the two-game winning streak…As long as Jones does a better job with his ball security, the Colts could easily win their next two contests.”

title: The Indianapolis Colts Are Still Searching for a Pass-Rush Fix
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered the offseason knowing they needed defensive end help.
Four weeks into the season, they're still looking for it.
Indianapolis had a glaring need coming out of last season and spent much of the offseason trying to boost its pass rush. There was no shortage of options, and the Colts came close on some.
But instead of landing the kind of addition that could change the position, things took a turn.
And now, with injuries piling up, the questions surrounding the position have only gotten louder.
To understand the Colts’ current predicament, we have to go back to the offseason. General manager Chris Ballard knew he needed to add some juice to the defensive line in order to elevate Indy’s pass rush.
“We’ve gotta address the front and make sure we have enough,” he said in his end-of-season press conference back in January. “You’ve got to find ways to be deep enough and have enough talent on the roster that you can still win games.”
The Colts saw plenty of turnover at the position, losing veterans Kwity Paye, Tyquan Lewis and Samson Ebukam to free agency. That left just Laiatu Latu and Jaylahn Tuimoloau from last year’s team still under contract.
Ballard knew what he had to do. And with former Bengals defensive end Trey Hendrickson, the 2024 sack leader under current Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo, available, he became the obvious primary target.
The Colts got real close to inking Hendrickson to a deal that would’ve transformed the defensive front. But they missed out at the last second, with Baltimore swooping in to snatch Hendrickson up on a monster four-year, $112 million deal.
Ravens signing DE Trey Hendrickson to a 4-year, $112M deal. (via @rapsheet , @tompelissero ) pic.twitter.com/Tjaf7Sv0Ae
That left Ballard with a decision to make. Indianapolis still needed to address the issue, but the team wasn't going to find another Trey Hendrickson sitting around waiting to be signed.
Instead, they took a more boring approach.
Indianapolis added Arden Key as a low-end starter option opposite Latu and later brought in Micheal Clemons as a rotational depth piece. Neither move carried the same weight as the Hendrickson pursuit, nor were they as flashy of moves, but together they gave Indianapolis two experienced bodies to help fill out the depth chart.
Later in the offseason, Ballard took two late-round flyers on rookies George Gumbs Jr. and Caden Curry, but that was it for additions. Instead of adding the game-changer, the Colts went for role players, an intentional decision that forced the Colts to bet on Latu breaking out in his third year. Which, in theory, could work. Latu would lead the way, Key would complement and the rest of the unit would do the rest.
But four games into 2026, and that plan has been tested significantly.
The team placed Clemons on injured reserve Sept. 22. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler announced Tuesday that Key, who suffered a hamstring injury in Indy’s 30-17 win over the Commanders , will miss around 3-4 weeks. So now, the Colts are right back where they started.
Colts pass rusher Arden Key is expected to miss about 3-4 weeks with a hamstring injury, per sources. Head coach Shane Steichen said Monday that Key, a starter, would miss ‘some time.’ pic.twitter.com/2qsGqC8dQQ
Assuming Key’s absence, Latu and Tuimoloau are Indy’s starting edge rushers, leaving Indianapolis in the same situation they were in a year ago: looking for a boost.
While the Colts pass rush is undermanned, the injuries also provide opportunity.
Curry and Tuimoloau, both of whom have played rotational roles this season, will be thrust into larger roles. Gumbs, who’s yet to make his NFL debut, will get the chance to suit up for the first time.
For Tuimoloau, his opportunity has finally arrived. After spending most of his rookie season on the bench, Indy’s second-round pick from 2024 has finally found his way into more playing time. But that comes with steep responsibility, and it’s unclear how ready he is.
And of course, there’s Latu.
While Latu hasn’t had a Hendrickson-like impact for the Colts through four games, the team is still banking on him establishing himself as the top dog. There have been flashes, as there have been throughout Latu’s career, but the final product hasn’t always been there. Now, there’s never been a better time for that to change for Latu than now.
The next few weeks will be crucial, not just for the pass rush, but for the team. As the defense adapts to life without Clemons and Key, the Colts will find out whether the bet they made on their young defensive ends can pay off, or if they’re better off exploring other options.

title: Is it Too Early for the Colts to Panic About Daniel Jones?
full_text:
Daniel Jones looked like a completely different quarterback once he entered Shane Steichen's system last season.
His legs paired with Jonathan Taylor's rushing ability and Alec Pierce's deep-threat presence created almost a perfect storm. For stretches, this offense looked unstoppable, and Jones was doing whatever he wanted with the football while still taking care of it.
Then came the Achilles tear.
Jones tore his right Achilles on Dec. 7 against Jacksonville, ending a career year in which he completed 68% of his passes for 3,101 yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions.
Just 280 days later, he was back under center for Week 1 against Baltimore.
And four games into his return, I think it is fair to start asking the question: Should the Colts be worried about Daniel Jones?
Nothing about Jones physically screams that Achilles is still bothering him.
He moved well throughout training camp, has shown he can escape the pocket and even scored his first rushing touchdown since the injury Sunday against Washington.
But we still haven't seen the same Daniel Jones who made defenses account for his legs every single play last season.
Jones rushed for 164 yards and five touchdowns in 13 games last year. Through four games this season, he has just 21 yards and one score.
Maybe that matters more than we realize.
An Achilles injury is brutal, especially for a quarterback whose athleticism was such an important part of what made this offense dangerous. Jones may technically be healthy, but expecting him to immediately have the same burst and confidence only nine months removed from surgery might not be completely fair.
We saw a version of this with Kirk Cousins after his Achilles tear. Cousins returned for Atlanta in 2024 and threw 16 interceptions in 14 games before eventually losing the starting job.
Obviously, that isn't a perfect comparison. Cousins was older and never had Jones' mobility to begin with.
But it does make me wonder how much an injury like this can impact a quarterback mentally, not just physically.
This is where my true concerns begin.
Jones has already turned the ball over seven times through four games, throwing four interceptions and losing three fumbles. He had 11 total turnovers across 13 games last season.
That simply cannot continue, and against Washington, it wasn't only the turnovers.
Jones finished 19-of-34 for just 143 yards, and there were several opportunities where receivers were open and the throw simply wasn't accurate enough.
Could Jones be trying to compensate for some of those explosive plays he used to create with his legs by forcing more with his arm? Maybe.
That's impossible to know from the outside, but something is clearly different right now.
Still, I'm not ready to panic, Jones is four games removed from a long and grueling rehabilitation process. He deserves some time to rediscover the rhythm that made him so good in this offense last season.
I still believe Jones can play at an elite level in Indianapolis, but the ball security has to improve immediately.
And if we know anything about the quarterback Indianapolis saw last season, Jones is going to work relentlessly to get back to where he needs to be.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Week 4 Snap Count Analysis: What’s Going on With CJ Allen?
full_text:
The Colts came home from London with a 30-13 win over Washington, but the Week 4 snap counts left behind a few questions worth digging into.
Some players are earning bigger roles. Others are somehow seeing theirs disappear.
Here are the three snap-count storylines that stood out most.
At this point, the situation is getting harder to ignore.
CJ Allen, the Colts' top pick in the 2026 NFL Draft at No. 53 overall, was active Sunday and did not play a single defensive snap. He has now played just 11 defensive snaps through four games, recording one assisted tackle.
That is strange enough for a second-round linebacker, but it gets even stranger when you consider how Indianapolis talked about Allen all offseason.
Lou Anarumo and his staff put the green dot on Allen almost immediately after he came off PUP during training camp. He wore it at Georgia, and Chris Ballard's scouting staff specifically highlighted his communication ability and green-dot potential.
Allen opened camp with a calf strain and later suffered a hamstring injury that Anarumo said set him back roughly a month. That explanation made sense early.
But we are now a month into the season, and Allen isn't just being eased in — he isn't playing.
Austin Ajiake had not logged a defensive snap entering Sunday and played 17 against Washington. Bryce Boettcher played 18, while Jaylon Carlies played 30.
There may also be a slight philosophical difference between Ballard's vision and Anarumo's.
Ballard's staff drafted Allen believing he could run the defense from the MIKE spot. Through four weeks, that vision has yet to materialize on Sundays.
Adebawore continues to make the most of every opportunity he gets.
He played 29 defensive snaps Sunday, or 45% of the defense, and split a third-down sack with Laiatu Latu.
More importantly, Adebawore currently leads Indianapolis in pressure rate despite still operating in a limited role.
He generated four pressures and 1.5 sacks against Houston in Week 3, then followed it up with another disruptive performance in London.
At some point, production has to earn more opportunity.
The Colts needed somebody to step up at receiver with Alec Pierce on injured reserve and Keenan Allen out with a groin injury.
Laquon Treadwell answered.
Treadwell played 56 offensive snaps, tied with Tyler Warren for the most among Colts skill-position players, and led Indianapolis with five catches for 42 yards on six targets.
He entered Sunday with four catches on five targets all season, but when his role expanded, his production followed.
Treadwell may not provide the same vertical element as Pierce, but he has done exactly what Indianapolis has needed from him.
Allen's continued absence is easily the biggest snap-count story to watch moving forward.
If Allen still cannot crack the rotation as the season moves deeper into October, the questions are only going to get louder. For a player the Colts once viewed as a potential green-dot linebacker from Day 1, 11 defensive snaps through four games is becoming harder to ignore.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Week 4 Stock Report: 3 Risers, 2 Fallers After Colts’ Strong Win in London
full_text:
After a worrying 0-2 start to the 2026 season, the Indianapolis Colts have worked their way right back into the thick of things in the AFC with back-to-back victories, most recently a 30-17 win over the Washington Commanders in London.
While four games is still a small sample size, each week brings us more information on which players are playing key roles for the Colts. Here’s a look at who’s trending up and who’s causing concern after an important victory overseas.
The Colts’ run game powered the offense on Sunday, accounting for just under half of the team’s total yardage and scoring all three touchdowns. And while Seth McGowan played a very small role, it’s becoming clearer that the Colts want him involved on the ground more as the season progresses.
On a season-high 19 snaps, McGowan logged his best statline so far: six carries for 31 yards and a seven-yard catch. He also added 102 kick return yards.
While the rushing numbers themselves are uninspiring, their proof that McGowan’s involvement in the offense is growing. For a team that leans so heavily on Jonathan Taylor to win games, having a developed and trusted backup to help keep Taylor fresh throughout the season will pay off in the long run.
Jaylon Carlies opened up the second half with a bang, coming away with the Colts’ first interception of the season. But it wasn’t just the splash plays that made for an impressive performance.
Carlies caught THAT. #INDvsWAS on NFLN pic.twitter.com/y0FdbDLmBM
Carlies paired five tackles with a 90.8 defensive grade from Pro Football Focus , despite playing a season-low of 30 snaps. While he was only on the field sparingly, the third-year man figured out a way to maximize his impact.
Given some of the questions surrounding the Colts linebacker group this offseason and into the season, having a guy like Carlies step up with an impactful showing in limited action helps the Colts get closer to figuring out the best possible rotation for their current linebacker group.
Sunday was perhaps the best game Charvarius Ward has played since joining the Colts.
Ward was dominant in coverage, allowing just two receptions for 13 yards on seven targets, adding three pass breakups as well. He consistently stayed stride for stride with Washington's receivers and made life difficult whenever they tried to throw his way.
After a rocky start to his Colts tenure, Ward is beginning to look more like the corner Indianapolis expected when it signed him. If Sunday was any indication, his play could be trending in the right direction at an important time for the Colts' secondary.
While Charvarius Ward was playing his best game as a Colt, Sauce Gardner was playing his worst.
Gardner allowed four catches on five targets for 117 yards and a touchdown, the most yards Gardner has allowed in a game in his career, according to Next Gen Stats. Even with third-string quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis in the game for Washington, their offense wasn’t afraid to attack the two-time All-Pro.
#Colts CB Sauce Gardner allowed 4 receptions for 117 yards and a TD on 5 targets in coverage against the Commanders in Week 4, the most yards allowed in a game by Gardner in his career, according to @NextGenStats .
The win helps to mask Gardner’s forgettable afternoon, which would’ve been under a microscope has the result fallen differently. Still, it was a noticeable step backwards from a player the Colts invested in to anchor their secondary.
Josh Downs simply wasn't involved nearly enough in a matchup that, when you look at it closely, seemed tailor-made for him.
With Indianapolis without their best deep threat in Alec Pierce, Ashton Dulin being banged up and Keenan Allen unavailable on Sunday, it seemed likely that the Colts pass game wouldn’t stray too far from around the line of scrimmage, and rely more on quick-hitting throws.
As a result, you’d think, would be a busy day for Downs, as he’s the Colts’ best separator and creator after the catch. And Indianapolis did try a heavy dose of the screen game.
But the 25-year-old Downs only logged four targets, three of which he caught for a meager 16 yards. To keep it blunt, that’s nowhere near the impact he should be having in these kinds of games.

title: Colts Week 4 Grades: Defense Takes Another Step Forward
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back to .500 after a 30-13 win over the Washington Commanders in London, and the biggest takeaway has to be the defense.
Granted, this two-week stretch came against a beat-up Houston offense and a Washington team forced to turn to a third-string quarterback, but the Colts defense finally looks like it is taking the right steps.
The frustrating part is that this game could have been even more lopsided if Daniel Jones could snap out of whatever funk he is in.
Here are my Week 4 grades.
Jones finished 19-of-34 for 143 yards, no passing touchdowns, one interception and a 53.9 passer rating.
He also lost a fumble on the second play and finished with the lowest offensive grade on the team, via PFF. Seven turnovers through four games simply is not good enough.
Jonathan Taylor handled business again.
Taylor finished with 97 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns, while Seth McGowan added 38 total yards on seven touches. Taylor is now the all-time leader in international rushing touchdowns with six.
This group had trouble consistently separating against a struggling Washington secondary.
Laquon Treadwell led the team with just 42 receiving yards, although injuries left the room thin. When guys did get open, Jones missed too many opportunities.
Tyler Warren caught all five of his targets for 41 yards.
With the receiver injuries, I would still like a little more production, but Warren and Mo Alie-Cox both held up better in pass protection. That was a much-needed step forward for Warren.
The run blocking was solid, but the pass protection left something to be desired.
Indianapolis rushed for 128 yards, but Jones was sacked twice and moved off his spot too often against a defensive line that entered the game ranked 31st by PFF.
The interior continues to be the strength of this defense.
Austin Ekeler's 29 rushing yards were the most by any Washington running back, and Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner were stout inside. I still need more consistent impact from the defensive ends.
Finally, some real progress.
Akeem Davis-Gaither earned a 91.7 defensive grade and Jaylon Carlies posted an 82.2, via PFF, the two highest defensive grades on the team. Carlies also recorded the Colts' first interception of the season.
This group was decent overall, but the deep shots are still concerning.
Sauce Gardner had arguably his roughest game as a Colt and was involved in two big completions downfield. Justin Walley helped in run defense and added a sack.
Cam Bynum was solid in coverage and against the run, but A.J. Haulcy had some issues on the back end.
Outside of the deep-ball breakdowns, this group did enough.
Spencer Shrader was money again, drilling field goals from 48 and 52 yards.
The punting operation also looked cleaner than it did early in the season, making this one of the better special teams performances we have seen from Indianapolis so far.
The Colts are back to .500, and for the first time this season, the defense is starting to look like a group that can actually be trusted.
Now the challenge is getting Jones back on track. If Indianapolis can pair this version of the defense with the offense we saw early in the season, this team could finally start putting together complete performances.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 4 Things We Learned About the Colts in Week 4 Win Against Commanders
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have gone from 0-2 and searching for answers to 2-2 with a legitimate chance to take control of the AFC South.
That's quite the turnaround in the span of two weeks. Indianapolis still has plenty to clean up, and Sunday's 30-17 win over Washington was hardly flawless, but the Colts have started to show some signs of what this team can be.
Four weeks in, we're starting to get a clearer picture of who the 2026 Colts are. Here are four things we learned from Sunday's win in London.
The Colts learned just how valuable Alec Pierce is to their offense on Sunday. (Hint: that four-year, $114 million contract was well worth it.)
Between Pierce being sidelined, Ashton Dulin banged up and Darius Slayton inactive, the Colts lack a true field-stretching threat at wide receiver, limiting their pass attack to the short and intermediate areas. As a result, Washington was able to play tighter to the line of scrimmage, making life more difficult for Daniel Jones and an offense that took a while to find its rhythm.
Had Pierce been out there, his mere presence alters the offensive approach significantly. The defense would have to respect the deep pass, opening up space underneath for other pass catchers. Without the threat of the big play, the defense had one less thing to worry about.
Pierce's value goes beyond his own production. The Colts offense looked much more limited without him. His return can't come soon enough, even if he doesn't return until next season.
I don’t know what it is, but there’s something about playing in Europe that gives Jonathan Taylor super powers .
After rushing for 95 yards and two touchdowns, Taylor became the all-time leading rusher in international games, now holding the records for most career yards (408) and touchdowns (6). Sunday was also his third multi-touchdown game of the young season, underscoring his strong start to 2026.
Across the three international games Taylor has played in, the Colts have won all three. Maybe it’s time to schedule a trip to Europe every season.
The Colts’ defense looked downright ugly through the first two weeks of the season. Indianapolis surrendered 1,029 yards in losses to Baltimore and Kansas City, with big plays coming far too easily and the unit struggling to get off the field.
But something has clicked over the last two weeks.
The Colts held Houston to 223 total yards and 17 points in Week 3 before limiting Washington to 13 points on Sunday. The pass rush has been much more disruptive, the defense isn't missing tackles and the communication on the back end has improved dramatically.
There’s still plenty to clean up, but the difference between the first two weeks and the last two is hard to ignore. After looking like one of the NFL’s worst defenses to open the season, Indianapolis is finding its footing on defense.
The Colts haven't put together a complete game yet. But they've still won twice, against Houston despite scoring just 19 points and beating a beat up Commanders team playing with their third-string quarterback. While they've won both, neither were in entirely convincing fashion.
But that's also what makes these last two wins encouraging. When the offense has struggled, the defense has picked it up. When the passing game hasn't been there, Jonathan Taylor has carried the offense. When the offense has stalled in scoring range, Spencer Shrader has delivered.
There’s still a lot this team needs to clean up, but the Colts are learning how to win without everything going right. That's a valuable trait for a team trying to establish itself as the team to beat in the AFC South.

title: Colts HC Shane Steichen Evaluates QB Play: Has Daniel Jones Been Good Enough?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts took the league by storm in 2025 after their first season with Daniel Jones leading the charge immediately paid dividends.
The Colts were on top of the NFL world after starting last season with an 8-2 record, and a big reason for their hot start was due to the offensive marriage between head coach Shane Steichen and quarterback Daniel Jones.
Jones had gotten the fresh start he needed, and Steichen got his ideal quarterback to run the offense as he envisioned, but it wasn't just their efforts that saw them start the experiment off with said success.
The 2025 Colts offense jumped out to a historically efficient start, and that's because Steichen and Jones were afforded the necessary supporting cast to reach the heights they knew they could.
However, even though the Colts largely ran it back on offense, something's changed through four weeks of the 2026 season.
Of course, Daniel Jones's infamous Achilles tear from Week 14 of the 2025 season has played a part in such regression: but is it a true regression, or is Jones trending back to his true self?
The Colts have managed to even up their overall 2026 record to 2-2 after four weeks, but it's largely been in spite of Jones's play.
Jones currently sports the second-most turnovers responsible for among any quarterback throughout the first month of the season with seven (four interceptions, three fumbles lost), trailing New England Patriots' Drake Maye (eight turnovers).
The Colts' starting quarterback has certainly looked like his peak 2025 self at times throughout the young 2026 regular season, but he's looked like his past self more often than not, and that's not a sustainable formula to bank on.
So, what did Colts' head coach Shane Steichen and Daniel Jones himself have to say about the team's quarterback play through four weeks?
Going into the Colts' Week 4 international matchup against the Washington Commanders, head coach Shane Steichen emphasized the need to take care of the ball moving forward.
Daniel Jones entered the week with five turnovers (three interceptions, two fumbles lost) through three games, but he didn't clean up his act after traveling overseas.
Jones threw an interception and lost a fumble against the Commanders, and Shane Steichen continued to put an emphasis on the non-negotiable that is not turning the ball over following the Colts' 30-13 victory.
"We just got to get those things cleaned up. That's part of the game. But you want to limit those turnovers as much as you possibly can," Colts' head coach Shane Steichen said about taking care of the football. "We'll go back and look at the tape and make sure we get that stuff cleaned up."
Daniel Jones hasn't been all bad through four weeks of the 2026 regular season, but he's certainly struggled more than he's thrived.
When asked to evaluate Jones's performance thus far, Colts' head coach Shane Steichen was brief but honest.
"I think he's done some really good things and some things we got to clean up," Shane Steichen said about Daniel Jones's performance thus far. "It's been four weeks into this thing and 2-2 right now, and so there's stuff to clean up, like always. But I think he's doing a good job."
I personally wouldn't say that Jones's performance thus far warrants praise, but at least the head coach and offensive playcaller still has confidence in his quarterback despite the rough start.
As alluded to, the Colts were able to thrive with Steichen and Jones leading the charge due to their complementary offense, but a lacking wide receiver core in 2026 has proven to be too much of a challenge thus far.
The Colts are without top wide receiver Alec Pierce for the foreseeable future as he rehabs his left heel injury that kept him out of the majority of the offseason, and this lack of a respectable deep threat has shrunk the offense, thus making it more difficult on the short passing game and run game.
Furthermore, veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen missed Week 4's game against Washington, but Ashton Dulin returned to the fray after missing multiple weeks with an ankle injury. Even though Indianapolis got a vertical threat in Dulin back, the offense still struggled to generate any explosive plays through the air.
The Colts brought in veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton to address this lack of an explosive downfield threat, reuniting him with Daniel Jones, but he's been a healthy scratch for both games since his addition.
Shane Steichen acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the wide receiver position, but ultimately decided that a revolving door of personnel should not dictate a quarterback's overall play, no matter how dire the situation presents itself.
"Darius [Slayton] is still learning the offense. He's getting into it. He's been here for two weeks. We'll see how next week goes. But I don't think so. I think that's part of the NFL. Guys are going to get hurt. Guys are going to get injured. It's next man up," Shane Steichen on the notion that Daniel Jones has started to showcase some poor tendencies because of his lack of a supporting cast through the air.
"I think [Laquon] Treadwell stepped up. Had some good catches. The ball got spread around a little bit, but overall it was not our best but it was good to win.
Throughout four weeks, Daniel Jones has been a below-average quarterback - and he knows it.
Entering Week 4, Jones sit among all NFL quarterbacks with the following statistics: 611 passing yards (23rd leaguewide), three passing touchdowns (T-23rd), three interceptions (T-24th), and is sporting the 25th-ranked QB Rating (38.9).
Against the Commanders, Jones did enough to get the job done, but he didn't start off hot. Jones had arguably his worst half in a Colts uniform to start the game, and he looked like the skittish, lost version of himself against pressure that forced him to part ways with the New York Giants.
In Week 4, Jones went 19-34 (55.9%) for 143 passing yards, one interception, was sacked twice, had one rushing TD, and lost a fumble.
It's fair to consider this a passable performance, especially considering the Colts ended up scoring 30 points overall, but in the grand scheme of things, this isn't cutting it come postseason pla -- the Colts' defense, who undeniably held up their end of the bargain against Washington, isn't going to face a depleted offense in the playoffs after all.
But as previously mentioned, Jones's lack of production is nothing compared to what's really holding the Colts' offense back; it's his second-most seven turnovers (four interecptions, three fumbles lost).
"Yeah, definitely got to play better. Got to clean that up. Can't afford to turn the ball over like that," Daniel Jones said about his performance through four weeks so far. "So, yeah, I think I just got to focus in on the details, understand can't do it and make better decisions."
So, if Jones knows that he's not playing up to standard, why does he continue to turn the ball over?
"I think they're all different," Daniel Jones said about his turnovers to start the season.
"Got to understand when to take a chance, when not to, when to protect the ball, when you have a chance to make a play. I think all that is something you're always studying and learning, and I definitely got to do a better job taking care of the ball."
On top of the concerning turnover rate to start the year, Jones has also started to panic in the pocket, and has been wildly inaccurate at times as a result. To be fair to him, the Colts' offensive line has taken a step back in pass protection, thus making life harder on Jones and the rest of the offensive passing game.
Entering Week 4, Jones had faced the 4th-highest amount of pressure among any NFL quarterback, according to Next Gen Stats.
Pass protection wasn't much better against the Washington Commanders, and Jones definitely deserves some grace, but he himself also needs to play better.
