title: Dolphins Wednesday Mailbag: How Will the Defense Deal with Mike Gesicki?
full_text:
Part 2 of the post-Vikings game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Hi Alain, with our problems covering TEs which needs to fixed ASAP, is Kyle Louis a potential solution if he returns and, if so, what is his timeline for return?
Hey Keith, Louis will be eligible to return from IR after the Week 5 game against the Bengals, but we have not gotten a progress report on his recovery from his knee injury, so I don’t know that he’ll be back for the Week 7 game against the Jets after the bye. I would suspect he’ll be given a shot to cover tight ends at some point, but I’d be concerned a bit about his lack of size being a problem there.
Why have the special teams been so awful and will we have to wait until next year to fix the problems?
Look at how the Dolphins have churned the bottom of the roster, which is where all of the special teams units get their players. Then add the inexperience factor with a lot of rookies involved. Then you can see where issues pop up. The group should get better as the season progresses, but it started from a difficult position.
Is the game too fast for Malik Willis ? He seems flustered at times, not seeing open receivers and often off target (inconsistent). Should we still view him like a rookie where the game has not yet slowed down?
Hey Zander, it’s a fair question, but how often is he flustered because there’s pressure and his receivers aren’t getting open? I’m not buying this “game is too fast” narrative, but he’s certainly more inconsistent than ideal with his passes and what’s pretty clear is he often doesn’t set his feet probably and relies too much on his arm strength.
Is it me or did anyone else get an uneasy impression from Malik Willis’ demeanor when the cameras were on him from the sidelines? Wouldn’t you be talking to your WRs and OC and trying to get organized and such, especially right before their last drive w/ 6+ minutes left.
Hey Bubba, yeah, I’m not on board that whole narrative. If there were specific issues that needed to be discussed before a drive, rest assured the offensive coach on the sideline would get with Willis to go over everything.
On the flight home, what was that conversation like between Hafley and the special teams coach?
Hey Jayco, it might have gone something like this, “Hey, Chris (Tabor), make sure you remind Malik (Washington) not to try fielding a punt around the 5-yard line and let’s keep coaching our young players so our kick coverage teams stop leaking, even though I understand you’ve got a lot of fringe NFL players and young guys on that unit.”
Hi Alain, thx for all the hard work. Why it seems that we have the same issues regardless of who's the head coach? Bad offensive line play, defending TE, has been an issue forever. Is it Grier been in charge for so long?
Well, everything this season boils down to the roster not being good enough and not having enough experience, so I guess you could pin that on Grier because of the roster overhaul the new regime deemed necessary.
Have you seen enough from Malik to say he is/isn’t the guy? I think it’s too early to say no, but it’s leaning that way.
You said it right there, it’s way too early for me. We’ve seen flashes here and there with some great off-schedule plays that we haven’t gotten from a Dolphins QB in maybe a decade, but the consistency just hasn’t been there. But the question is whether the consistency is lacking because Willis just isn’t the guy or because the supporting case currently just isn’t good enough and that consistency will show up once it improves.
Hi Alain, I watched the game hoping to see some improvement. On defense I did but one area is still bad. Why can’t this team cover a tight end? The running game was better, but there seems to be a real issue with our passing game. Lack of talent or chemistry? Maybe next week.
Hey Mark, yeah, this doesn’t have anything to do with chemistry. The Dolphins just don’t have that one guy who can cover tight ends one-on-one and they’ve left big holes in their zones at times, and then you’ve had some busted coverages. It’s a combination of several factors, none of them good.
At Monday’s presser Hafley did something I’ve never really seen him do. Perk asked him about a third-and-goal play where Willis had to choice to run for the end zone or make a pass attempt. Perk asked if he made the right choice on that particular play and he said something to the effect of everything happens so fast that it’s Willis’s choice to make. To me it was a deflection. It’s his job as coach to look at every play and make a determination of what the right thing to do is. I looked at play in real time and thought he had a lane and should have ran for the end zone. Even if he doesn’t make it, he would have been stopped very close to the end zone and the Dolphins would have had a choice to go for it on fourth-and-short. I thought Hafley for the first time was copping out. Are we to the point where the coach is excuse-making and deflecting? Do you think Willis should have ran for it ? Also currently Willis has one of the lowest completion percentages in the league; how concerning is that stat?
Hey Dana, first off, I’m on board with Hafley saying Willis has to make that decision because the last thing you want is a QB playing robotically and do you really want a coach publicly second-guessing a player’s decision after the fact? Do you eliminate the possibility that Hafley told Willis privately that if the situation presents itself again he should go for it? It’s very easy for fans and the media alike to look at a replay and decide what a player should have done; it’s not the same thing at full speed. Even if Hafley agreed with you that he should have run, I think we’ve seen he’s not willing to criticize his players publicly and I’m not going to fault him for that. Just like Malik Washington fielding a punt around the 6-yard line seemed like a clear mistake, but Hafley answered a question about the muff without saying that. And the completion percentage stat itself doesn’t bother me because a throw at the line of scrimmage just to get that number up doesn’t accomplish anything (as we saw for most of 2024 and in 2025). I would like to see more success in the passing game, period.
Will Storm Duck replace Jason Marshall in lineup or will Chris Johnson slide inside to the slot more? Seeing some All-22 tape on our receivers getting separation, it seems like Willis is struggling reading the field, with his decision-making, and knowing where to go with the ball in the pre-snap read. Do you believe this is something that can be taught and worth 2-3 years invested?
I wouldn’t assume anything about Duck immediately going into the starting lineup. You got all that about Willis from the All-22? If you’re accurate about your assessments there, no, it’s not worth investing 2-3 years. Or it could be that Willis needs to be more consistent at everything and he needs more help from the offense.
I’m wondering what the answers the Dolphins may try to limit tight ends running roughshod over our defense. I like the growth I've seen so far, but this is going to continue to be an issue until we find a coherent response.
Correct, and the answer isn’t easy and requires improvement in several areas, whether in man or zone coverage.
Hey Alain, after hearing Hafley's press conference last week about getting Greg Dulcich more involved, I was surprised to see that he didn't even get a target. He's probably our most accomplished receiving threat and one would think that he would be a safety blanket for Willis (kinda like Murray to Hockenson was). Hard to believe he can't be schemed up to get open, especially on a designed rollout where the tight end kind of runs a 5-yard out toward the sideline. Tua did in a couple of those a game for us last year and they always seem to work. And I was also disappointed in Willis not reading the field properly, because if you look from the All 22 he had receivers open, yet couldn't pull the trigger or was not…

title: Dolphins Tuesday Mailbag: What's the Biggest Issue with Each Unit?
full_text:
Part 1 of the post-Vikings game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
I’ve been following you for years and you always give us the truth no matter how hard it is to hear sometimes. My question is even though it’s early this draft seems solid; is there a chance we found a GM and possibly coach for the future?
Hey Mark, yeah, the early returns from the 2026 draft have been pretty encouraging that GM Jon-Eric Sullivan can pick good players, though I’d caution against anointing any draft pick a hit just yet. We also don’t know what Sullivan can do in terms of landing big-name free agents because that wasn’t on the agenda this year with the lack of cap space. And the same applies to Jeff Hafley as a head coach, it’s just too early to make a call. Let’s see what the Dolphins look like toward the end of this season.
Bobby Slowik seemed to finally found something on the lone TD drive by rolling Malik out & having him throw on the run. Could this be the game plan moving forward?
Hey Lu, that touchdown drive consisted of just four plays after the bad punt by Minnesota. And only one of those plays was a completion of a rollout and I’m not even sure that was a designed rollout as opposed to Willis moving to his left to avoid pressure up the middle before throwing a dart to Malik Washington. I would like to see more of that, but I get the feeling the Dolphins want to establish a traditional from-the-pocket passing game first (though I could be off the mark with that, which wouldn’t be a first).
We should have had Gordon spell Achane way before he got hurt. Love seeing that dude hit the hole. Great to see the left of the line provide so many gaps. Do you think the right side of the line, cough cough Jackson, finally gets it together at some point this season?
Hey Dean, I sure would hope that Austin Jackson’s game would get better as the weeks go by, and the same goes for Jonah Savaiinaea, who already has made progress, but the fact is the left side always is going to be the strength of the offensive line and I’m not sure it’ll ever be close with the current personnel.
Alain, my fellow Canadian Dolphins fans and I were shocked at the bad look Willis stretched out and disinterested on the bench in 2nd quarter and in the 2nd half? Was he lost in thought?  Did that 1st hit give him a concussion?  Does he not need to be talking and engaged with coaches?  Looking at an iPad?  Where is his leadership and working on plays with the WRs?  Can you ask the question? I have not had a chance to listen or read your latest articles. It was a bad look…if I was the GM or coach I would have sat his butt on the bench.
Hey Jeff, a quarterback looking at an iPad to see what the video is telling him about coverages and what the defense is doing is completely and totally par for the course. There’s really nothing there.
Morning, Alain. This is the 2nd or 3rd game I didn’t notice Jonah. Is he turning the corner?
Hey John, I think it’s actually more accurate to say he’s already turned a corner. Now, nobody is suggesting he’s getting a Pro Bowl or All-Pro nod this season, but he’s clearly a much better offensive lineman than he was as a rookie (admittedly a low bar).
From Jorge Francisco boyd:
Hi Alain, do you think Malik Willis looks into his progressions; how much better would he look with Caleb Douglas playing again; do you think he sees the open receiver all the time or makes poor choices?
Hey Jorge, yes, Malik Willis goes through his progressions, he clearly would be significantly better with Caleb Douglas, the one downfield threat the Dolphins had before he was sidelined with that ankle injury, and no quarterback sees the open receiver all the time and every quarterback sometimes makes poor choices. What Willis has to do is get more consistent in all areas, but he also needs help from his receivers in getting open and the line in giving him more time.
Mike Gesicki over / under 200 yards Sunday?
Ha! We have a comedian in our midst. The former Dolphins tight end may very well be a big factor for the Bengals passing game on Sunday given the injuries to Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
Is anything going on with Wright besides he was injured? He doesn’t look good at all.
Hey Jorge, Wright was dealing with injuries last week, so he probably wasn’t at 100 percent in the Minnesota game, but I don’t know that it explains everything because he indeed didn’t look great against the Vikings.
Four part question: 1) Biggest problem for the offense so far? 2) Biggest problem for the defense so far? 3) Biggest problem for the special teams so far? 4) Biggest team-wide problem? This would help to check what they fix the rest of the way.
Hey Erick, will answer those, but it doesn’t mean there are easy fixes. Biggest problem on offense I would say is the lack of dynamic options in the passing game, which makes everything more difficult. Biggest problem on defense is covering tight ends now that the pass rush came to life against Minnesota. Biggest problem on special teams is poor kick coverage. The biggest problem overall is a lack of depth and a lack of experience.
Will Chris Bell eventually cut out the mistakes, step into his potential, and get in the end zone this year? Aka will he become a consistent contributor year 1?
Yes, it’s fair to expect Bell to eliminate the mental mistakes he’s been making and I certainly would expect to get into the end zone at some point, but I’m not sure I would count on him reaching his potential this season as he works his way back from his November 2025 ACL injury and I’d also temper expectations in terms of how much contribution he can provide for the offense.
Hi Alain, why are people saying that Grant can help with the pass rush? That isn't, and never has been, his game. Also, much was made about how bad the Vikings offense is, plus without JJ, but now the Dolphins defense is getting props? Explain it to me like I'm 5, please.
Hey Jason, last things first, the Dolphins could only play the opponent in front of them Sunday, so it’s not their fault the Vikings offense stinks. It doesn’t take away from what overall was a solid performance, but it wasn’t as dominant as it could have been (particularly allowing four first downs on each of the final two drives) and it also shouldn’t be viewed as a sign that the defense has arrived. As for Grant, he’s viewed as being able to help the pass rush from the IDL spot in part because Jordan Phillips and Zeek Biggers offer next to nothing in that department and while it may not be Grant’s game, he’s still better in that area than any DT on the roster not named Zach Sieler. Now, here’s your lollipop.

title: Dolphins Week 5 Power Rankings Roundup: Baby Steps Recognized
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins remained winless following their loss against the Minnesota Vikings, but after their closest call yet this season they're inching their way out of the bottom of the NFL power rankings.
The Dolphins finished just one point behind the Tennessee Titans in our weekly survey of national outlets — Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, The Athletic, NFL.com, USA Today, Pro Football Talk, FOX Sports, The Sporting News, CBS Sports — with an average ranking of 31.4 compared to 31.3 for the AFC South team.
The Dolphins did get a ranking as high as 29th, that coming from Nick Shook of NFL.com.
The average ranking position for Miami's Week 5 opponents, the Cincinnati Bengals, was 14.2 after their loss against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Paycor Stadium on Sunday dropped them to 2-2 on the season.
Before we get to our weekly rundown of the Dolphins placement in the rankings with the accompanying commentary, we'll again examine the other winless teams.
The Dolphins were one of five teams that started 0-3 along with the Houston Texans, Titans, Los Angeles Chargers and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and remarkably (or perhaps not) all five of them lost in Week 4.
In a quick ranking of most disappointing starts among the winless teams, based on preseason expectations, the distinction of ranking at the top there comes down to either Houston, which some analysts had pegged as a legitimate Super Bowl contender, or the Chargers, whose offense was supposed to ignite with former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel as their new OC but instead has been a comedy of errors.
We are assured of having no more than four teams without a win after Week 5, barring a tie, because Houston and Tennessee will be facing each other. The Dolphins will be at home against Cincinnati, the Chargers will be at home against Denver, and Tampa Bay is playing the Thursday night game at Dallas.
Los Angeles Chargers — Their offense finally showed signs of life in the second half of their Week 4 loss at Seattle, but they already trailed 27-6 by that point. It was bad enough again Sunday that head coach Jim Harbaugh was asked about McDaniel's job security in the aftermath. Houston Texans — Houston wasted C.J. Stroud's best performance of the season because its vaunted defense couldn't stop Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb. Tampa Bay Buccaneers — The Bucs are in a major trouble with QB Baker Mayfield expected to miss a few more games and the current option at quarterback being undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels. Tennessee Titans — The Titans gave the Baltimore Ravens a pretty good game in Week 4, but couldn't overcome mistake like running back Tony Pollard deflecting a shovel pass from Cam Ward into the arms of a defender for an interception. Miami Dolphins — The Dolphins gave themselves a chance to win in the fourth quarter their last two games, and now it's a matter of being able to finish.
The Sporting News (Vinnie Iyer)
Analysis: The Dolphins played with more defensive energy in Minnesota and are trying to do what they can with now Malik Willis and Ollie Gordon II leading the offense. They still are dealing with an overall talent deficiency from week to week.
Analysis: Their offense is so limited right now, which showed up against the Vikings. The defense actually played a solid game and kept them in it.
Analysis: They haven't led for a single minute of any game so far.
FOX Sports (Ralph Vacchiano)
Analysis: Yes, they’re movin’ on up! But don’t get comfy up this high. They still stink. And they’re probably still the worst team in football. But they deserve a reward for pushing an undefeated (though likely overrated) Vikings team to the limit. They only lost by five points (though it would’ve been 12 if Minnesota TE T.J. Hockenson hadn’t slid at the 1 to let the clock run down with two minutes remaining). RB Ollie Gordon did a nice job replacing the injured DeVon Achane (100 yards on 9 carries, albeit 53 on one). But QB Malik Willis is still as bad as many of us thought he’d be.
Analysis: Haters who haven’t watched the Dolphins will call them the worst team in the league. I am not a hater. Miami is on a slow-but-steady track of improvement, showing signs of progress with each week. It's still a low-ceiling offense and the team remains winless, but I see the vision Jeff Hafley has for the Fins.
The Athletic (Chad Graff and Josh Kendall)
Analysis on concern level (not as high as you'd think): Without De’Von Achane, Ollie Gordon ran for 100 yards and a touchdown on nine carries, while the defense looked good against the Vikings. They’re a rebuilding team headed for an ugly record, but there have been some brief moments of hope along the way.
Analysis: Through the first two weeks of the season, the Dolphins looked like they weren't ready to compete. In Weeks 3 and 4, however, their defense pushed a pair of undefeated division leaders to the brink. On Sunday, the Dolphins recorded 17 pressures and four sacks -- their first sacks of the season -- while holding an admittedly struggling Minnesota offense out of the end zone. First-year coach Jeff Hafley said his team is "starting to believe." Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez said the team is close to its first win: "The physicality and the want-to are there. ... We've just got to learn how to win." -- Marcel Louis-Jacques
Pro Football Talk (Mike Florio)
Analysis: Could the first team to go 17-0 go 0-17?
Sports Illustrated (Conor Orr)
Analysis: Until Miami gets a win, this will become a Jacob Rodriguez bot account. I have Rodriguez right there in the Defensive Rookie of the Year conversation.
Yahoo Sports (Frank Schwab)
Analysis: The Dolphins battled at Minnesota, and if they didn't get unlucky on Chris Bell barely stepping out of bounds before catching a long touchdown and getting an illegal touching penalty, maybe they'd have a win. But it's another loss, and Miami's offense is still hard to watch. Unfortunately for Dolphins fans, it's a familiar feeling.

title: Breaking the Dolphins Monday Roster Move and Injury Updates
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins made a roster move Monday in the aftermath of their Week 4 game against the Minnesota Vikings, though it probably was more a matter of official record than anything else.
The Dolphins announced they had waived running back Carlos Washington Jr., two days after they signed him to the active roster off their practice squad. And the best guess is that Washington will be right back on the practice squad by Wednesday, assuming he doesn't get claimed off waivers.
Washington was signed to back up Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II for the game against the Minnesota Vikings and the Dolphins couldn't simply elevate him from the practice squad because they needed their two moves to add defensive line depth with both edge Rodney McGraw and interior lineman Mazi Smith.
The Dolphins realistically could have done the move they made with Washington with any of the three players because any of them can be signed off the practice squad anyway if another team wants them badly enough (the only stipulation being that players signed off another team's practice squad have to be kept on the active roster for three weeks).
It just so happens the Dolphins have an opening on the practice squad, the one created when they signed Washington the active roster.
The Dolphins have another running back on the practice squad at this time, trade acquisition Jarquez Hunt, but it says here that Washington being brought back is a very solid bet.
Though he was active against the Vikings, Washington did not get into the game.
Head coach Jeff Hafley offered some injury updates Monday, the best news being that defensive tackle Kenneth Grant will be back at practice Wednesday for the first time in the regular season.
Grant missed the first four games of the regular season after being placed on IR on August 30, but he's now eligible to return to game action.
If Grant can get through the week of practice without any issues, he should be in line to make his 2026 season debut against the Cincinnati Bengals next Sunday and his addition could prove valuable to an interior D-line group — Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers — coming off its best performance of the season.
The news wasn't quite as encouraging when it comes to wide receiver Caleb Douglas, who missed the past two games because of an ankle injury.
Hafley described Douglas as day-to-day and said "we'll see" in terms of whether Douglas would be able to practice Wednesday.
Keeping in mind that the Dolphins have their bye following this game against Cincinnati, don't be surprised if they err on the side of caution and keep Douglas out one more game, which would give him two more weeks to get back to 100 percent or close to it.
Hafley also put safety Dante Trader Jr. in the day-to-day category after he injured a knee against the Vikings but later returned to the game, and said special teams cornerback Reece Taylor would be week to week with his quad injury.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers From Week 4 Dolphins Loss
full_text:
In their third road contest in four games, the Miami Dolphins had one of their best chances to win this season, but could not get the job done, falling to Minnesota 15-10.
It feels like there was genuine progress made by Miami. After being blown out by Las Vegas and San Francisco, the Dolphins hung around longer than expected against Kansas City and were a TOE away from a possible win against the Vikings.
Bottom line? This "progress" is too slow, and even though the list of winless NFL teams is shrinking, the Dolphins are firmly on that list no team wants to be on. Some players stood out for the Dolphins on both sides of the ball for good and bad reasons, but the same problems persist.
The biggest what-if of the season occurred in the second quarter when Bell caught a 68-yard touchdown to give the Dolphins the lead — except it didn't count because Bell BARELY stepped out of bounds before catching the ball, leading to an illegal touching penalty and wiping the score off the board.
Knowing how the game transpired, it's a brutal mistake for Bell to make. Every play matters more in a game that was this close. But if you were to take away that play, Bell was still a non-factor in this game, targeted three times but not recording a single catch. He was expected to build on a solid performance against Kansas City, but it didn't come close to happening.
One of the biggest negatives of Miami's season up to this point was the lack of a pass rush; opposing quarterbacks' jerseys were way too clean. However, the Dolphins found their groove against the Vikings, and Sieler was the poster boy of the group with three tackles, two tackles for loss, and, most importantly, TWO SACKS.
It's his best overall performance this season, hands down. He set the tone with his first sack, which came on the first play of the game. There was genuine synergy between him and some of the other Dolphins in the trenches, like Chop Robinson and Jordan Phillips.
Don't think this is a sign that Miami's pass rush is "fixed," and that they can continue this moving forward. But they found success against a really solid Minnesota offensive line, and will now take on a historically shaky Cincinnati O-line back in Miami Gardens, so let's see where they go from here.
Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores had his way in terms of getting to Miami's quarterback. Willis had an abysmal 85 passing yards, lost a fumble, and was sacked twice. While he didn't throw an interception, he shucked some questionable throws that could have been picked off.
When he had some solid completions here and there, he couldn't keep it going for back-to-back plays, or there was a penalty that wiped it off the board. In terms of being a dual-threat QB, he wasn't a threat at all in the run game.
I've tried my best to keep Willis off these lists so far this season, but his performance against Minnesota was the breaking point. Miami's offense had opportunities in this game to win, but it genuinely looked like Willis held the offense back at times.
The keys to the run game were given to Gordon following Achane's injury, and he didn't disappoint with 100 yards and a touchdown off nine carries.
His 53-yard pick-up coming out of halftime gave the Dolphins the spark they needed on offense, though it sadly led to a field goal. He could have even done better if one long-distance run hadn't been called back because he was "supposedly" touched at the line of scrimmage after stumbling down, though no TV angle was provided that actually showed that.
Regardless, Gordon was electric in this game and had to put the offense on his back at times. The flashes of speed, agility, and ability to break tackles in prior games culminated in one of his best performances in the NFL, and it was well needed.
In Paul's defense, the officiating crew for this game didn't give the Dolphins any favors, but players eventually need to adjust when they're getting hammered with penalties. Paul did not do that and was hit with three holding penalties. He negated a few quality plays from the offense, including the best run of the game for Willis in the second quarter.
It's a shame, because Paul did look good when blocking for Gordon and company. He had a great game against Kansas City and genuinely looked like he was turning into a quality pass blocker.
However, he regressed against Minnesota and visibly looked frustrated, not just with the officiating, but also with how the O-line struggled — Austin Jackson wasn't any better; it's just the matter of three holding penalties by Paul that put him on this list.
There needs to be a serious discussion about Rodriguez and how he deserves to be in the running for the NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year Award. He's done everything asked of him by Miami and then some, and seems to only be getting better as the weeks pass.
His performance against Minnesota was his best so far—- 18 total tackles (nine of which were solo) on 78 defensive snaps, leading the team in all three categories (tied in snaps). His 18 tackles in a single game are the most by ANY defensive player in the NFL this season in the NFL so far.
Rodriguez always seems to find his way to the football. His ability to wrap up quarterbacks, running backs, and wide receivers is currently unmatched in the NFL, especially considering he's 24 years old. Getting by Rodriguez with the ball in your hand has become a near-impossible task, cementing him as one of the brightest spots on the team this season.
On one hand, this was a decent game for Brooks by the numbers with 13 tackles. However, this slot truly represents everyone who attempted to contain TJ Hockenson, who had one of the best games of his career. Postgame, Brooks claimed ownership of the defense's struggles to keep up with the eighth-year tight end.
With Justin Jefferson not playing, there was hope that Miami's defense could silence Minnesota's passing game, but Hockenson turned out to be the hero that the Vikings needed. He racked up 13 receptions for 119 yards, including some of their biggest plays on offense as the game progressed.
The cherry on top was the final play before the two-minute warning, with Hockenson going down at the 1-yard line to ice the game as Miami had no more timeouts. Jordan Addison and the rest of Minnesota's wide receivers had mediocre performances in comparison; Hockenson was at the right place at the right time to become one of the most unexpected reasons why the Vikings won.
So far, Uche has had a pedestrian season for the Dolphins, but he provided solid snaps for Miami against the Vikings, finishing the day with six tackles and a sack in the second quarter.
He did some of his best work in the second half, including one of the most critical tackles of the game. On 3rd & 8, he stopped Aaron Jones dead in his tracks for a gain of three yards. Minnesota had to settle for a field goal, giving the ball back to Miami's offense, trailing by five points with just under seven minutes to go.
The Dolphins' offense didn't come through, but you can't say the defense didn't give them the opportunity needed to win the game.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 4 Snap Counts Stories: (Overly) Busy Day for the Defense
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 15-10 loss against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, where the biggest news involved two players again being out with injuries — Caleb Douglas and Robert Beal Jr.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord, offensive lineman Andrew Meyer and running back Carlos Washington Jr., who was signed to the 53-man roster off the practice squad Saturday.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies after tight end Will Kacmarek joined Week 3 starters Chris Bell at wide receiver, fullback DJ Herman, guard Kadyn Proctor, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- What stands out here is the ridiculously low number of offensive snaps the Dolphins got, which was 39. That was exactly half the number of plays run by the Minnesota offense.
-- Jaylen Wright got the start at running back with De'Von Achane on IR with a torn ACL, but he quickly gave way to Ollie Gordon II, who ended up with a 22-12 snap advantage and clearly established himself as the current RB1 after rushing for exactly 100 yards.
-- For the first time this season, Kacmarek got more snaps at tight end than Greg Dulcich, with 24 compared to 20.
-- Veteran Jalen Tolbert was active for the second time, but he again barely was a factor on offense as he played only six snaps, two more than special teams specialist Ryan Miller. The Dolphins did use three wide receivers at the same time quite a bit, but this is where we point out that Malik Washington is more like a utility player on offense — a halfback/receiver, if you will — than a pure wide receiver.
-- The Dolphins used a sixth offensive lineman again, though this time it was only one snap for Caedan Wallace.
-- Four players were on the field for all of Miami's 78 defensive snaps: linebackers Jacob Rodriguez and Jordyn Brooks, Taaffe and Johnson.
-- This not surprisingly was a season/career high for the three rookies. The previous high for both Rodriguez and Johnson came in the season opener when both played all 68 snaps against the Las Vegas Raiders. Taaffe's previous high was 52 snaps against Kansas City. It was the second-highest total of Brooks' career, topped only by his 81 snaps for the Seattle Seahawks in a 33-13 victory against the Houston Texans in 2021, his second year in the NFL.
-- The Dolphins opened the game in the nickel and played most of the game with that five-DB alignment. JuJu Brents got 69 snaps at cornerback and Jason Marshall Jr. got 60.
-- Dante Trader Jr. again started at safety alongside Taaffe, but he left the game with a knee injury before returning, and Zayne Anderson wound up playing 29 snaps in Trader's place.
-- On the defensive line, what stood out was Josh Uche, who was very active, getting the most snaps on the edge with 55, five more than Chop Robinson, who also had his moments rushing quarterback Kyler Murray.
-- Practice squad elevations Rodney McGraw and Mazi Smith played 12 and nine defensive snaps, respectively, and each made a play or two, McGraw as a pass rusher and Smith getting penetration on a run that led to a tackle for loss.
-- Eight non-specialists saw action only on special teams — Seydou Traore, Andre Jones Jr., Jackson Woodard, Julius Wood, Jaylin Simpson, Jarrett Kingston, Reece Taylor, and newcomer Shaka Heyward.
-- Speaking of special teams, Traore again led the way with 23 snaps, followed by 18 fo r Miller, Wood and Heyward, who was signed off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad last week.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to Dolphins-Vikings Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins battled back late, but lost a 15-10 decision against to the Minnesota Vikings. Let’s overreact to the fourth straight loss to begin the Jeff Hafley era.
For the third time in four weeks, Miami was dominated in the third phase. The Dolphins gave up multiple big returns to Myles Price, and muffed three kicks of their own.
In a game that ultimately was decided by one score, having the worst special teams group in the league is going to keep moral victories from translating into material ones. The unit is sloppy, consistently out of place, and hasn’t shown any redeeming qualities outside of a nice Jaylen Wright return in Week 1.
An argument can be made that continuity will help this group over time, but Miami’s offense and defense don’t look nearly as out of place as its kicking game, despite also being made up of plenty of new players. This unit feels substantially worse than the rest of the team, and churning whatever you can of that portion of the roster seems like the best way forward.
The Dolphins' passing game was awful against Minnesota. Malik Willis finished 9-of-17 for 85 yards, and the team went 2-for-9 on third downs. Their biggest play, an out-of-structure touchdown from Malik Willis to Chris Bell, was wiped off the board due to the rookie stepping out of bounds before making the catch.
Outside of Malik Washington making a couple of nice plays in space and finishing with 67 yards, the receiving corps feels razor thin. Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr. missed out on crucial chemistry-building time this offseason, but have been vaulted into vital roles in the absence of Caleb Douglas.
Douglas’ return would not only re-adjust the pecking order, but also add some much-needed size and verticality to an aerial attack that seems insistent on pushing the ball deep down the field a few times a game.
Week over week, Miami is watching its rookies find increased comfortability, and several of them made major impacts on this game.
Jacob Rodriguez was all over the place, logging 18 total tackles, while Kadyn Proctor flashed on some big runs by Ollie Gordon. Michael Taaffe, Chris Johnson, Chris Bell, and Will Kacmarek all also had individual moments that showcased their potential.
Each have missed assignments, and the overwhelming amount of youth on this team is a major factor in Miami’s 0-4 record, but in a season where the team is looking for flashes, they’ve certainly gotten them so far.
Week One’s defensive woes seem like a distant memory compared to the most recent exposure we got against Minnesota. The team grabbed their first four sacks of the season , held Minnesota to zero touchdowns, and held their own on the backend for a majority of the game.
The front four had their best game of the season. Chop Robinson and Josh Uche were impactful, and the interior duo of Zach Sieler and Jordan Phillips appear to have settled in, with both making highlight plays.
The last couple of drives were rough, as Minnesota iced the game on the back of TJ Hockenson, but Jeff Hafley and Sean Duggan have this unit playing hard consistently, and their ascension has kept Miami in their last two games.
For as many individual high-points as there were in this game, there were just as many lows. For instance, following Miami’s lone touchdown drive, they allowed Minnesota to drain over eight minutes of clock, and after rallying to force a field goal, Jaylen Wright struggled to come up with a knuckling kick, knocking Miami’s offense back for their potential comeback drive.
This has been one of the major stories of this season. Penalties inside opposing territory, flags negating game-changing plays, and crucial clock and personnel gaffes late. These moments are to be expected of a young team, but the quantity and timing of them are becoming unacceptable. Whether this is simply the youth or a potential coaching problem is something that needs to be sorted out as soon as possible.

title: Dolphins Week 4 Instant Takeaways: So Close, Yet So Far
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins continue to be a tough out, but they still can't get that elusive first win under head coach Jeff Hafley.
In many ways, the Dolphins let one slip away against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium, dropping a 15-10 decision that moved their record to 0-4.
The Dolphins gave the undefeated Vikings all they could handle, though in fairness Minnesota is a pretty unimpressive 4-0 team on offense, but again mistakes and missed opportunities made the Dolphins come up short.
And that's the plight of a team overloaded with young and unproven players, though some of the culprits on this day were not rookies but rather young veterans with starting experience.
While running back Ollie Gordon II proved a bright spot with his work in the absence of De'Von Achane, the bottom line is the Dolphins once again failed offensively with a fourth consecutive game with fewer than 14 points.
The defense gave the team a chance to win until the end, but then couldn't get the stop needed to give the offense a final opportunity to pull out a late victory.
-- The Dolphins don't have to hear about not having any sacks on the season anymore and they took care of that issue right from the start, courtesy of Zach Sieler. By the time they were done, the Dolphins had four sacks, two by Sieler and one each for Josh Uche and Chop Robinson.
-- Robinson ended with a game-high three QB hits, including back-to-back pressures in the first half and a sack like we haven't seen from him before where it wasn't about his speed and get-off but rather about pushing back right tackle Brian O'Neill into the lap of Kyler Murray.
-- The legend of Jacob Rodriguez continues to grow, this time with a game-high 18 tackles, which is the highest total in the NFL this season. What was lacking from his game this time was a tackle for loss or an impact third-down play. In other words, his performance was good, but maybe it was overblown a bit if you were to believe the folks at FOX and the gushing they were doing.
-- For all the good work of the defense — and it was a good performance, albeit against a mediocre offense missing its best player (Justin Jefferson) — it failed to deliver in the clutch. Needing the ball to try to come back, the Dolphins defense gave up four first downs on each of Minnesota's final drives, the first of which ended in the field goal and the second ending with kneel-downs to end the game.
-- Meanwhile, the Dolphins went three-and-out the only time they had the ball in the fourth quarter, which led to a time of possession advantage for the Vikings in that fourth quarter of 14:00 to 1:00.
-- Covering quality tight ends is not easy for any defense, but the Dolphins must do better than letting T.J. Hockenson completely own the game down the stretch, including the game-sealing third-down reception where he could have scored but instead gave himself up at the 2-yard line to run out the clock.
-- This is a recurring theme, but one we should get used to when we're dealing with so many young players.
-- It also sure looked like the Dolphins couldn't catch a break from the officials the entire game on a day when there seemed to be blown calls or questionable calls all over the place.
-- There were three significant close calls that all went against the Dolphins in this one, the most notable the call that Chris Bell's got a piece of the sideline to nullify his 68-yard touchdown off a brilliant off-structure play by Malik Willis. There also was the replay-assisted decision to rule that the Minnesota player had tipped the ball and therefore the roughing-the-punter penalty that would have given the Dolphins a first down had to be erased. And lastly there was that run where Ollie Gordon II stumbled at the line, got up and raced down the field, only for the officials to rule he was touched before getting up when TV replays didn't clearly show that at all.
-- And we won't talk about the three holding penalties called on left tackle Patrick Paul, all on plays where similar circumstances didn't produce a flag. Let's just say the Dolphins got a flag-happy crew on this day.
-- Willis' final stats again won't look very good for him without telling the real story because he was under duress. But maybe the Dolphins can take some comfort in holding the Vikings to two sacks after they had at least four in each of their first three wins.
-- Back to Gordon, that was some impressive running by the second-year tailback, and it sure looked as though his success came up the middle or over the left side.
-- Malik Washington showed once again why he's the most reliable and dependable wide receiver on the team and his work after the catch was some kind of impressive.
-- We addressed this in our halftime observations, but yes the special teams were rough, but that often happens when you have a talent-defiicient roster and the players on the back end of that roster are those playing in the kicking game.
-- So now the Dolphins are 0-4 for the sixth time in franchise history, the first time since that 2019 season. This 0-4, though, continues to look nothing like the 0-4 of 2019 when they lost by 20 or more points each time.

title: Breaking Down the Week 4 Dolphins Inactive Info
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins ' inactive list for their Week 4 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings once again was led by rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas.
The list included the team's other injured player, edge Robert Beal Jr., along with the usual group of young players.
Tight end Justin Joly, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Denver Broncos after they released the fifth-round pick from N.C. State, returned to the inactive list after making his NFL debut against the Kansas City Chiefs last week.
With Douglas out for a second game because of his ankle injury, veteran wide receiver Jalen Tolbert again will be active after not being in uniform for the first time two games of the regular season.
As expected, running back Jaylen Wright will be active after missing the Kansas City Chiefs because of his stinger/foot issue.
He'll be joined at running back by Ollie Gordon II and new 53-man roster member Carlos Washington Jr., who was signed off the practice squad Saturday.
We hit on all of our inactive list projections for the second time in four games.
Edge defender Rodney McGraw has a chance to become the 12th Dolphins rookie to make his NFL debut after being elevated from the practice squad Saturday. The Dolphins have 14 rookies on their roster, with Kenneth Grant and Trey Moore on injured reserve, and sixth-round pick DJ Campbell is the only rookie on the active roster yet to make his NFL debut. Practice squad member Max Llewellyn got playing time in Week 2 when the seventh-round pick was elevated for the game in San Francisco.
Campbell and fellow offensive lineman Chukwuebuka Godrick will be inactive for a fourth consecutive game, with Brady Cook once again serving as the emergency third quarterback.
Cornerback Marcellas Dial Jr. will be inactive for a third straight straight week after playing in the season opener against the Las Vegas Raiders.
Godrick and Campbell also were expected inactives based on the fact the Dolphins are carrying 10 offensive linemen on their active roster and the normal number is eight for game day, and they're the two least established of the group.
The Vikings' inactive list is headed by wide receiver Justin Jefferson, who was ruled out Friday because of the ankle injury he sustained in Week 3.
The list also includes B Max Brosmer, S Jakobe Thomas, P Brett Thorson, CB Chuck Demmings and DL Elijah Williams.

title: UDPATE: Why It Was the Right Time for the Dolphins to Kick the Tires on Another Former First-Round Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins, at the risk of repeating ourselves, are on a quest to find core players for the future this season as much as they are looking for wins.
This is not bold statement because we've seen it manifest itself time and time again through the personnel transactions the team has made going back to the spring where the only newcomer of significant or financial commitment the team added was Malik Willis — and that in and of itself should be the only evidence anyone needs to understand he's not just a bridge quarterback.
Among the many new players brought in were a couple of former first-round picks looking to revive their NFL career and after the first experiment failed, the time has come to see about the second one.
Specifically, it's time for the Dolphins to find out what they have in defensive tackle Mazi Smith, and that's just what they made happen Saturday when they announced he was one of the two practice squad players elevated for the Week 4 game at Minnesota — just like we had suggested minutes before the move became official (and, no, we didn't get advance notice).
Also elevated was edge defender Rodney McGraw, who'll be in line to make his NFL debut, while running back Carlos Washington Jr. officially was signed to the active roster off the practice squad.
Smith failed as a first-round pick of the Dallas Cowboys in 2023 out of Michigan before he was included in the trade with the New York Jets that sent defensive tackle star Quinnen Williams to Dallas.
After they saw him for three games last year, the Jets cut Smith this offseason and the Dolphins signed him to their practice squad in the hopes that he perhaps could rediscover the form that had made him a disruptive force for the Michigan defensive line, where in 2022 one of his teammates up front was Kenneth Grant.
Smith started 17 games for Dallas in 2024, but never became that presence in the middle of the defensive line for the Cowboys.
The Dolphins' current interior defensive line group is down to three players after Kenneth Cooper Jr. was waived this week, though Grant could be back pretty soon from injured reserve with the Week 4 game at Minnesota being the last one he has to sit out regardless of health.
For that game against the Vikings, it was difficult to envision or rationalize the Dolphins going with only three IDLs — Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers — because just one injury would have put an unfair burden of the other two.
That meant the Dolphins likely needed to elevate a defensive tackle from the practice squad.
The Dolphins certainly could elevated Cooper since he did play in the first three games and was re-signed to the practice squad after clearing waivers, but the mere fact they were willing to expose him to waivers in the first place suggests his long-term future with the team isn't overly solid.
And since the 2026 season is about evaluation, why not get a look at Smith?
Head coach Jeff Hafley said Friday that Smith had made steady progress since joining the practice in the first days of September.
"He keeps getting better, and hopefully we'll be close to seeing him on a Sunday," Hafley said. "But he's making improvement, learning the defense and doing everything that (DL coach Austin) Clark asks him to do. I think he's getting himself in better shape, which is important. I've seen improvement, and I'm excited about the progress that he's made and eventually we're going to see him on a Sunday."
This Sunday will be that day.

title: Vikings' Odell Beckham Jr. Signing Raises More Questions Than Answers
full_text:
Just over a week after the J.J. McCarthy trade, the Vikings had another surprise move in store as Week 5 began. On Wednesday morning, the Vikings added a big name by signing veteran wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. to the practice squad , according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
BREAKING: Odell Beckham Jr. is signing with the #Vikings , per sources. pic.twitter.com/30XQwSTBvi
The addition comes after an ankle injury to Justin Jefferson and some lackluster play from the rest of the receiver room.
Beckham spent this summer and the first few games of the season with the Giants before getting released in what ended up being a messy separation. He left his second stint with New York without recording a reception and had just nine catches in 2024 with Miami.
After starting his career with three-straight 1000-yard seasons, the 33-year-old Beckham hasn't notched one since 2019, and injuries have largely derailed his promising career. So what's the deal here?
The Vikings' receiving corps has looked shaky behind Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, but does a receiver who hasn't been productive for a few years now really add anything?
Beckham certainly has an impressive resume and even connections with head coach Kevin O'Connell, so let's break down what his signing means and what type of role he could carve out.
First things first. Jefferson's injury has always been considered day-to-day, and there's little reason to think that it's changed in that sense. The ex-Giant's arrival, however, does let the Vikings give Jefferson more time to heal if they want to rest him against the Saints, since the bye week follows immediately.
Still, Beckham's addition likely has more to do with the less-than-impressive performances from the rest of the Vikings' receivers.
The Vikings signed Jauan Jennings earlier this year to be their WR3 in hopes of rounding out what could have been one of the best trios in the league. With just two catches this season, though, it's clear his addition hasn't provided the type of production fans hoped for after Jennings put up over 1,500 yards over the last two seasons with San Francisco.
Behind Jennings, Tai Felton and Myles Price have failed to carve out much of a role either, and the pair have combined for just three catches. For perspective, DeeJay Dallas, a backup running back added at the buzzer, has more yards and catches than Jennings, Price, or Felton. Not great.
Adding Beckham, who does have some familiarity with O'Connell from their time with the Rams, gives the Vikings another option as the fourth or fifth guy. It's doubtful he'll ascend enough to replace Jennings, but O'Connell may look for a more reliable route runner ahead of Felton or Price despite the obvious physical limitations.
Beckham hasn't been able to produce at a high level for several years now, but Minnesota clearly thinks it can squeeze whatever juice he has left out of his game in a reserve role.
Ultimately, signing a veteran with a scheme fit for a veteran minimum feels like a harmless move. There's little reason to expect Beckham to come in and be a difference-maker, but if it means getting a bit more production out of the bottom of the receiver depth chart, it's hard to hate the signing.
This will either be a fun redemption, or Beckham may be looking for another new home by November.

title: Making Sense of the Vikings' Latest Flurry of Roster Moves Heading Into Week 5
full_text:
It's safe to say that the Vikings had a busy Tuesday, making multiple roster moves as the Purple and Gold prepare for a Week 5 showdown against the Saints in New Orleans.
In total, six players were on the move as the Vikings try to manage players coming both on and off injured reserve, among other things. One big loss and the return of a friendly face headlined some of the action, so let's break down a busy day of transactions for Nolan Teasley and company.
The #Vikings have announced the following roster moves - Placed G Donovan Jackson on IR - Signed T Tristan Leigh to the practice squad - Released CB Natrone Brooks, P Johnny Hekker and RB Devin Neal from the practice squad - Waived CB Tyreek Chappell from IR
This one stings, as Donovan Jackson was arguably playing like the Vikings' best offensive lineman through three weeks. Leading up to Sunday's game, Jackson had allowed just two pressures and zero sacks , according to Pro Football Focus . His season is now over with a torn meniscus, and all eyes now turn to backup guard Joe Huber, who took over against Miami when Jackson went down.
Huber has been an ascending player behind the scenes, and while he's not on the level of the first-rounder Jackson, he could be a good enough stopgap for the remainder of 2026. The Vikings could also play around with a few different combinations over the Week 6 bye, but there's no question this team just got worse with Jackson's untimely injury.
After getting signed as an undrafted free agent out of Clemson, Tristan Leigh was waived by the Vikings ahead of the season. He played both left and right tackle during the preseason, and Minnesota apparently saw enough to bring him back to the practice squad for his "Electric Boogaloo" sequel.
The Vikings' practice squad has seen non-stop turnover since the start of the season, and it's hard to say whether Leigh's return will last six months or six days. Still, there's never enough offensive line depth, and he has familiarity with the scheme.
The Vikings released three players from the practice squad:
Hekker's release surely means rookie punter Brett Thorson is on the mend and will be ready to go for New Orleans. That, or Hekker's abysmal display on Sunday, was enough for the Vikings to trust someone else with the all-important duty of holding for Will Reichard. Either way, Hekker's days in purple are over.
Brooks, meanwhile, just learned his coaches' names after spending only five days on the practice squad before getting released again.
In a similar vein, Neal was added to boost an underwhelming running back room, but was also cast aside after just a few days with the team. General manager Nolan Teasley is bouncing running backs around more than a beach ball at a Nickelback concert. After signing and then cutting Jerome Ford, Jaret Patterson and now Neal, it's hard to understand what his plans are with any of these additions. Luckily, Jordan Mason is just one week and then a bye away from his return.
The Vikings made a move with Tyreek—no, not that one—officially waiving Chappell after placing the young corner on injured reserve back in August. The undrafted free agent out of Texas A&M will look to find a new home in 2027.

title: Vikings Verdict: Judging Offensive Line, J.J. McCarthy & Other Overreactions Entering Week 5
full_text:
The Vikings remain just one of three undefeated teams after a win against the Dolphins , but plenty of questions remain. While certain groups are pulling their weight, others are falling short, and the Purple and Gold are still searching for the elusive complementary football.
Is the special teams unit historically great? Is the offense in trouble after a brutal injury?
It's time to judge some potential overreactions spilling in as the Vikings head into Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season.
The Vikings' special teams unit has won them multiple games this season and is one of the most well-rounded groups in the NFL. In fact, Pro Football Focus has Minnesota's special teams as the top-graded unit through four weeks (91.3).
Will Reichard is a perfect 12-for-12 on the year and has accounted for nearly half of the Vikings' total points this season. Meanwhile, returner Myles Price leads the league in return yards and boasts the only return touchdown so far this season. Those two are well on their way towards first-team All-Pro selections , but could the Vikings sweep all four?
Long snapper Andrew DePaola also has four straight All-Pro honors and could make it five, leaving the biggest question mark at punter. Rookie Brett Thorson needs to get healthy and then go on a pretty dominant streak to earn some recognition after starting the year with a pedestrian 45.8-yard average. He's likely the odd man out, but three out of four is still an unbelievable feat.
The Vikings lost both Christian Darrisaw and Donovan Jackson to injury against Miami, leaving the left side of the line in shambles heading into New Orleans this week. Darrisaw left with a concussion and could feasibly play as early as this week, but the coaching staff may opt to let him take the week and then the bye to get fully healthy. Jackson was unfortunately lost for the season with a torn meniscus after an impressive start to his sophomore campaign.
Jackson is a big loss, and the Vikings may have to get creative to replace him. Joe Huber filled in during Jackson's absence last week and could be in line to start the rest of the season. That's a fairly steep drop-off, though, after Jackson had allowed just two pressures through three games, and Huber already has two himself in just 43 pass-blocking snaps. There won't be much worthwhile available via trade yet, so Minnesota may need to find ways to shield Huber, although Darrisaw's cloudy future only complicates things.
Still, unless Darrisaw misses significant time, the line will be fine. Worse, but fine.
Trading J.J. McCarthy ahead of Week 4 was certainly... a choice.
There wasn't a Godfather offer on the table, and fellow quarterback Kyler Murray had already missed time due to injury this year. McCarthy's days as a starter in Minnesota were all but over weeks ago after getting demoted to QB3, but the timing of the trade felt odd.
After a brief uproar from fans, Minnesota has largely been able to move on, which now seems like the ultimate goal.
Until McCarthy starts taking snaps from the ever-polarizing Jameis Winston in New York, Vikings fans have (mostly) moved on, and there's no longer the 23-year-old former first-rounder breathing down Murray's neck. The offense was slightly improved against Miami , and another improvement against the Saints may be the last whack of the amnesia hammer fans need to finally put this debacle behind them.
Head coach Kevin O'Connell may never be fully forgiven for failing to develop McCarthy, but winning fixes a lot, and heading into the bye at 5-0 is hard to fault.

title: The Biggest Decision Kevin O’Connell Got Right vs. the Dolphins (And What It Means Moving Forward)
full_text:
The Vikings are 4-0, but online discourse about their offensive struggles suggests they’re one of the most confusing teams in the league. The team’s current situation is complicated, to say the least. Sunday marked the second time in four games this season that the team failed to score a single touchdown ( shoutout to Will Reichard ).
Starting quarterback Kyler Murray has only one touchdown on the year as well, after missing most of Week 1 and all of Week 2 with a concussion. Safe to say, finding the end zone could go a long way toward helping this offense build confidence.
So why did head coach Kevin O’Connell and his offense intentionally pass up an easy TD opportunity at the end of Sunday’s win over the Dolphins?
The answer is simple: the 2026 Vikings want to win even if it doesn’t look pretty along the way .
The Vikings led 15-10 as their offense finally found a flow late in the game on Sunday, with Kyler Murray going 13-for-14 for 120 passing yards and a 102.4 passer rating over the team’s final two drives (h/t: VikingzFanPage). Top that off with a touchdown, and you have quite the momentum train to ride into Week 5. The team had a chance to do just that with just over two minutes left in the game.
Minnesota had the ball on third-and-five near Miami’s 10-yard line when Murray faked a handoff to Aaron Jones before hitting tight end T.J. Hockenson for a wide-open completion about five yards past the line of scrimmage. In front of him? A clear path to the end zone.
Instead, the eight-year NFL veteran slid to the U.S. Bank Stadium turf , setting the team up to kneel out the clock and end the game (h/t: NFL).
Savvy play by TJ Hockenson to stop short of the end zone MIAvsMIN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/z81tAE4wNy
Reactions to this play were mixed, to say the least. I even took to X to see what fans thought of the decision as it happened and was honestly surprised by how divided people seemed. Some loved the safe decision. Others wanted the team to build offensive momentum with the score.
Then there was the loud group whose Sunday parlays were destroyed by the play.
Would the Vikings have won the game after a touchdown and extra point increased their lead to 12? Probably. Would it have been guaranteed? Not exactly.
Hockenson shared after the game that the decision for him to go down in bounds was made in the huddle and was part of O’Connell’s focus on being “situational masters" (h/t: VikingzFanPage), a term the head coach has used throughout his tenure.
#Vikings TE TJ Hockenson said he was told in the huddle to go down and not score a TD on the last play of the game: “There was a lot of grass in front of me. Seeing paint is always fun, but again, whatever it takes to win this game, that’s the whole mindset of this team.” pic.twitter.com/7dNp2mfKsO
The selfless play indicates O’Connell’s focus on winning football over flash or stats, a theme that has carried through their nine-game win streak going back to last season. The risk in scoring? Allowing Miami to score a touchdown, recover on an onside kick, and score again.
As wild as it sounds, it would not be the first time we’ve seen it happen.
The Jets notoriously beat the Browns 31-30 in 2022 after the Browns scored to take a 30-17 lead with less than two minutes to go . It may be rare to lose after going up by two scores that late, but it’s certainly not impossible.
O’Connell prides himself on his passing game, and while he's certainly shown frustration with the lack of success so far, decisions like this suggest he’s prioritizing the right things as the team works to find its offensive identity.
If he keeps making sound decisions while he and Murray build the right offensive system, we could see O’Connell lay the foundation for his first taste of Vikings playoff success.

title: Vikings Rookie Report Card: Grading 2026 Draft Picks After First Month of the Season
full_text:
Drafted by interim general manager Rob Brzezinski, the Vikings' 2026 rookie class is certainly a unique one . The production hasn't been huge early on, but there's still been plenty to like from a class that figures to only get better as the NFL season goes on.
That said, we're now in October, meaning this year's Vikings rookies have played about a quarter of their first season as pros, giving a large enough sample size to evaluate.
From first-round pick Caleb Banks all the way down to sixth-rounder Demond Claiborne, it's time to look at who has impressed and who has left some meat on the bone.
Let's get into some grades.
Giving a 'B' to a first-round pick who has notched just 75 snaps in four games might seem overly generous, but context is key.
Banks missed most of the summer with a known injury and, on top of that, was always looked at as a bit of a project. The tools and physical attributes are there, and he's flashed some of that potential at certain points during the season, especially against the Bears, where he racked up six tackles—including one for loss.
While the Vikings would certainly benefit from Banks being a bit more pro-ready, they're staying patient, and there's no reason to be alarmed until at least 2027.
Much like Banks, despite getting selected highly in this year's draft, Jake Golday has played sparingly.
Golday got his first defensive snaps against Miami in Week 4, but his lack of playing time (likely) isn't a reflection on his ability. An off-ball/EDGE tweener, Golday is stuck behind four established starters and was clearly a pick for the future. He'll get to redshirt for 2026 in a sense, and could find some more playing time in 2027 with Andrew Van Ginkel, Eric Wilson and Blake Cashman all on the wrong side of 30. He'll be judged much more critically next season.
Grab some honey because it's another 'B' for the Vikings' rookies. No, this record isn't broken, as Domonique Orange has played sparingly along the Minnesota defensive front.
Orange's numbers won't jump off the page with just four tackles and one pressure, but at 6-foot-4 and 325 lbs, he's been a third- or fourth-and-short specialist. The Vikings' defense boasts an NFL-best 22.6% conversion rate on third-down, and Orange has been a big part of that. He has a niche role and he's doing it well.
Demond Claiborne was a late-round pick, so he's earned a bit of grace here, but not much. After averaging just 2.6 yards per carry in the preseason, Claiborne has just 13 yards on six carries to start the season. Despite the loss of Jordan Mason, Claiborne has been unable to carve out a role in the Vikings backfield, and his 4.37-second 40-yard dash speed (h/t NFL) has been a complete non-factor early in his career.
Until Claiborne can improve his vision, ball security and pass protection, he will revert to riding the bench once Mason returns.
Of the remaining picks, only fullback Max Bredeson has seen much action, and even that's been limited to about 10 snaps per game. Caleb Tiernan could potentially get some reps in the near future with Christian Darrisaw ailing, but the Vikings will likely rely on veteran Ryan Van Demark if Darrisaw misses time.
Jakobe Thomas has been inactive for much of the season after working through some back issues in preseason, and preseason darling Charles "Chuck" Demmings is now on ice due to a hamstring injury.

title: How Vikings' Looming IR Returns Could Give Offense Some Much-Needed Relief
full_text:
Every NFL season brings adversity for every team, and the undefeated Minnesota Vikings aren't an exception . Despite the vibes being at an all-time high in the middle of a 4-0 start to the campaign, the Purple and Gold are dealing with key injuries on the offensive side of the ball that have contributed to their struggles to score.
Heading into Week 4, the Vikings already had wideout Justin Jefferson out with an injury, while tight end Josh Oliver and running back Jordan Mason continued their injured reserve stints. Unfortunately, Minnesota's injury list expanded after the 15-10 win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, with starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw now in concussion protocol and No. 1 left guard Donovan Jackson's season likely over due to a meniscus tear .
The Vikings' offense isn't firing on all cylinders at the moment, averaging 21.5 points (18th) and 262.8 total yards (31st) per game, along with an NFL-worst 4.4 yards per play. That said, being without Jackson and Darrisaw for any amount of time won't exactly help the Purple and Gold find the end zone more often.
Even though perfectly replacing any injured player won't be easy for head coach Kevin O'Connell, the Vikings' bench boss should at least feel a tiny bit of optimism knowing that potential reinforcements are on their way.
Now that we're four games into the 2026 NFL season, players who started the season on injured reserve are finally eligible to make their debuts. For the Vikings, that means potentially seeing center Michael Jurgens and tight end Ben Yurosek return to the field sooner rather than later, after head coach Kevin O'Connell confirmed Monday that they'll return to practice this week (h/t team writer Lindsey Young).
Getting Jurgens back would certainly be a boost for the Vikings' interior o-line after the Wake Forest product started the season on IR due to an undisclosed injury. The former 2024 seventh-rounder played 309 offensive snaps in 15 games (three starts) for Minnesota last season and finished with 62.0 run-block and 61.3 pass-block grades on Pro Football Focus .
Jurgens's eventual return could allow the Vikings to move pieces around during their Week 6 bye. Blake Brandel has been operating as Minnesota's top center so far after being converted from left guard, but getting him back to his natural position would help with Jackson sidelined.
A healthy Jurgens would make that possible and help to keep an already-delicate offense afloat.
And considering how the Vikings' TE depth beyond T.J. Hockenson is essentially just Gavin Bartholomew (who was invisible in Week 4), it'll be nice to get Yorusek back, too.
The 24-year-old pass-catcher, who's been on IR due to an undisclosed injury, made 12 appearances as an undrafted rookie with the Vikings last season. He didn't see much action (three targets), but he made the most of it by catching two passes for 14 receiving yards and a first down. If he's healthy enough, he could build on that in Week 5 against the New Orleans Saints, who are allowing the fifth-most catches (29) and receiving yards (306) to tight ends this season.
On top of that, Yorusek shone in pass protection, with a 79.6 blocking grade , per PFF . With Darrisaw sidelined, having another reliable pass-blocker to give quarterback Kyler Murray as much time as possible would be huge for O'Connell & Co.
Jurgens and Yurosek are the kind of reinforcements the Vikings need right now, especially if they hope to remain perfect throughout October and beyond.
That said, both injured players need to return to practice and prove that they're healthy enough first. They might get close to that stage in the coming days, but O'Connell might decide that holding them out of Sunday's tilt and letting them heal during the bye week is the best course of action.
There might be some rust to shake off, and it could take time to get back into mid-season form, but it's encouraging to know positive injury updates could be on the horizon for the Vikings after mostly bad news since the season started.

title: Nolan Teasley Must Have Clear Priorities as He Navigates Vikings' OL Injuries
full_text:
The vibes around the 4-0 Vikings are high, but news around the left side of the team’s offensive line may have brought the mood down quite a bit at TCO Performance Center on Monday.
Left guard Donovan Jackson will likely miss the remainder of the season after tearing his meniscus in Sunday’s matchup with the Dolphins. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw is also in concussion protocol after initially being cleared to return in Sunday’s game.
Not exactly ideal for a 4-0 team that has managed to remain undefeated despite serious offensive inconsistency.
Losing Jackson for the season is especially difficult, as the 2025 first-round pick was dominant early in the year, allowing only two total pressures through three full games. Now, general manager Nolan Teasley will face one of his first major roster-building decisions since being hired in June, and he’ll have a delicate line to walk.
We are about to learn a lot about Teasley’s long-term roster-building philosophy.
The argument can be made that the team’s undefeated start and need for offensive consistency should lead to an aggressive pursuit of help on the left side of the line. Unfortunately for those looking for a big swing, several factors may complicate that approach.
First, NFL teams rarely put starting-caliber offensive linemen on the trade market, and when they do, the price is at a premium. Second, the Vikings simply cannot afford to burn through 2027 draft capital to solve a temporary need. They will enter the 2027 offseason with uncertainty at quarterback, running back, tight end, center, linebacker and cornerback at minimum. Teasley will need to retain premium draft capital to provide maximum flexibility come April.
If the team can find a guard they like for a Day 3 price tag, Teasley may need to pull the trigger. After all, they have a shiny new 2027 fifth-round pick burning a hole in their pockets. The simplest option, however, is likely the safest one.
While backup guard Joe Huber played as well as expected in relief for Jackson, he may not be the most secure option going forward, given the circumstances. Luckily, a new option may be able to step in at LG for the Vikings, and he currently starts at center.
Blake Brandel is in his first season at center after being a key utility piece on Minnesota’s offensive line. If there’s a position in the trenches, he’s probably filled in. But so far, Brandel has looked less at home at his new spot than he did elsewhere. Makes sense, given he hadn't played the position until last season. Turns out, there may just be a way to solve multiple needs.
Head coach Kevin O’Connell announced on Monday that backup center Michael Jurgens is set to return for his 21-day practice window after being placed on IR in August (h/t: Vikings). While Jurgens showed inconsistencies in 2025, he may just be the key to flexibility for the OL going forward.
If O’Connell and Teasley trust Jurgens to take the starting role, they could slide Brandel over to the left to take Jackson’s place for the remainder of the season. This would provide stability at the guard spot while keeping draft capital in-house. Ultimately, though, it comes down to the staff’s confidence in Jurgens ability to ramp up and develop.
Luckily, the Vikings enter their bye week after this week’s matchup against the Saints in New Orleans, providing Teasley with ample time to sort through his OL plans.

title: Vikings Stock Report: Who's Rising (and Falling) After Gritty Week 4 Win
full_text:
The Vikings are winning ugly, but there's certainly some beauty in the struggle. After a gritty 15-10 victory over Miami , Minnesota is one of just three undefeated teams remaining. Powered by an elite defense and a dominant special teams unit, the Vikings are simply finding ways to win .
The team is clearly being carried by a select few at the moment, so while certain players are doing more than enough, others are left needing to show some signs of life.
Whose stock is up and whose is trending down after the Vikings' Week 4 win?
It's hard to imagine Reichard's stock going any higher than it has been, but he's put up some incredible—or depressing—numbers as of late.
After going 5-for-5 in the win over Miami, Reichard now accounts for half of Minnesota's total points scored this season. He's also been the only source of points in two of the four games. His dominance at a position historically viewed as a liability in Minnesota is refreshing, but maybe at some point the offense will lighten his load a bit.
It was a rough day all around for the offensive line, which allowed the Dolphins' first, second, third and fourth sacks of the season. Losing Donovan Jackson and Christian Darrisaw didn't help , but Brian O'Neill got bullied by Chop Robinson several times throughout the day, allowing a whopping eight total pressures. He also allowed three pressures on the day , according to Pro Football Focus , after surrendering zero in the two previous games.
His performance was more likely an anomaly than a concerning trend, but O'Neill will have his hands full if his counterparts miss time.
After taking back an 86-yard punt for a score against Tampa Bay, Myles Price followed it up with another impressive performance. A 47-yard kick return and a 36-yard punt return highlighted another strong day for one of the most electric returners in the game. " All-Pro 4," anyone ?
Despite the absence of Justin Jefferson, Tai Felton failed to make any impact in the receiving game, notching just one catch for 14 yards. To add insult to injury, cornerback Zemaiah Vaughn was absolutely electric as a gunner (h/t NFL) in his first action of the season, and could potentially usurp that role from Felton.
Gunner teach tape by Zemaiah Vaughn 😳 MIAvsMIN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SKLJbp9TLA
It's getting late early for the former third-round pick to find a home, and Felton's roles seem to be diminishing every week.
Kyler Murray found a friend in T.J. Hockenson, whom he linked up with 13 times in the win over Miami. While it may have been a flash in the pan, it's still encouraging that Murray and Hockenson have seemingly developed some nice chemistry.
Ideally, Murray will look to push the ball down the field to receivers more in the future, but seeing Hockenson step up without Josh Oliver was promising for the offense moving forward.
Head coach Kevin O'Connell apparently finally realized that Murray works best out of shotgun, and the Vikings ran 54 snaps from it against the Dolphins, which was the most in a game (h/t The Athletic 's Alec Lewis) during O'Connell's tenure.
They also ran the ball 18 times from shotgun, and if that trend continues, it will push Max Bredeson off the field more and more. The fullback notched just 14 snaps this week, and he has yet to eclipse his Week 1 emergence of 24 snaps.
