title: New 2027 Mock Draft Sees Titans Double Down on Generational WR Talent
full_text:
Forgive us for looking into the future, but the current state of the 0-4 Tennessee Titans suggests that the 2027 NFL Draft will be another huge one for this franchise. Carnell Tate led what is turning out to be a productive draft class for Robert Saleh, but next year's pool could end up just as important, if not more so.
As is the nature of mock drafts, we're already seeing early returns based on the first month of this season. As one of only four remaining winless teams in the league, the Titans are topping charts with a predicted high pick next year. Justin Melo, with NFL Draft On SI, has Tennessee at the second spot.
With that selection, Melo forecasts a potentially surprising - and all too exciting - grab. In his latest mock, the Titans take Ohio State Buckeyes WR Jeremiah Smith. A bold pick? Potentially, but Smith is perhaps the most undeniable prospect in the 2027 class.
He's a superstar in the making, and his addition to Tennessee's WR room would make it perhaps the most promising group in the entire league.
"Cam Ward isn't playing well enough, but it'd be premature to move on from a sophomore No. 1 overall quarterback," Melo explained. "Instead, the Tennessee Titans take a generational talent in Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith."
For detractors waiting to point out that Tennessee just took an elite Buckeye receiver this past draft, that's exactly the appeal of this selection. As Melo points out, adding more talent to Ward's arsenal would give the second-year passer an even better chance to reach his ceiling.
If Ward doesn't pan out? You're still reuniting a pair of Ohio State pass-catchers that defined one of the best offenses in college football together. Both of those guys together have the potential to make any offense better, whether or not the team has a defined answer under center.
Carnell Tate just went off against the Baltimore Ravens for the best game of his rookie campaign. The first-year receiver hauled in nine catches for 145 yards, completing a late two-point conversion in the process. He leads Titans receivers comfortably with 22 receptions and 268 yards on the year.
Smith, on the other hand, already has nine scores and 823 yards for Ohio State through just five games. He's pacing for a third straight campaign with 1,000+ yards and double-digit touchdowns. Smith has the most receiving yards, receptions, and touchdown catches of any WR in Ohio State history.
The Titans simply could not pass on Smith if he's available, no matter why they end up on the draft ladder. The prospect of pairing him with Tate is one of such promise that it appears franchise-saving.
This season is far from over, and Saleh should be worried about winning games with the group he has right now. But if the Titans end up in a position like the one posed here, taking Smith could lay the foundation for an unstoppable pass-catching duo for years to come in Nashville.

title: Titans Snap Count Analysis: Carnell Tate Breaks Out, Backfield Depth Limited in Week 4
full_text:
For the second consecutive season, the Tennessee Titans are 0-4 after falling to Baltimore 24-18 on the road.
Tennessee's defense shut out the Ravens in the second half after QB Lamar Jackson was sidelined with an ankle injury, but the Titans were unable to capitalize on multiple promising drives. The Titans are unable to score more than 20 points in a game this season.
There isn't much for Titans fans to celebrate, but taking a look at the snap count trends reveal the coaching staff's direction against Baltimore.
Despite the Titans' continual offensive woes, rookie WR Carnell Tate had a beastly performance. The rookie played 54 snaps, which was the most of any Titans skill player aside from QB Cam Ward.
He tied a franchise record shared with A.J. Brown for the most receiving yards in one game for a rookie with 145 against the Ravens. Tate's 145 receiving yards and nine receptions rank as the most by a rookie in a single game this season.
The only blemishes from Tate were coughing up two fumbles; the one he lost came on a key drive before halftime. Ravens K Tyler Loop to hit a field goal shortly after the fumble to go up 24-10 after the first half.
Nonetheless, Tate is showing early makings of a superstar, a sight Titans fans would love to see.
On Sunday, WR Elic Ayomanor has been held to only one reception for one yard. In Week 3, Ayomanor played 48 snaps, but against Baltimore, he only played 40 snaps.
It marked the third time Ayomanor has been held to one reception this season. His role in the Titans offense is firmly behind the likes of Tate and Wan'Dale Robinson.
This season Ayomanor has only five receptions on 11 targets for 118 yards and one touchdown.
For the second consecutive week, RBs Nick Singleton and Tyjae Spears make my snap count losers list.
Starting back Tony Pollard continues to gobble up touches in the Titans backfield; he had 18 touches for 50 yards and a touchdown from scrimmage against the Ravens. Meanwhile, Spears and Singleton combined for six touches.
Pollard recorded 34 snaps against the Ravens, which is two more than the week prior. Spears played five fewer snaps from last week, and Singleton played eight snaps but only had three touches.
For reasons unknown, the Titans coaching staff strongly favors Pollard. Pollard failed to score on the goal line after four consecutive runs. An inexplicably bad play call . Still, Spears and Singleton may not see an uptick in touches for quite a while at this rate.

title: Tony Pollard Just Had a Solid Game — That’s Exactly Why Titans Should Trade Him
full_text:
Contrary to the hopes of a fanbase that has to be tired of all of this by now, the Tennessee Titans' rebuild is clearly far from complete. Robert Saleh is 0-4, and yesterday's loss to the Baltimore Ravens only continued to confirm some of our worst fears about this team. They're simply not "there" yet.
It's the young talent giving this franchise hope for the future. Carnell Tate just broke out for an outrageous 145 yards receiving. Anthony Hill Jr. continues to stun at the LB spot as one of the NFL's most efficient tacklers, full stop. Some veteran pieces appear awkward as a result.
Tony Pollard leads the latter list. The 29-year old back is in the final year of his contract. He's been with Tennessee for three seasons now. Against Baltimore, Pollard scored his first touchdown of the season on a hefty 16-carry workload.
That uptick in production is exactly why the Titans should make a move to trade him. Things might be different if Tennessee weren't still in the midst of their unending rebuild, but the state of this franchise demands a reset just about everywhere. The backfield is up next for an overhaul.
I'm not the only one ringing this bell, either.
ESPN's Adam Schefter mentioned Pollard as a sensible trade candidate just before the Titans kicked off against the Ravens, on Sunday NFL Countdown. "Tony Pollard fits the profile of somebody who could be dealt before the trade deadline," said Schefter.
For those keeping tabs, the trade deadline is Tuesday, November 10.
"A team that's not winning with a player in the last year of his contract. If there's a team that needs running back help, Pollard might be the first call," Schefter continued. To be fair, it's all speculation at this point. But Pollard being on the trade block is almost a given.
Moving on from Pollard may mean Tennessee sacrifices some surefire production, but with both Tyjae Spears and rookie Nick Singleton waiting in the wings, the team's split-backfield approach would remain in-tact. If anything, it would be an opportunity for Singleton to settle into a larger role.
Pollard is doing his job with Tennessee right now; this is not a plea to dump a guy who is falling short. But due to Pollard's age and waning role as a go-to starter, the Titans are facing an ideal window to move on from him at maximum value.
The veteran has done more than enough to leave this backfield in good shape when he goes. A Pollard trade feels like the natural next step in the Titans' rebuild. Fans should keep an eye on this potential move as we get closer to November.

title: Washington Keeps Talking About Fixing Its Penalties. The Numbers Say Otherwise — Commanders Daily
full_text:
While the Washington Commanders aren't the most penalized team in the NFL, they keep finding new ways to shoot themselves in the foot at the worst time. More importantly, the problem the team keeps talking about controlling is actually getting worse over the last two games. Since the start of the season, Washington has 30 accepted penalties for 224 yards, which is the 16th-most in the league (Cleveland has the most with 43). Game-by-Game Penalties - Philadelphia: 6 for 45 - Dallas: 5 for 38 - Seattle: 9 for 57 - Indianapolis: 10 for 84 Offensive coordinator David Blough openly addressed the issue the first moment he got a chance after the Seattle game. "Truthfully, man, it was not really up to our standard as an offense," Blough said. "Too many pre-snap penalties, too many third downs where we couldn't convert. And it starts with me and coaching it and teaching it better." Looking back at his words, I'm realizing his accountability can only go so far if he can't get this under control now, after pinpointing it as an issue, only to have it actually get worse. London gave Washington another example of exactly what Blough was talking about . Late in the third quarter, with the Commanders trailing 20-13, Athan Kaliakmanis hit Antonio Williams for what looked like an 87-yard touchdown. Instead, an illegal shift where Dyami Brown never came to a complete stop wiped it off the board, and Washington went from being an extra point away from tying the game to facing third-and-16 from its own eight-yard line. Kaliakmanis scrambled for eight yards on the next play, and Tress Way came out to punt.
Here’s the play where #Commanders WR Antonio Williams’ 87 yard TD was nullified by two penalties: Illegal shift & Offensive Holding on Dyami Brown pic.twitter.com/LRYOfqokcP
That wasn't the only time Washington hurt itself Sunday, either. Treylon Burks was called for a false start early in the second quarter, the Commanders took a delay of game late in the fourth, and the penalties stretched across all three phases. That's the part that makes this harder to dismiss as one bad afternoon or one position group having problems . When the offense, defense, and special teams all contribute, it becomes something much bigger than cleaning up one guy's mistake. Quinn addressed that this week when talking about how he wants Washington practicing moving forward. "That's what I want to make sure in practice: we're seeing all three phases connected. But let's make sure, man, let's go battle forward, but no fouls that are before the snap. After the snap, those ones, let's handle business between the whistles." That's the distinction Washington has to make now. A hold or pass interference can come from trying to finish a play, but a false start, illegal shift, or delay of game happens before the opponent has really done anything to you. At 1-3, the Commanders already have enough problems without creating extra issues before the ball is even snapped. The Giants game will give them another chance to show this is actually getting fixed, not just talked about. Washington doesn't have to suddenly become the least-penalized team in football, but the number can't keep climbing every week while the same mistakes continue showing up in critical moments. title: Austin Ekeler's First Game Back Reveals Surprising Truth About Commanders Backfield
full_text:
Running back Austin Ekeler was set to join the Carolina Panthers ' practice squad in Week 4 when the Washington Commanders called. What's wild is that after being signed back to the roster just a few days earlier, Ekeler not only made the trip across the pond ; he played 17 offensive snaps (27%) against the Indianapolis Colts. That may not sound like much, but Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led the backs with 29 snaps (45%), Ekeler was next with 17 (27%), and rookie Kaytron Allen played 12 (19%). There are two ways to look at this: either Washington already highly trusts a 31-year-old Ekeler coming off an Achilles tendon injury he suffered in Week 2 of the 2025 season, or Allen may not be as far along in the pecking order as we thought. Either way, Bill still got the lion's share of the snaps, even though Ekeler gained more yards on fewer carries and neither back lit things on fire (Ekeler had 4 carries for 29 yards, and one catch for 11; Bill had 9 carries for 15 yards, and two catches for 35 yards). While the initial signing is certainly more about adding another dimension than replacing the current back, the truth is generally in the numbers, which will undoubtedly shift again when White returns. The player this should worry is Allen, who saw Ekeler come in and get officially signed when the team was in the process of making a trip to London , and then get more snaps than him. Obviously, Ekeler wasn't brought in for depth, since the team knows what he can bring when healthy, but it's interesting to see how quickly the younger back rotation shifted. That makes what happened with rookie Robert Henry Jr. even more interesting. Henry flashed during the preseason but was cut and re-signed to Washington's practice squad after a bit of fumblitis, until Seattle signed him away Monday. The Seahawks then decided not to sign veteran Joe Mixon after his physical, potentially opening an opportunity for Henry. Washington, meanwhile, chose to bring back Ekeler and immediately gave him more snaps than Allen.
We've signed RB Robert Henry Jr. Read more » https://t.co/rRC44HuDF0 pic.twitter.com/ciiUr52L9y
The team still appears committed to Croskey-Merritt as its lead back, but Ekeler getting 27% of the snaps right off the street tells me that the coaching staff believes he can help now. I was already expecting him to lead from experience , help in passing-down work and protection, and give the offense a dependable veteran option rather than becoming a volume runner again. We'll have to wait until White gets back before we get a clearer picture of how Washington wants to divide this backfield. title: Three Takeaways from Athan Kaliakmanis' Commanders Debut
full_text:
Jayden Daniels is just two weeks removed from another elbow dislocation. Marcus Mariota sprained his MCL for the second time in the same knee this season. Athan Kaliakmanis is the Washington Commanders' suddenly elevated quarterback, and watchers of the team may as well start analyzing what the third-stringer brings to the team's floundering 1-3 situation .
Aside from earning the distinction of being the first rookie quarterback to check into a 2026 regular-season game, he left a strong impression on anyone curious to see how the backup to the backup would fare in his first taste of NFL action. He arguably outshone his Indianapolis Colts counterpart , Daniel Jones, tossing for 186 yards to the veteran's 143, with a boom-or-bust style sure to elicit strong opinions from the Washington fan base depending on how long they'll have to ride his young arm.
If nothing else, the 23-year-old is hungry for big plays, a feature that shouldn't be taken for granted amongst backups, often more worried about holding onto their tenuous depth chart position than anything else.
The Rutgers product doesn't have to worry much about superior competition, currently standing alone in the position group's room. That willingness to play freely helped him stand alone as the only quarterback in the league to attempt six or more passes of 30-plus yards in a game this season, as well as the first-ever Redskin/Commander/Washington Football Team participant to convert on multiple 40+ yard heaves in his Washington debut.
Athan Kaliakmanis goes DEEP for a beauty of a touchdown! @INDvsWAS on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JXB6CmxI9w
Kaliakmanis' pre-draft scouting report described exactly the sort of quarterback we saw: someone armed with a strong enough arm to go for the home run play whenever he spotted an open target downfield. He credited his confidence and decisiveness in a prior interview with On SI, though his accuracy on such bold ideas still has some work to do before he's contending for anything resembling a starting spot anywhere.
As bold as he can get in his explosive play hunting, Kaliakmanis was never known for his pinpoint passing. Though he peaked as a 62.2% completion artist as a collegiate senior, he also totaled 27 interceptions and 55 touchdowns in his career thanks to that same aggression before the pros came calling.
He wasn't completely innocent in his messy debut, recording his first NFL pick when he dared to try and make something happen on the run. Like most fresh backups, he'll need some time before he resembles the comfortable decision-maker he knows he can be, a commonality that'll require a healthier context than the one he was suddenly dropped into.
Shifting from Daniels to Mariota on a dime last month never sounded unreasonable to Washington's coaches. Though Mariota is safer and lacks that same big-play upside, both are mobile quarterbacks capable of extending plays with their legs.
Kaliakmanis does not fit that same mold. He's more of your classic hungry gunslinger who's happier to sit back and wait for his most grandiose routes to develop, though he's already proven happy to sprint into space and break out a surprise spin move that sort of-almost worked.
Athan Kaliakmanis with the little spin move @INDvsWAS on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SgaeFSMZWc
Unfortunately for everyone involved, Washington's offensive line isn't where anyone looking for sustainable cover should hide. They're down their two strongest pass-blockers, Laremy Tunsil and Sam Cosmi, leaving behind a ragtag band of overtasked starters and rotating reserves to keep the offense afloat. That's a tough position for any quarterback to have to navigate — let alone a rookie in his first-ever bit of NFL action.
He'll greatly benefit from Terry McLaurin's return to the starting lineup as the squad's go-to endzone target out deep, as well as a healthy and diverse receiver room to spread the field and give the less-dynamic athlete in Kaliakmanis options.
Even if Daniels is trending toward returning before the bye week, it wouldn't hurt for the coaching staff to remain prepared for alternatives such as their newest signal caller. He's already here and likely to stay as a recent draftee, so they may as well make his life as quarterback as easy as they can.

title: Washington Finally Found the Takeaways. Now Comes the Harder Part — Commanders Daily
full_text:
After Week 2, we emphasized that after an offseason spent focused on creating them , Washington was heading into the Seattle game with no takeaways. New defensive coordinator Daronte Jones made that a major priority of his offseason program. The unit broke through, getting three against the Seahawks and two in London against Indianapolis. With the takeaway faucet on, the conversation has shifted from whether they're getting them to whether they're turning those extra possessions into points. Jones talked about it before the season: "Well, we've been preaching it, but it's just a mindset. I think it's their intentionality with it. When you're seeing a ball carrier break through at practice and guys are trying to take shots on the ball rather than just going for a tackle, different things like that," Jones said. "Trying to attack the ball at high points, tracking the ball. I think you just want to create a conscious level with that." The Seattle game is the perfect template for how takeaways are supposed to work. The team got to work early with cornerback Amik Robertson peanut-punching the ball out of rookie running back Jadarian Price's hands and defensive tackle Tim Settle recovering it at the Seattle 21. Four plays later, the Commanders scored on a six-yard touchdown pass from Marcus Mariota to Rachaad White. Early in the third, rookie linebacker Sonny Styles intercepted a Sam Darnold pass that skipped off Settle's helmet; Washington scored three plays later on a 30-yard Mariota-to-Terry McLaurin touchdown. The day was, of course, capped off by LB Kain Medrano's 50-yard pick-six, giving Washington 20 points on three takeaways (they missed an extra point after Frankie Luvu was flagged for running onto the field to celebrate while not in uniform). Before the Seattle game, Jones was adamant that sticking to the process was the way to go. "It just takes that one, and the ball will start rolling... Meek had a couple of good shots out on the perimeter on the ball," Jones said, talking about Amik Robertson . "So you just got to keep going at it. Got to keep just chopping wood, and eventually the tree will fall." Robertson got the first takeaway; from that point through London, Washington produced five takeaways in less than eight quarters of football after having none through its first eight quarters. The issue is that in London, the team didn't capitalize. On the Colts' opening possession, Odafe Oweh forced and recovered Daniel Jones' fumble after pushing his man back into the quarterback; Washington took over at the Indy 21. Four plays later, the team settled for a Drew Stevens 31-yard field goal. In the second quarter, Rasul Douglas picked off a Jones pass and returned it to Washington's 37; the Commanders gained nine yards on the ensuing possession before getting stopped on fourth-and-1 at their own 46. Seattle: 3 takeaways → 20 points → win. Indianapolis: 2 takeaways → 3 points → loss.
🚨 Interception CB Rasul Douglas catches a meatball sub from Daniel Jones. #Commanders defense has forced 2 turnovers already this game. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/UvZxQhG4ZH
After the loss in London, Quinn acknowledged the issue : "I loved the way the defense started, creating some takeaways, but to only get field goals out of those, I thought those were ones that we needed to nail." He went on, "I thought between the penalties and not converting on some touchdowns on the takeaways, those were two big parts of the game," Quinn said. Quinn has a point. For the process to work, the offense has to follow through. If no one is maximizing the opportunity by scoring, then getting takeaways means a lot less. One side of this conversation points to a defense that should be encouraged by getting the five takeaways in the last two games, which is real progress. But the last two games have given Washington radically different examples of the value of those takeaways. Against Seattle, they turned extra possessions into points; in London , they turned them mainly into missed opportunities. Washington finally found the takeaways it spent the offseason setting up for. Now comes the part that decides whether they actually change games: doing something with the football once the defense gives it back. title: Commanders Make Jayden Daniels’ Return Plan Clear Ahead of Week 5
full_text:
Washington Commanders head coach Dan Quinn finally put a clear target on Jayden Daniels' return from a dislocated elbow. "The goal… is for him to have a full week of practice, full week, and start on Sunday," Quinn said. That's a much clearer answer than Washington was willing to give last week . Quinn had already identified a full week of practice as the next step , but Daniels remained limited and was eventually ruled out against Indianapolis. Now the Commanders want more than just participation; they want him to get through the entire week and be ready to start. The team has no interest in skipping a step in the process. This is what Quinn wanted from the start: for Daniels to progress naturally and return when he's ready, not because the situation forces him back. After Marcus Mariota injured his knee and left the game early on, the Commanders had to turn to rookie Athan Kaliakmanis to finish the game , which is not something the team wanted to do coming into the year. That makes Daniels' availability all the more important, with Washington already having to reach further down the quarterback depth chart than it ever wanted to this early in the season. While the team has tons of faith in Kaliakmanis , nothing about the way this quarterback room was built suggested Washington ever expected him to take meaningful snaps this early in the season. Now that the timetable has been set and the goal is known, Wednesday's practice becomes the first real checkpoint to watch. While participation obviously matters, stacking good days without any setback is what the staff is looking for as they prepare to make a decision on him this week. Overall, the mystery now shifts from what the plan is to whether Daniels can complete it. title: Commanders QB Marcus Mariota Suffers Second MCL Sprain, Expected to Miss Time
full_text:
The Washington Commanders' quarterback room took another hit Sunday in London , and this one could make Jayden Daniels' upcoming practice week even more important. According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , Marcus Mariota suffered an MCL sprain during Washington's loss to the Indianapolis Colts . It's the second MCL sprain Mariota has dealt with this season after suffering the first during the preseason.
Better view here on Marcus Mariota’s right leg. Ouch. Ankle pinned by defender and knee bent inwards. Might get X-Rays to rule out fibula injury. Probably mostly concerned on an MCL injury and/or high ankle. Good thing Jayden Daniels might play Week 5.. https://t.co/FOMDsXsTdL pic.twitter.com/FM9rhFvLol
Mariota left Sunday's game in the first quarter and did not return, forcing rookie Athan Kaliakmanis into action much earlier than anyone expected. The seventh-round pick had some promising moments, including his first NFL touchdown pass, but Washington obviously didn't enter the season expecting him to be one snap away from becoming its starting quarterback. That leaves Washington with a quarterback situation that could get thin quickly. The good news is Daniels was already moving toward the next step in his return before the Commanders left London. Quinn said last week that the plan was to get him through a full week of practice once the team returned, and Mariota’s injury only makes that checkpoint more important. That doesn’t mean Washington should suddenly rush Daniels back because Mariota is hurt. If he’s ready, he’s ready. If he isn’t, Kaliakmanis may be the guy they have to lean on until Mariota can return. Either way, the Commanders entered this week hoping to get a better answer on Daniels. After losing Mariota too, they may need that answer a little more than they expected. title: Washington’s 17-Point London Loss Looks Stranger the Deeper You Go — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders outgained the Indianapolis Colts 317-257, averaging 5.2 yards per play, gaining 88 more passing yards and finishing the game plus-one in turnover differential (two takeaways). Now, if you stopped right there and didn't read a single thing further, you'd think Washington won, not lost by 17 points , as those numbers are not something normally associated with losing a game. To understand the loss, you have to go back over the painful ordeal, starting with Odafe Oweh forcing and recovering Daniel Jones' fumble on the Colts' opening possession. Washington took over on the Colts' 21-yard line and gained just eight yards before sending Drew Stevens out for a 31-yard field goal. On the very next Commanders possession, they drove 70 yards to the Indianapolis 5-yard line before Mariota was sacked, and the drive ended on another Stevens FG. Literally, the first quarter closed with Indy having only 20 yards in total offense. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said , "I loved the way the defense started, creating some takeaways, but to only get field goals out of those, I thought those were ones that we needed to nail." Three categories tell the tale of the tape in this game: third downs, fourth downs, and red zone efficiency. Washington was 2-of-15 on third downs (13.3%), while the Colts were 5-of-16 (31.3%). On fourth downs, the Commanders were 1-of-4, and the Colts were 1-of-1; in the red zone, Washington was 0-for-2, and Indianapolis was 3-of-3. One of the day's oddest numbers: Washington had only 12 first downs despite gaining 317 yards; in short, they generated chunks of offense without sustaining enough drives to finish them. The penalty situation told an odd story in this game: Washington had 10 accepted penalties for 84 yards, while Indianapolis had only one for five yards. Amik Robertson's penalty was ticky-tacky at best, and allowed a drive that produced a Jonathan Taylor touchdown to continue. Quinn after the game: "I thought between the penalties and not converting on some touchdowns on the takeaways, those were two big parts of the game." If one play wrapped the whole afternoon into a nice little package, it came late in the third quarter. Trailing 20-13 and facing third-and-11 from their own 13-yard line, Athan Kaliakmanis connected with Antonio Williams for what appeared to be an 87-yard touchdown that would have put Washington an extra point away from tying the game. Instead, an illegal shift wiped the play off the board. An offensive holding penalty was declined; Washington backed up to third-and-16, Kaliakmanis scrambled for eight yards, and Tress Way came out to punt. Now, no one is saying here that, by rule, this wasn't an infraction; the timing of both flags coming out was odd if you follow the refs, and this doesn't get called every time it's done in the league (the holding was a complete phantom call, it never happened).
Here’s the play where #Commanders WR Antonio Williams’ 87 yard TD was nullified by two penalties: Illegal shift & Offensive Holding on Dyami Brown pic.twitter.com/LRYOfqokcP
That's how you end up looking at a box score Monday morning, wondering how any of this adds up . The Commanders created explosive plays, moved the ball better than Indianapolis in stretches, and did enough defensively to give the offense extra opportunities. What they couldn't do was stay out of their own way long enough for any of it to matter. The staff didn't help much, as the team seemed unprepared at times and also decimated by injuries at other times . Indianapolis didn't need to dominate Washington between the 20s. They simply won when the field got shorter, and the downs became more important. The Colts scored touchdowns on all three red-zone possessions, while the Commanders failed to score a touchdown on either of theirs, failed on three of four fourth-down attempts, and spent too much of the afternoon trying to overcome their own mistakes. Washington gained 317 yards Sunday, but yards were never really the problem. Turning them into points was, and that’s how a game the Commanders statistically had every reason to be competitive in ended with a 17-point difference on the scoreboard. title: Commanders Report Card: Who Deserves the Blame for London Collapse?
full_text:
For a few days, an optimistic future for the Washington Commanders was finally easy to envision.
All that stood in the way of their return to .500 was the Indianapolis Colts in a London-hosted Week 4 matchup. After a wave of season-opening injuries crested with Jayden Daniels' prior elbow dislocation , longtime backup quarterback Marcus Mariota and his reawakened defense had inspired hope that Washington's supporting cast could hold the line until his impending return.
No such luck followed the Commanders' trip overseas. Anyone who checks a game score online can guess as much, with a 30-13 defeat doing little to convince anyone that the remaining group fought to the bitter end in their fall to 1-3. The Colts, the injury bug, and yet another week of questionable coordination stymied the team's potential resurgence, leaving few position groups limping out of the breakdown unscathed.
The combination of what Mariota provided before exiting early in the first half and third-string understudy Athan Kaliakmanis' debut left very few meaningful takeaways for fans to analyze. Mariota fit in as smoothly as ever in the Commanders' offense before his knee injury, while Kaliakmanis looked like a seventh-round rookie who'd yet to be tested from behind his spotty offensive line.
That is to say, he still warranted that recent draft selection with some obvious throwing talent. He isn't the most accurate deep-ball slinger, but he's certainly less afraid to give his sprinting receivers a chance than your average deep-cut rookie. The few connections he made on 30+ yard tosses were the kind to make anyone stand up, with one particular beauty to Treylon Burks earning him his first professional touchdown credit.
Athan Kaliakmanis goes DEEP for a beauty of a touchdown! @INDvsWAS on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JXB6CmxI9w
If nothing else, he'll be a fascinating developmental watch as the season trudges on, though his lack of play-extending legs makes him a tougher fit in a pocket known to give up pressure. In the meantime, the Commanders may find it tough not to reconsider Daniels' return timetable following his predictably raw entrance.
Rachaad White getting ruled out earlier in the week certainly hurt the remaining backs' odds of flourishing, but the Commanders' rushing leaders on the afternoon should clarify just how much Bill Croskey-Merritt has disappointed as the lead option on the ground. He was outgained by Mariota, who played for less than one quarter; Kaliakmanis, who'll only use his legs if he has the chance to deploy the earliest open-field spin move imaginable; and, most strangely of all Austin Ekeler , the familiar Commanders player who was still on the couch this time last week.
As fun as Croskey-Merritt's dashes off of short catches were, 15 rushing yards on nine carries just doesn't scream efficiency, especially with Ekeler looking as smooth as he did. This wasn't the ideal setting to fully judge the Commanders' run game, with the coaching staff trying to figure out how to set Kaliakmanis up for success in real time, though it's clear that White will be welcomed back with open arms as a versatile Daniels battery mate.
This position group may as well get an "Incomplete" grade. They were even more hampered without Mariota in the game, and while the backs had to trek on without their RB2, Terry McLaurin had to watch this one from the sidelines, too.
That effectively removed much of the threat the receivers had of stunning the Colts, given their sudden dependency on a rookie decision-maker, though Stefon Diggs and company did their best to meet Kaliakmanis on his long-range prayers (even if Diggs himself ended up getting outmatched by a pair of reserves in Burks and Dyami Brown). There was some solid role-playing, though little game-changing playmaking when most of the platoon wideouts were called upon.
This was an especially disappointing outing for the tight end room, especially now that starting option Chig Okonkwo has returned to Washington's starting lineup. He only recorded five yards on two receptions, not nearly enough to make up for his positional peers.
John Bates wasn't up to his usual excellent blocking standards within a scheme that's especially needy for playmakers, and that's not to mention the still-silent Ben Sinnott. Kaliakmanis could really benefit from a big target to get open in the flat with a simple move or two, and he's clearly still without that jumbo pass-catcher as things currently stand.
The Commanders' blocking rotation is a disaster. Even if they were fully stocked with their best blockers, Laremy Tunsil and Sam Cosmi, they'd still be lugging several subpar starters on their roster.
For one, they couldn't do much to keep Mariota safe from Indianapolis' sack threats; in a sick reflection of the poor blocking that once plagued Daniels' pocket, more shoddy guard depth haunted the quarterback room yet again. Nick Allegretti was nowhere to be found- the previously starting center seemed to have been demoted once again after a brief foray at right guard, completely superseded by the likes of Matt Gulbin and Lucas Patrick.
For those asking Nick Allegretti wasn't on the injury report all week. He's healthy, just not playing.
Injuries are one thing, but the Commanders' front office absolutely has to locate some alternatives if their previously envisioned lead center can't make it a month before hitting the pine.
The defense gave it all they had, playing with enough tenacity to disrupt Daniel Jones' passing attack during the game's early going. Odafe Oweh recorded a sack and a fumble recovery early on; the Colts' attempts at screen catches were repeatedly halted, and Frankie Luvu's presence was felt.
Odafe Oweh pushes the tackle into Jones and causes a sack and fumble. Washington's ball. #RaiseHal pic.twitter.com/tLAPSwQMN1
They didn't let go of the rope so much as they ran out of the necessary stamina to hold their grip on the game, soon succumbing to their quick 6-0 lead once the Mariota-less offense stalled. Even when Kaliakmanis was able to occasionally troop down the field for a moment of relief, these guys never seemed to get a break before eventually collapsing as Indianapolis outscored Washington 30-7 the rest of the way.
The league leader in aerial touchdowns allowed heading into Week 4 didn't relent a single strike to Jones and any of his pass-catchers, a big step in the right direction as the Commanders look to figure it out without the currently injured Trey Amos and the relegated Mike Sainristil .
Amik Robertson and Rasul Douglas were everywhere, sprinting down from deeper coverage into the action without Nick Cross to help. Together they recorded 15 tackles, and Douglas got his first interception of the season on an errant Jones idea .
They're doing as good a job of persisting past occasional injury scares as anyone, and it's shown with a cohesiveness that's only improved as the young season has progressed. Even if such a defeat shouldn't leave anyone feeling great, the defensive backs can walk away from this one with their heads up.
Another week of ho-hum play from the special teams. Tress Way continues to punt about as well as anyone could ask, while Drew Stevens enjoyed a perfect 3/3 outing on field goals and extra points, though the return team still raises an occasional eyebrow at the play.
Jaylin Lane had to be carted off the field after an ankle injury during the game's second half. Another area in which the coaching staff will have to improvise.
Dan Quinn and his merry band of signal-callers deserve a little grace for the situation they fell into, with Kaliakmanis lacking the mobility they're used to with Daniels and Mariota, making for a tougher on-the-fly fit, though he could have been utilized better considering his lack of experience. Going for it on a fourth-and-one with fringe running back Craig Reynolds, surrendering the ball on downs and allowing the Colts to commence their scoring wave,…

title: Everything Dan Quinn Said After Commanders’ Loss to Colts in London
full_text: The Washington Commanders’ trip to London didn’t go the way they hoped, and the loss came with even more injury concerns. Dan Quinn spoke afterward about Marcus Mariota, Jayden Daniels , the costly penalties and where Washington goes from here. Opening statement “I’ll get rolling with some updates on some injuries. Talk about Marcus. I was just gutted for him. I thought he really started off strong. Long run, playing well, and I thought he had an excellent week of practice leading up. The team thinks it’s an MCL injury, and when we get the scan tomorrow, we’ll have further knowledge of what we’re dealing with and length and all those. Charles Omenihu hurt his groin again. Same thing. We’ll find out more tomorrow as we’re going. Jaylin Lane had a serious ankle injury. The hope is that he’s flying back tonight, but I’ll get a better update with you as well when we get back home into that. Then past that, I thought AK came in after 12 plays. It’s not the ideal space to begin it, but I thought he also showed a lot of confidence, some fearlessness with that, and made some of the throws to highlight why he is where he is. As far as a full team, I didn’t think we did enough around him into that spot. I loved the way the defense started, creating some takeaways, but to only get field goals out of those, I thought those were ones that we needed to nail. Our team is really tough, and I told them tonight, man, we are the ones that are built for this type of adversity. We’re back to a division game, and we’re going to do all we can to get ourselves ready. We’ve got a 70-man roster, and we’ll lean into that as we find out more about some of the guys on injuries and also some returning from injuries.” How much does it change things with Marcus going out, and how much did the Colts change things after that? “Yeah, it’s a significant change because you don’t do quite the same. I thought he was off to an excellent start. But it’s a factor for sure, when there’s less things that you have to deal with offensively. So, it was a factor.” And then Terry, what happened? How did he get hurt on Friday, and how does that impact everything? “Yeah, he was injured Friday, and we wanted to give him every chance to see if he’d have a shot, and it was best to hold him out. He desperately wanted to go. I should have a good update of where we’re at as we get into some work with him into Wednesday, but it was just the best play to hold him out, John. It was during Friday, and we just said, okay, let’s see what the next day looks like and then into the next day, and it just made the most sense to hold him.” What went into the decision to start Matt? “I think we want to just keep competing where we’re at at the O-line spot, finding the five with Sam being out. We liked some of the things that we saw with Lucas, and we’ve liked some of the things we’ve seen in practice with Matt. We thought, okay, let’s put him into the space as well. Nick got a little bit banged up at the end of last week, and he was going to be limited at the start. So we thought this was the best chance for this week of where we’d go. That’s all it was.” Not necessarily a longer-term move? “No, I don’t see it that way. And we’re hopeful Sam’s turning quickly, too. So if that’s the case, we see Matt center first, but inside when you’re not starting, you’re playing two spots. And we thought that gave us the best space heading into the game.” What did you make of the penalties, and how do you guys continue to clean those up? “Yeah, and you probably saw me upset with that. There’s as much of that just the entire day, 10 to one to go. Whether it’s points off the board or once the hit on — we certainly got plenty of work to do. I’d like to look at them and see. But I thought between the penalties and not converting on some touchdowns on the takeaways, those were two big parts of the game.” Despite all that, Antonio gets the 87-yard play. It looks like it’s going to be the tying score and then there’s the penalty. How disheartening was that? “It was hard. At the time, I didn’t see what or who for the illegal shift. But I think it’s indicative of the two of them. Antonio’s got it, and so to be outside and rip the ball to him, that was a big play. I like the way he’s developing, Ben, at receiver and making some plays. But definitely it was deflating for sure, and those are difficult to overcome because points were difficult to come by. So when you get a big, long one, that’s what we needed to get done, and so it definitely was tough.” Do you anticipate looking at a veteran quarterback, or is there optimism Jayden could possibly come back? “That’s the hope for sure for us, for Jayden coming back. He’ll have a full week of practice beginning Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. That’s the goal, Ben, that he could get into that space. And once we see where Marcus is, that part too, we’ll have a better understanding. But that’s the goal for Jayden, to throw a full-on week. He was able to do some limited this week, and this week would be the plan for him to do all the reps.” Can you take us through the fourth-down decision? “Sure. In that spot, different parts of the field, JP, it’s okay, we’d be a go from two or a go from one. So we had one that we thought had good design for that time where we shifted people in to go. In that instance, man, we’ve got to get the space to create it. It was less than one. When you go for it, there’s risk involved. We thought this one was the best plan to go after it at that distance. So with different ones, you punt or go, but that one we thought, hey man, this gave us the best spot to go for it.” And Reynolds was the back on that play. Was that by design or did that just happen? “It was by happenstance. We did an on-the-ball shift, so it was more by happenstance. We didn’t full sub. It was a specific package that we had worked on.” How does the risk on that play factor in when it’s not Jayden or Marcus at quarterback, but it’s AK, and the field position might be better? “Yeah, I get what you’re saying, Ben. For sure, I thought we were off to a good start defensively, but I also have a lot of confidence that inside a yard like that we’ll get the down. So that part, I don’t want to overthink it just based on the result.” Did the referees explain why they rescinded the pass interference? “They said that another official had a view that it wasn’t. I’m looking forward to watching it, but that was their reasoning: that a deep judge had a different view that said, ‘Hey, it wasn’t a foul.’ In that spot, it’s not something to challenge. You kind of have to just take it and move it on.” With Jayden potentially getting back out there, that would be a huge lift for the offense as a whole. But around him, how do you think the offense is supporting him as he comes back?" “I thought Jayden, at the start of the Dallas game, was exceptional because he’s on the move. So the second play with him is critical, where he can get outside the pocket, and he ripped a bunch of throws in that space. For us, having the run game is going to be a big deal. Hopefully Sam’s on his way back, too. So when you’re putting those two together, to me that’s the sweet spot, where you can balance both of them together. We don’t want to make it where he’s a drop-back player, and they do all your magic on every time. So the run, the run action, certainly owning the ball is a big piece of it. Jayden’s exceptional at that in terms of the location, where to go. That’s always been his case. So that’ll be a big piece to it, too.” If you have a call you don’t agree with, what is the process for documenting that and talking to officials about it? Do you do it right after the game? “No. We collect them, and then we send them in Tuesday by a certain time, and then we get responses back. So it’s the same process for everyone. It’s probably good you’re not on Monday, so it’s the next day. You’re limited to a certain number. More often than not, I want the…
